World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.title: Germany deploys soldiers to Poland to help reinforce eastern borders
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany has deployed soldiers to Poland to help reinforce defences on NATO’s eastern flank in response to the threat of Russia. While Poland already hosts various allied forces, the presence of German troops is particularly symbolic given the two countries’ difficult history. “United, we will prevail,” wrote the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces (SGWP), announcing the deployment. “This is what allied cooperation looks like in practice, which translates into greater military readiness and strengthens NATO’s defensive potential.” Polscy i niemieccy żołnierze razem wzmacniają granicę z Rosją. Takie rzeczy możliwe tylko za Tuska ☺️ pic.twitter.com/oNBME2gBsv — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 22, 2026 Last December, the Polish and German defence ministries revealed that a “mid-double-digit number” of German troops would be deployed from mid-2026 until the end of 2027 to support implementation of Poland’s East Shield operation, which seeks to bolster defences along the borders with Belarus and Russia. They said that the German personnel would mainly engage in engineering work, such as digging trenches, laying barbed wire and constructing anti-tank barriers. Today, Poland’s SGWP confirmed that “several dozen” German troops, including “highly specialised engineering forces” along with their equipment, had since June been temporarily deployed to “support the Polish armed forces in expanding defence infrastructure on NATO’s northeastern flank”. It emphasised that the East Shield project is “purely defensive in nature” and comes in “response to threats stemming from, among others, Russian aggression against Ukraine”. While the armed forces did not reveal the location of the deployment, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk indicated in a social media post that it was on the Russian border. Poland has a 210-km frontier with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. German public broadcaster Deutsche Welle reports that the activities of the German sappers are focused in particular on improving defences around the so-called Suwałki Gap, a strategically important stretch of land around the Polish-Lithuanian border between Belarus and Kaliningrad. “Together, we are ensuring Europe’s security,” said Lieutenant General Alexander Sollfrank, the Bundeswehr’s operational commander, announcing the deployment today. “Through our engagement in Poland, we are strengthening NATO’s defence capabilities and underscoring the alliance’s unwavering commitment to ensuring peace through unity and credible deterrence.” Poland and Germany have signed a bilateral security agreement that will see the two neighbours and NATO allies increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity https://t.co/6BPX2WxvxH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 SGWP, which shared footage of Polish and German forces installing anti-tank barriers, said the work aims to “hinder and delay an aggressor’s actions in the event of a threat”, thereby “increasing the time for a response from the Polish armed forces and the entire [NATO] alliance”. It also seeks to “create conditions for the efficient reception, deployment and use of NATO forces on Polish territory”. SGWP welcomed “the involvement of the German contingent as a practical expression of allied solidarity and the result of consistently developing military cooperation between Poland and Germany”. It also noted that the cooperation would help the two sides improve their ability to operate jointly, including “developing the competencies necessary for conducting a joint defence operation”. However, it emphasised that the current deployment is focused on training and engineering, with no combat component, and that the German troops are unarmed. SGWP also emphasised that the East Shield operation remains entirely a Polish national programme. The leaders of eight countries on the EU's eastern flank have met in the first summit of its kind to discuss closer security cooperation. Finland and Poland announced that they would jointly lead an initiative, Eastern Flank Watch, to bolster defences https://t.co/fxRHpkM6w9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 The deployment of German troops to Poland comes shortly after the two countries signed a defence cooperation agreement in which they pledged to increase cooperation in areas such as military mobility, logistics infrastructure, maritime security in the Baltic Sea, and cybersecurity. The agreement is a sign that the two countries now stand “shoulder to shoulder, as equals”, declared German defence minister Boris Pistorius. Poland is also currently seeking a new permanent US military base on its territory, after President Donald Trump recently pledged to boost American troop numbers. Last week, Tusk also announced that Poland will host military exercises involving France and the UK this autumn. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. Poland’s climate and environment ministry has inaugurated the first of 11 planned “community forests” around large cities, with the aim of giving residents a place for recreation and contact with nature while also helping to fulfil the government’s pledge to reduce logging. Plans for the forests were announced in 2024, and the first has now been established around Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city. Ten other major urban centres, including Warsaw, Kraków, Poznań and Łódź, are set to follow. Dotrzymujemy słowa. Powołaliśmy pierwsze lasy społeczne w Polsce, to lasy ochronne wokół Wrocławia. Kolejne miasta przed nami. @MKiS_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/RxhsMZShj9 — Paulina Hennig-Kloska (@hennigkloska) July 21, 2026 “This is a historic moment and the beginning of a new approach to forest protection – with residents in mind first and foremost,” said climate and environment minister Paulina Hennig-Kloska at an inauguration ceremony outside Wrocław on Sunday. “Community forests are places where residents can relax, play sports and simply spend time close to nature,” she added. “At the same time, they are crucial to our security and quality of life: they retain water, regulate the climate, purify the air and protect the soil.” An area covering 13,000 hectares (32,124 acres) has been designated as a community forest around Wrocław. Forest management there will now be aimed at “maximising the forest’s social functions”, says the ministry, while timber harvesting is also restricted. The area will be divided into three zones, including “natural forests”, where nature will be left to take its course, and “near-natural forests” with minimal intervention. However, the largest zone, amounting to over 8,000 hectares, will be “social forests”, which the state forestry agency says “will be managed in a way that ensures the comfort of those who use the forest and its benefits related to wellbeing, physical exercise and recreation”. Hennig-Kloska noted that, in the latter area, educational trails as well as hiking and cycling paths would be established. However, given that such facilities already exist in many forests, it remains unclear how the new community forests will differ. The ministry is now conducting consultations and analysis on establishing community forests around ten other designated urban centres: Bielsko-Biała, Tricity (Gdańsk-Gdynia-Sopot), Katowice, Kielce, Kraków, Łódź, Poznań, Szczecin, Toruń-Bydgoszcz and Warsaw. On Sunday, Hennig-Kloska said that the “next in line” to have their community forests established are Kielce and Bielsko-Biała, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Shortly after coming to power in December 2023, the current government announced that it would halt planned logging in some forests. The former Law and Justice (PiS) administration had faced criticism for overseeing an increase in logging, especially in Białowieża Forest. The current government also launched plans to create Poland’s first new national parks in over two decades. However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed that move, arguing that it would “block the economic development of the region” and threaten Poland’s security. Poland has joined a European Union project developing a secure satellite internet service that would provide an alternative to networks such as Elon Musk’s Starlink. Warsaw has committed €656 million (2.8 billion zloty) to the IRIS² programme, with the money coming from Poland’s EU post-pandemic recovery funds. In return for joining the project, Poland will gain access to the secure satellite communications network for government institutions, the armed forces and emergency services, while the growing Polish space industry will be eligible to compete for contracts linked to the development of the constellation Today Poland🇵🇱joins the EU🇪🇺space programme #IRIS² w/additional €656 mln. 🇵🇱 is on a remarkable space journey to build a strong space economy & secure connectivity for the defence of Poland, the Eastern Flank & 🇪🇺. IRIS² brings greater unity & strength for the entire Europe. pic.twitter.com/TwS59vpXtm — Andrius Kubilius (@KubiliusA) July 21, 2026 “This is a big day for Poland, the eastern flank and the entire European Union,” declared the EU’s defence and space commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, at a signing ceremony in Warsaw on Tuesday. “By investing in space, Poland is investing in its security, its economy and its future.” Speaking alongside him, Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said that IRIS² would help “ensure our security and strategic independence” while “demonstrating that Poland aims to be a leader in the European space industry and remain at the centre of EU security efforts”. “No single country is able to build such a [satellite] constellation so efficiently, which is why we are joining this major project – to be part of it and one of its managers,” he added. The IRIS² programme aims to deploy a constellation of nearly 300 satellites in low and medium Earth orbit, providing encrypted, interference-resistant communications for governments, defence agencies, emergency services and selected commercial users across the EU. First announced in 2022, the project is part of the EU’s efforts to reduce dependence on non-European satellite operators amid growing concerns over cybersecurity, hybrid threats and the resilience of critical infrastructure following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. “It is super important for Europe to have a sovereign capacity, and Starlink will never do that,” said Eva Berneke, CEO of Eutelsat, one of the companies involved in the project, quoted by Politico Europe. The project is expected to cost €10.6 billion, including €6.5 billion in public funding and around €4 billion from private investors. IRIS² is expected to become operational in 2030. 🇪🇺 The IRIS program is Europe's replacement for Starlink. The constellation will consist of over 300 satellites to serve Europe alone. Security and sovereignty! Like Galileo, it could surpass its US counterpart. Fewer satellites, smarter coverage. Eventually more could be added pic.twitter.com/Uswmuotw7F — Mariska den Eelden 🇪🇺🇳🇱 (@eeldenden) February 22, 2025 As part of its contribution to IRIS², Poland will finance six large satellites in medium Earth orbit (MEO) and six smaller satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO). It will also build a ground gateway station in Warsaw to connect the satellites with GovNet, the country’s secure government fibre-optic communications network. Earlier this year, the Polish government approved the use of money from its share of the EU’s post-pandemic reconstruction fund to cover its contribution to IRIS². Sięgamy gwiazd!! Polska przystępuje do europejskiego programu budowy bezpiecznej łączności satelitarnej 🛰️📡! W ten sposób zaspokoimy wszystkie potrzeby łączności służb i administracji państwowej. IRIS² zapewni nam bezpieczeństwo i niezależność. Dziękuję @KubiliusA za współpracę pic.twitter.com/c8u2QH0Wyn — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) July 21, 2026 Once the system is up and running, Poland’s police, border guards and other emergency services would be able to use the network during natural disasters, power outages and other emergencies when terrestrial communications infrastructure is unavailable. The system would also make it possible to provide temporary connectivity for civilians through emergency hotspots, says Poland’s interior ministry. Polish companies will now also be able to compete for contracts covering satellite manufacturing, telecommunications equipment, software and ground infrastructure, expanding the country’s role in Europe’s space industry. “It is estimated that each zloty invested in the project will generate a five-zloty return through new jobs, innovation and the development of domestic technologies,” the ministry said in a statement. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last week, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that it will open a new security centre in Warsaw. One of its areas of operation will be satellite communication, including the use of satellite imagery to monitor critical incidents such as natural disasters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk also revealed that Poland and the ESA are working on the first Polish spacecraft, which would provide servicing, refuelling and other services for satellites Last year, Poland launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest ever contract with the ESA, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. World.title: Archaeologists uncover synagogue in Warsaw Jewish cemetery destroyed by Germans in WWII
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Archaeological work at a Jewish cemetery in Warsaw has uncovered the foundations of and many objects from a former synagogue and funeral home that was destroyed by the Nazi-German occupiers in 1943. The finds were made at the cemetery on Okopowa Street, which, at around 33.5 hectares in size and with some 250,000 people buried there, is the second largest in Poland, after the Łódź Jewish cemetery, and one of the biggest anywhere in the world. Following the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of 1943, the Germans liquidated the ghetto, sending most of its remaining inhabitants to the gas chambers and destroying the buildings that remained there, including the synagogue and burial houses. In June this year, archaeological work began at the site of the former synagogue, commissioned by Warsaw’s Jewish community, which owns and manages the cemetery. The two-storey building, designed by architect Adolf Schimmelpfennig, a Pole of Dutch Lutheran descent, was constructed in 1877 and existed until 15 May 1943, when it was destroyed with explosives. The archaeological work aims to “uncover, document and preserve the remains of this historic complex, maintaining the memory of this place and passing it on to future generations”, says the office of the conservator of monuments for Masovia, the province in which Warsaw is located and which is supervising the work. Archaeologists have so far discovered numerous items that offer “silent testament to the daily life of the community that was connected to this site for decades”, says the conservator. They include ceramic floor and wall tiles, glass bottles and tiles from stoves used at the funeral home. “Every discovered brick, fragment of flooring or piece of furniture helps reconstruct the history of one of the most important buildings in historic Warsaw,” adds the conservator. Among the finds is an item that relates to a well-known and tragic story from the war, a door plaque from the office of the then-director of the cemetery, Abram Pozner. Pozner brought members of his extended family to the funeral home at the start of the war, where they were initially able to remain in relative safety, away from the horrors of the ghetto that the occupiers forced Jews to live in. As life became ever more brutal and dangerous for Jews, Pozner created an underground hideout within the cemetery. The Germans eventually found the bunker and killed most of those hiding there. However, two of them managed to survive imprisonment in German labour camps, one of whom, Avraham Carmi, remains alive today and lives in Israel. The current archaeological work is expected to be completed by the end of July, after which the foundations will be re-covered with earth. Warsaw’s Jewish community then hopes to restore the previous building, adapted to current conditions and needs, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “The goal is to determine whether the funeral home could be rebuilt on these remains, or whether it would make more sense to display them as a monument within a newly constructed building, and also whether erecting a building on this site is even realistic,” cemetery director Witold Wrzosiński told the newspaper. Archaeologist Szymon Lenarczyk, who has led the work at the site, says he has proposed that the structure of a future building should feature an underground room where discovered artefacts can be displayed. Before World War Two, Warsaw was home to around 350,000 Jews, a third of its population and more than any city in the world other than New York. However, the vast majority were killed in the Holocaust, meaning that only a small Jewish community remains today. World.title: Kraków launches €43m “pre-design” tender for planned metro system
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A planned metro system in Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has moved a step closer after the authorities launched a 188 million zloty (€43 million) tender for “pre-design” of the project. City authorities say the plans – which will include a feasibility study, environmental report, geological research, and assessment of the project’s impact on existing buildings – are a major milestone in the development of what would be only Poland’s second underground railway network. #Krakow #metro #projektowanie #przetargi 🚇Kraków ogłasza przetarg na opracowanie dokumentacji przedprojektowej dla budowy metra. W ramach uruchomionego postępowania powstaną m. in. dokumenty, analizy i decyzje, które pozwolą przygotować dokumentację niezbędną do finalnego… pic.twitter.com/0jcYL4HGRq — Kraków (@krakow_pl) July 13, 2026 The idea of building a metro in Kraków has been discussed for decades and, in 2014, 55% of residents who took part in a referendum voted in favour of the project. However, only in 2024 did the city’s then-mayor, Aleksander Miszalski, announce plans to build a system. In September last year, the city unveiled the metro’s planned route, with two lines travelling through the city’s historic centre from its southwestern and southeastern suburbs to its eastern outskirts. In May this year, Miszalski, who had made developing the metro part of his election campaign in 2023, was removed as mayor in a recall referendum. But the project has nevertheless continued, with the municipal authorities last week announcing a tender for pre-design of the metro. The work will include confirmation of the planned structure of the system as well as the location of stations, tunnels and other infrastructure. The city has allocated 188 million zloty for the pre-design in its budget for 2026 to 2031. Studies of feasibility and impact are particularly important given that the planned route of the metro envisages it skirting around Kraków’s Old Town, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site that contains many historical structures. The tender follows months of preparatory work, initial market consultations, analyses and discussions with experts, said Maria Wojtacha, director of Kraków’s public works department. “Although this process doesn’t yet mean that construction has begun, it is one of the most important steps that the city can take individually,” Wojtacha added. “Our goal is to prepare Kraków for the next stage – the ‘design and build’ phase.” The experiences of other recent major infrastructure projects in Poland, such as a major new airport and transport hub and Warsaw’s second metro line, show that environmental and tender procedures need not slow investments down, said Marek Grochowicz of the city’s strategy and European funds department. However, it is clear that the earlier timeline for Kraków’s metro outlined is slipping. Last September, the city said that it hoped construction would begin in 2030 and that the system would be finished by 2035. However, the current acting mayor, Stanisław Kracik, announced last month that construction is unlikely to start until between 2040 and 2045. Even the current tender for “pre-design” work envisages a timeline of up to 50 months for that work alone. Warsaw has announced 56m zloty for “pre-design” work on a fourth metro line. The mayor says improving public transport is an "absolute priority". World.title: Attempted illegal border crossings from Belarus to Poland down over 98% this year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland says that the number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants over the border from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%. It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally. “The effectiveness of [border guard] officers and the Polish armed forces discourages migrants from taking risks,” says Poland’s interior ministry. Bezpieczeństwo na granicy z Białorusią w pierwszej połowie 2026 r. w liczbach: 📉 Ponad 65-krotny spadek prób nielegalnego przekroczenia (ok. 235 vs ponad 15,5 tys. w pierwszym półroczu 2025 r.) 🛡️ 0 udanych prób nielegalnego przekroczenia granicy 💯 Skuteczność ochrony: 100%… pic.twitter.com/1lTXV56JdW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) July 18, 2026 Since 2021, large numbers of migrants and asylum seekers – mainly from Africa and Asia – have tried to irregularly cross the border from Belarus to Poland with the help and encouragement of the Belarusian authorities. In 2021 alone, just under 40,000 attempted illegal crossings were recorded. While Poland subsequently strengthened border infrastructure and sent thousands of additional officers to bolster security, attempted crossings remained high: there were just under 30,000 in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have now fallen dramatically in the first half of this year, when Poland’s border guard recorded only 235 crossings, compared to 15,500 in the equivalent period for 2025. Meanwhile, the interior minister says that the number of successful crossings by migrants – i.e. those who managed to get across the border and were not apprehended – has fallen to zero so far this year, down from around 1,700 in 2025, 5,000 in 2024 and 12,000 in 2023. However, when presenting such figures on successful crossings, the ministry does not indicate how it calculates them, given that successful crossings are often inherently undetected. Most of those who manage to cross do not remain in Poland, instead heading westwards, in particular to Germany. “The statistics clearly show that the 3 billion zloty (€692 million) investment in the security of the Polish-Belarusian border has delivered the intended results – we are effectively protecting our country from illegal migration organised by the Belarusian regime with the support of the Kremlin,” declared the ministry. Poland says that “specialists from the Middle East” have been brought to Belarus to dig tunnels under the border for migrants to cross into Poland. Four such tunnels have been discovered this year, including one last week that was used by 180 migrants https://t.co/4ConkQnj8z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 16, 2025 Among the measures taken to protect the border are a 5.5-metre-high steel fence as well as an electronic monitoring system that detects attempts to cross and dispatches officers to the scene. In 2024, following the death of a soldier who had been stabbed by a migrant attempting to cross the border, Poland also loosened the rules on the use of firearms by officers posted there. Since last year, it has banned asylum claims by people who cross from Belarus. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, also praised Poland’s “impressive” efforts “to stop illegal migration” and said that it was vital for the EU to offer financial and logistical support. World.title: Spicy, Not Spicy: How This Chef Is Bringing Authentic Chinese Street Food to Prague
World.content:
At Manifesto Market, the aroma of Sichuan peppercorns and chili oil stands out among the usual mix of street food and drinks.

It comes from Lá Bù Lá Street, the more casual sibling of the restaurant Lá Bù Lá, both founded by Wen, a Chongqing native who wants to introduce Prague diners to the real flavors of her hometown.

Wen arrived in Prague in 2019 after being accepted into a Master’s program at the Prague University of Economics and Business. But studying was only part of the reason she moved. At 22, she wanted a new beginning and the chance to discover a different version of herself.

“There was something about Prague that attracted me immediately,” she says. “The architecture, the pace of life, the atmosphere of the city —

it all felt very charming. I wanted to see what kind of person I could become here.”

That decision eventually led her into the restaurant business, with four concepts launched over the years — two that closed and two that continue today.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lá Bù Lá Street (@labula_street)

Beyond the Stereotypes

For Wen, opening a Chinese restaurant in Prague was never only about selling food. It was also about showing people that Chinese cuisine is far more diverse than many stereotypes suggest.

“China is a huge country, and every region has its own culture and food traditions,” she says. Through her restaurants, she hopes guests become more curious about where dishes come from, how ingredients are used, and how different regions eat.

She also wants Chinese food to be seen as something connected to special occasions, not only a quick meal.

“Chinese food can create beautiful memories too,” she says. One example is Chongqing chili, which is often associated only with heat. Wen says there is much more to it.

“Many people think Chongqing chili is only about being spicy. But it is also about aroma,” she explains. The same applies to Sichuan peppercorns, where the famous numbing sensation is only part of the experience.

Learning the Hard Way

Wen’s path has not been simple. Her first two projects, Chi Xiao Mian and Mi I’m, did not succeed as she had hoped, but she sees them as important lessons.

“They taught me how to work with people, how to manage a team, and how important communication is,” she says.

The experience also taught her to stay focused on her original vision. Running a restaurant requires listening to others, but also knowing when to trust your own ideas.

“Building something meaningful always requires finding a balance between dreams and reality,” she says.

A Restaurant, and Then a Street

Today, Wen runs two concepts: Lá Bù Lá and Lá Bù Lá Street. The name, meaning “spicy, not spicy,” reflects the idea that Chongqing cuisine is about much more than just heat.

The original restaurant offers a deeper introduction to traditional Chongqing dishes, while Lá Bù Lá Street at Manifesto Market has a more relaxed atmosphere.

“It is more spontaneous and more social,” Wen says. The concept is inspired by street food culture in Chongqing, where people gather, share dishes, and spend time together.

At Manifesto, surrounded by music, travelers, and international crowds, the idea has naturally evolved. Some dishes work better for sharing, while others simply encourage people to stay longer.

“For us, food tastes better when shared,” Wen says. “Passed around a table. Offered to a friend. Or quietly stolen from someone else’s plate.”

Growing Step by Step

Like many restaurant owners, Wen faces daily challenges, from managing a team to introducing unfamiliar flavors to new customers. Building a group of people who share her values has been one of the most difficult parts.

When asked about opening more locations in Prague, she says the ambition is there — but there is no rush.

“Of course, I would love for more people to discover the food of my hometown,” she says. “But I am not in a hurry.”

For now, Wen is focused on improving the restaurants she already has and building a stronger team.

“When my team and I are truly ready, we can always begin the next journey,” she says. “For now, we are happy to keep growing step by step.”

World.title: Prague and Stockholm Launch Cross-Border Public Art Project
World.content:
Visitors in Prague and Stockholm will soon be able to communicate across borders through a pair of interactive public art installations designed to exchange anonymous messages between the two cities.

The linked installations, created by the Czech initiative Praho! project and its Swedish partner Stockholm! project, will open in Stockholm on August 20 and in Prague on August 31.

The installations are designed as private spaces intended for one visitor at a time.

After entering, participants answer a series of questions before listening to an authentic audio recording left by someone in the other city. They are then invited to record their own message, creating an ongoing exchange between residents and visitors in Prague and Stockholm.

According to the project team, the concept explores what happens when anonymous thoughts become personal through the human voice.

“The installation creates a space where you first listen to someone else—and only then can you speak,” the organizers said. “We want to explore how connecting two different cities through shared experiences can foster understanding.”

The initiative is part of Art & Design Without Borders, an international collaboration supported by the Erasmus+ programme. The project brings together organizations from the Czech Republic and Sweden to promote participatory art, community engagement and new approaches to public space.

Although they work closely together, Praho! project and Stockholm! project operate as independent non-profit organizations. Their partnership reflects a shared history rather than a branch structure.

Praho! project was founded in 2021 and focuses on participatory art in public and digital spaces. Through text-based interventions and an online platform, it has collected more than 30,000 anonymous responses addressing personal experiences and broader social issues. Those contributions have since been transformed into publications, exhibitions and artistic installations.

The concept, however, began even earlier. Founder Annamarie Čermáková first developed the idea in 2019 while studying at Stockholm University of the Arts. Returning to Sweden inspired the creation of Stockholm! project in 2025.

The project extends beyond the installations themselves. Organizers will also host workshops, educational programmes, international internships and prepare a methodology guide documenting best practices in participatory public art across different European settings.

World.title: BAY55: 114 Luxury Apartments Planned for Prague’s Riverfront in Smíchov
World.content:
One of the last undeveloped riverfront plots in central Prague is set to become home to a new luxury residential project.

Developer Daramis has unveiled plans for BAY55, a development featuring 114 high-end apartments on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov, just steps from the railway bridge and within walking distance of the city center.

According to Daramis, BAY55 is designed to compete with premium residential developments in leading European and North American cities. The company says the project will emphasize architecture, technology, privacy and resident services alongside its prime location.

The residence will include a wellness and fitness center covering roughly 600 square meters, a private residents’ lounge and hospitality facilities.

A restaurant or café is also planned on the ground floor, serving both residents and visitors. The developer says the level of amenities is intended to match those found in luxury hotels.

Designers have also focused on balancing density with comfort. Every apartment is planned to include either a spacious balcony or terrace, complemented by integrated shading systems intended to provide greater privacy despite the urban setting.

Before construction of the residential complex can begin, significant work will be carried out along the riverfront.

The existing Smíchov embankment will be extended, creating additional public space and improving pedestrian access along the Vltava. The infrastructure upgrades are expected to become part of the wider transformation of one of Prague’s fastest-growing neighborhoods.

Daramis acquired the land from BPD Development in 2024. Although the developer has not disclosed the value of the investment, it says BAY55 represents the largest and most expensive project in the company’s history.

Costs are driven not only by the location and construction standards, but also by flood protection measures, advanced building technologies and architectural features planned for the shared spaces.

The project is currently progressing through the permitting process. If approvals proceed as expected, construction of the new embankment will begin first, followed by the residential development itself.

Completion is currently scheduled for around 2030.

World.title: From Müller to Krispy Kreme, Global Chains Are Coming to Czechia
World.content:
International drugstores, fashion retailers, discount chains and restaurant concepts are preparing to open their first locations in Czechia, adding new competition for established players.

Here are some of the biggest brands expected to enter the Czech market.

Müller

German retailer Müller is preparing to launch in the Czech Republic. The company has already established a Czech branch and website, although it has not yet announced the opening date of its first store.

Unlike traditional drugstores, Müller combines cosmetics and personal care products with toys, stationery, household goods, pet supplies and organic food.

The chain operates nearly 1,000 stores across nine European countries and will compete with established Czech market leaders such as dm, Rossmann and Teta.

Krispy Kreme

American doughnut chain Krispy Kreme is reportedly searching for a location in central Prague and could open its first Czech store soon.

Founded in North Carolina in 1937, the company became famous worldwide for its Original Glazed doughnuts and stores where customers can watch the production process.

Ochnik

Polish fashion brand Ochnik plans an ambitious expansion in the Czech Republic, with 15 to 20 stores expected by the end of 2026.

The company specializes in leather jackets, footwear, luggage and accessories. It previously considered acquiring Czech brand Kara but decided to build its own network instead.

OVS

Italian fashion retailer OVS is also preparing its Czech debut.

The company focuses on affordable clothing for the whole family and is particularly strong in children’s fashion. It is positioned between discount retailers and mainstream brands such as H&M, C&A and Reserved.

Normal

Danish discount chain Normal is preparing to enter the Czech market after establishing a local company.

The retailer sells cosmetics, household products, snacks and everyday goods at permanently low prices. Its stores are designed to encourage impulse shopping, with customers walking through a changing selection of products.

MR. D.I.Y.

Malaysian discount retailer MR. D.I.Y. has some of the biggest expansion plans among new arrivals.

The company plans to open around 20 stores in Prague and eventually grow to more than 100 locations across the Czech Republic. Its first Czech store is expected to open at Forum Nová Karolina in Ostrava.

MR. D.I.Y. sells household equipment, DIY products, electronics and stationery.

Burgermeister

Berlin burger chain Burgermeister will enter the Czech Republic as part of its European expansion.

The brand started in 2006 inside a converted toilet building near Berlin’s Schlesisches Tor station before growing into a chain with more than 30 restaurants.

It focuses on its own production, including burgers made with Irish beef and ingredients prepared in Berlin.

Dave’s Hot Chicken

American fast-food chain Dave’s Hot Chicken is preparing to compete with KFC and Popeyes in the Czech market.

The brand specializes in Nashville-style spicy fried chicken, offering chicken tenders and sandwiches with different levels of heat.

Founded in Los Angeles in 2017, the chain has expanded to more than 400 locations worldwide.

Arthur Gelato

Slovak premium ice cream brand Arthur Gelato has already opened its first Prague location on Francouzská Street.

The company focuses on handmade ice cream, fresh ingredients and unusual flavors. It plans further expansion through franchising.

Sticks’n’Sushi

Danish restaurant group Sticks’n’Sushi will open its first Prague location this autumn.

The concept combines Japanese sushi with grilled skewers and will operate a three-story restaurant on Jungmann Square with around 160 seats.

World.title: Five Things to Know Before Flying From Prague Airport This Summer
World.content:
Passengers departing from Prague Airport this summer are being advised to plan ahead as the airport prepares for its busiest travel season in years.

To help travelers avoid unnecessary delays, the airport has released a list of practical recommendations covering transport, security screening, travel documents and baggage rules.

Leave Extra Time to Reach the Airport

The biggest challenge this summer is expected to be road access to the terminals. Construction at the Aviatická–Lipská intersection may cause traffic congestion on routes leading to the airport.

Airport officials recommend using public transport whenever possible, as buses are not affected by the roadworks. Travelers arriving by car should allow extra time to reach the terminals, particularly during peak holiday periods.

Self-Service Check-In Can Save Time

Passengers can speed up the departure process by using the airport’s self-service facilities. Prague Airport now offers 31 check-in kiosks and 32 self-service baggage drop counters, available for flights operated by 18 participating airlines.

Before heading to the airport, travelers should also verify the entry requirements for their destination. Those flying to the United Kingdom, for example, now need an Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) before departure.

Bring Physical Travel Documents

Although many travelers rely on digital wallets and electronic documents, Prague Airport reminds passengers that electronic IDs and passports cannot be used during passport control.

Travelers should carry a valid physical passport or national identity card, depending on the requirements of their destination.

Security Rules Depend on the Terminal

Passengers departing from Terminal 2 will notice a faster security process thanks to newly installed CT scanners.

The new technology allows travelers to leave electronics and liquids inside their cabin baggage during screening. In addition to the standard one-liter transparent bag containing containers of up to 100 milliliters each, passengers may also carry one extra liquid container with a capacity of up to two liters.

These updated rules currently apply only in Terminal 2. Security procedures in Terminal 1 remain unchanged.

Pack Power Banks Correctly

The airport is also reminding travelers about one of the most common packing mistakes.

Power banks, laptops and tablets must always be transported in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage. In addition, lithium batteries must not exceed 100 Wh unless specifically approved by the airline. Ignoring these rules can lead to delays during security checks or, in some cases, passengers being refused boarding.

World.title: Czechia Debates Social Media Ban for Children as France Moves Ahead
World.content:
France is moving toward stricter rules on children’s use of social networks, while a similar debate is gaining attention in the Czech Republic.

Lawmakers, educators and experts are increasingly discussing whether children should face age restrictions on social media and tighter limits on smartphone use in schools.

The issue has grown across Europe amid concerns about excessive screen time, cyberbullying, online safety and children’s exposure to unsuitable content.

France has become one of the first European countries to push forward with legislation that would prevent children under the age of 15 from creating accounts on social media platforms. The French Senate has approved the proposal, which still requires approval from the lower house of parliament before it can become law.

If adopted, the measure would take effect on September 1 and require online platforms to introduce age verification systems. Companies would also have to remove accounts belonging to underage users within four months.

The French proposal also includes restrictions on mobile phone use in secondary schools, reflecting a wider European discussion about the role of smartphones in children’s lives.

Czech Republic considers stricter rules for smartphones in schools

The Czech Republic has so far focused mainly on regulating mobile phone use during school hours rather than banning social media accounts for children.

This week, the Czech government backed a proposal that would introduce a nationwide restriction on the use of mobile phones and other electronic communication devices in schools. The regulation is expected to come into force in September 2027.

Concerns over gaming, online content and cyberbullying

Supporters of stricter rules argue that unrestricted access to smartphones can expose children to risks ranging from harmful online content to addictive behaviour.

Experts have raised concerns about easy access to pornography, excessive gaming and the development of unhealthy digital habits among young users.

Many Czech schools have already introduced their own rules. Some require students to hand in their phones when they arrive, while others collect devices at the beginning of lessons.

Several European countries, including Spain and Denmark, are preparing similar measures aimed at protecting children online.

World.title: Charles Bridge Undergoes Careful Cleaning as Restorers Protect Historic Stonework
World.content:
The Prague Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) has started regular maintenance work on Charles Bridge, with restorers and specialists currently removing algae, moss and unwanted vegetation.

The work is aimed at protecting the bridge’s sandstone elements from long-term damage caused by moisture and biological growth.

According to TSK, the maintenance will continue over the coming weeks and will not affect pedestrian access or tourism on one of Prague’s most visited landmarks.

Specialists are carrying out the work using climbing equipment and a support boat, allowing them to reach areas that are difficult to access from the bridge itself. The method enables detailed cleaning while avoiding any need to close the bridge to visitors.

Experts say removing vegetation is an essential part of preserving Charles Bridge. Plants and microorganisms growing on the stone surface can retain moisture, which gradually weakens the masonry and accelerates natural deterioration.

Restorers use traditional cleaning techniques

The maintenance is being carried out manually using traditional restoration methods. Workers remove algae and other growth with controlled water pressure, silicone brushes and specialised tools.

After cleaning the stone surfaces, restorers inspect and repair the joints between individual blocks. Damaged sections are cleaned to a depth of around two to three centimetres before being refilled with traditional lime mortar designed to match historical construction techniques.

Charles Bridge is among the most valuable architectural landmarks in the Czech Republic. Construction began on July 9, 1357, under the reign of Emperor Charles IV, after the previous Judith Bridge was destroyed by floods.

World.title: Canadian International High School in Prague: Your Pathway to Top Universities Worldwide
World.content:
Earning an internationally recognized high school diploma and preparing for admission to top universities no longer requires moving abroad.

Canadian International High School in Prague (CIHS) offers students in Grades 10-12 a fully English-language education based on the Canadian curriculum.

Located in the heart of Prague, CIHS combines the strengths of Canada’s education system with the quality of life and accessibility of the Czech Republic. Students receive a globally recognized diploma while studying in a familiar European environment, avoiding the higher costs and challenges of relocating overseas.

An International Diploma Recognized Worldwide

Graduates earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD), Canada’s official high school credential, recognized in more than 20 countries. The diploma provides access to over 30,000 universities and colleges worldwide, including leading institutions across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Europe.

Unlike the Czech education system, which typically spans 13 years, the Canadian program is completed in 12. As a result, students graduate a year earlier, begin university sooner, and gain an additional advantage as they build their academic and professional future.

Learning the Canadian Way

CIHS delivers its academic program in partnership with Toronto Imperial School, ensuring that students follow authentic Canadian educational standards. Courses are taught using modern curricula, teaching methods, and learning resources aligned with those used in Ontario schools.

English is the language of instruction across all subjects. An international faculty, including teachers from Canada, creates an immersive English-speaking environment that helps students strengthen their academic language skills and confidently transition into universities abroad.

To maintain high academic standards, all teachers undergo a rigorous selection process followed by professional training led by Canadian educators and the school’s academic partners.

Outstanding Value

Tuition is, on average, two to three times lower than at many international schools in Prague while offering an extensive range of included benefits.

Tuition covers:

the Ontario Secondary School Diploma (OSSD)

an iPad for both academic and personal use

for both academic and personal use a complete school uniform

an annual gym membership

continuous academic guidance and support

and support educational trips to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany

to the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and Germany participation in the Exchange program in the United States.

International Experience Beyond the Classroom

Education at CIHS extends well beyond the classroom. Each semester, students have the opportunity to join educational trips to Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Switzerland, and other destinations. These experiences include university campus visits, meetings with admissions representatives, and valuable insight into international higher education systems.

Students may also participate in the Exchange USA program, spending one or two semesters at one of 40 partner high schools across the United States. The program offers full immersion in American school life while strengthening English proficiency and developing valuable intercultural experience.

For students planning to continue their education in the U.S., CIHS also offers the opportunity to transfer to an American high school during Grade 12 on an F-1 student visa, complete their final year there, and graduate with a U.S. high school diploma.

A Modern Campus in Central Prague

The school is located in Holešovice, one of Prague’s fastest-growing and most vibrant districts. Its central location makes the campus easily accessible from virtually any part of the city by public transportation, while convenient parking is available for families.

The campus occupies a modern business complex close to parks and the Vltava riverfront, providing an ideal balance between study and recreation. Students also benefit from an on-site cafeteria and access to medical professionals, including general practitioners, dermatologists, immunologists, and allergists. Sports facilities, swimming pools, cafés, and shops are all within walking distance.

Personalized University Preparation

Beginning after Grade 10, students choose one of two academic pathways: Business & Social Science or Engineering, allowing them to focus on subjects aligned with their future university studies.

Throughout the program, experienced teachers and academic advisors provide personalized guidance, helping students develop essential academic skills, explore career options, and build competitive university applications.

Graduate Outcomes

By the time they graduate, CIHS students have gained far more than a high school diploma. They leave with:

the internationally recognized Ontario Secondary School Diploma

strong academic English proficiency

experience studying in an international environment

university admissions guidance

a global network of peers

participation in international educational programs

access to leading universities across Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom, Europe, and beyond.

Canadian International High School in Prague welcomes prospective students and their families to visit the campus, meet the faculty, and learn more about its Canadian curriculum. It’s an opportunity to experience a truly international education and earn a globally recognized diploma – while staying in the heart of Europe.

World.title: PM Magyar press conference: pay caps, VAT cuts and wealth probes announced
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar presented a wide-ranging package of government reforms on Thursday, including salary caps at state-owned companies, possible VAT reductions, retrospective wealth investigations and a review of public-spending oversight. The Péter Magyar press conference also addressed Hungary’s budget deficit, fuel prices, the election of an interim president and investigations into projects inherited from the previous government.

According to MTI, the announcements were made at a government press briefing in Budapest on 23 July. Several measures have already been approved, while others remain under preparation or will require new legislation.

State company boards and executive salaries to be cut

The government will reduce the number of supervisory and management board members at state-owned companies to the minimum required by law. Remuneration for board members will also be lowered.

A gross monthly salary ceiling of HUF 3.6 million, approximately EUR 9,900, will apply to executives at state-owned companies. Ministers and state secretaries serving on company boards will no longer receive additional compensation, while deputy state secretaries will be entitled to no more than half of the standard board fee.

PM Magyar said the changes could save the state tens of billions of forints annually. He also claimed that earlier cuts to MPs’ expense budgets had already produced savings of around HUF 50 billion, or EUR 137 million.

Why it matters

State company positions have frequently been criticised in Hungary as highly paid appointments with limited transparency. The real impact of the reform will depend on how many positions are abolished and whether the government publishes company-level information on salaries, board memberships and savings.

PM Magyar press conference outlines integrity reforms

The government wants to authorise the National Tax and Customs Administration, known as NAV, to investigate the wealth of senior politicians and people living in their households going back 20 years.

The proposed system would cover approximately 1,000 people. Investigations would be selected through risk analysis, according to Magyar, while newly elected MPs and recently appointed ministers could become subject to checks after two years in office.

The government has also ordered a review of the State Audit Office. Its supervisory powers, responsibilities and leadership structure could be changed, although the legislative process is only beginning.

Magyar also said conflict-of-interest rules applying to former ministers would be tightened. His comments followed questions about former foreign minister Péter Szijjártó taking a position at Chinese electric vehicle manufacturer BYD.

Why it matters

The proposals could substantially expand scrutiny of political wealth and public spending. Their credibility, however, will depend on legal safeguards ensuring that investigations are independent, proportionate and not used selectively against political opponents.

VAT cuts planned for medicines, firewood and food

The government plans to reduce VAT on prescription medicines from 5 per cent to zero. Magyar estimated that the measure would cost the budget HUF 7 billion, approximately EUR 19.2 million, over a full year.

A reduction in VAT on firewood from 27 per cent to 5 per cent is also being prepared and could be approved before winter. The government additionally intends to double the HUF 5 billion, or EUR 13.7 million, social firewood fund and extend the programme to settlements with between 5,000 and 20,000 residents.

A broader proposal to reduce VAT on healthy food to 5 per cent remains at an earlier stage. Depending on which products are included, the measure could cost the budget between HUF 150 billion and HUF 300 billion, approximately EUR 412–823 million.

Magyar acknowledged that VAT reductions do not automatically result in equivalent consumer price cuts. He said an accessible price-monitoring system would be needed to prevent retailers from retaining the benefit. Details here: Hungary prescription drug VAT scrapped as government widens tax overhaul

Interim president and constitutional changes

Parliament must elect a new president within the 30-day period prescribed by law, Magyar said. An interim head of state is expected to be chosen in August and remain in office until a new constitution is adopted. As we wrote earlier, Hungary’s next president: two women temporarily take the country’s top constitutional posts.

The government plans to launch a broader constitution-making process in September, involving citizens, civil organisations and professional groups. The resulting text would be submitted to a referendum and could change the method used to elect future presidents.

Under Hungary’s current constitutional system, the president is elected by parliament rather than directly by voters.

Asbestos fund and EU security programmes approved

The government has created a HUF 3 billion, or EUR 8.2 million, fund to tackle roads built with asbestos-contaminated material. Municipalities will be eligible for support if they possess an asbestos map, continuously monitor pollution levels and submit reports every three months.

Officials said 667 inspections had been conducted and above-limit readings had previously been recorded in six locations, although Magyar said no location currently exceeded the health threshold.

The cabinet also approved programmes worth HUF 122.8 billion, approximately EUR 337 million, using EU home-affairs funds. The money will support security-related information technology, measures against terrorism and irregular stays in the Schengen Area, as well as education and employment programmes for refugees, particularly those arriving from Ukraine.

SUBSCRIBE to our daily newsletter to never miss a bombshell!

Gondosóra programme and state events face review

Magyar said the government had removed the Gondosóra elderly-support programme from an EU-funded package because it did not meet the relevant milestones and commitments. He alleged that the technology was outdated and the project overpriced.

Authorities are already examining the programme, while the government is preparing its own report and may file a separate criminal complaint. The programme’s objective – providing emergency assistance to elderly people – would not be abandoned, he said.

The prime minister also announced plans to rebuild the state’s internal capacity to organise major public events instead of relying heavily on private contractors. He said no advance payment had been made on an HUF 8 billion, or EUR 22 million, contract connected to the 20 August fireworks display.

Deficit reduction and possible fuel-price intervention

Magyar said the 2026 budget deficit could be reduced to 7.5 per cent of gross domestic product, partly because EU funds had become available. A decline below 6 per cent was expected in 2027, while reaching the EU’s 3 per cent threshold by 2030 remained possible if economic and fiscal conditions developed favourably.

On fuel prices, the prime minister said retail prices had so far remained close to the government’s protected reference level despite rising wholesale costs. He warned that further increases were possible but said the government was prepared to intervene if households, farmers and businesses faced a major price shock.

Fixing prices at substantially lower levels could cost the budget around HUF 50 billion, or EUR 137 million, per month, he added.

The measures outlined at the Péter Magyar press conference combine immediate spending cuts with longer-term reforms of political accountability, social policy and state capacity, although many of the proposals still require legislation and detailed implementation rules. Magyar also briefly confirmed that criminal complaints had been filed over four Eximbank transactions worth approximately HUF 1,000 billion, or EUR 2.74 billion, which are covered in a separate Daily News Hungary report.

World.title: Hungarian government seeks Eximbank investigations over EUR 2.74 billion in deals
World.content:
The Hungarian government has filed criminal complaints over four transactions linked to the state-owned Eximbank, requesting investigations into financing worth more than HUF 1,000 billion – approximately EUR 2.74 billion. The Eximbank investigations will examine whether the high-value transactions were approved with adequate safeguards and in accordance with the relevant rules.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced the complaints on Thursday, saying that the Ministry of Economy and Energy had identified the cases while reviewing the activities of institutions previously overseen by other ministries. The complaints were filed against unknown perpetrators, meaning that the authorities will determine whether any criminal offence occurred and who may be responsible.

Eximbank is wholly owned by the Hungarian state and was originally established to support Hungarian exporters and companies seeking to expand abroad. Its financing activities have since grown considerably: the bank reported total assets of HUF 3,967 billion, or roughly EUR 10.9 billion, at the end of 2024.

Eximbank investigations cover four major transactions

According to the government, the four cases share several characteristics, including substantial financial exposure, high-risk classifications and what the ministry considers insufficient collateral or guarantees.

HUF 59 billion loan for Budapest luxury hotel

The first complaint concerns HUF 59 billion, approximately EUR 162 million, approved in June 2025 for the redevelopment of the former Sofitel Budapest Chain Bridge hotel and the neighbouring former MALÉV office building.

The government said Eximbank’s board had only two days to consider a 145-page proposal before approving the financing. The project had reportedly received a high-risk rating under the bank’s own system, while exemptions were granted from several internal requirements.

The ministry also said questions had arisen over the project’s expected revenues and whether they would be sufficient to support the financing. Hungarian media have linked the hotel investment to business interests associated with István Tiborcz, the son-in-law of former prime minister Viktor Orbán.

State-backed financing for an African road project

The second case involves HUF 126 billion, around EUR 346 million, in bond financing provided by Eximbank and the also state-owned Hungarian Development Bank in November 2025.

The money was intended to support a Duna Aszfalt infrastructure project connecting Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The development includes a 184-kilometre motorway, a 362-metre border bridge and a border-crossing facility. Duna Group has described it as its largest international investment.

Both countries were placed in Eximbank’s highest risk category, according to the ministry. Nevertheless, the Hungarian state reportedly guaranteed 80 per cent of the financing, equivalent to approximately HUF 101 billion or EUR 277 million.

The government said the Eximbank investigations should establish whether the financing and state guarantee were justified given the country, legal and project-related risks.

Egyptian railway carriage contract faces delays

The largest individual transaction concerns a HUF 576 billion – approximately EUR 1.58 billion – loan to Egyptian National Railways. The financing supported the purchase of railway carriages manufactured under a Hungarian-Russian cooperation involving Ganz-MaVag and Dunakeszi Járműjavító.

The Russian partner withdrew following sanctions introduced after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the project continued under a restructured arrangement from 2022. More than 200 carriages had still not been delivered shortly before the original contractual deadline, the government said.

The ministry added that the Hungarian state bears the risk of non-performance. Liquidation proceedings were launched against the Hungarian rolling-stock companies in 2025.

The government also highlighted dividend payments totalling approximately HUF 10 billion, or EUR 27 million, including HUF 2 billion paid from retained earnings after a year in which the company recorded a HUF 15 billion loss.

If you missed it – Hungary’s richest reshaped by the Orbán era: Mészáros wealth surges by 284,400% in 15 years!

Nearly EUR 1 billion lent to North Macedonia

The fourth complaint concerns two unrestricted loans provided to North Macedonia, worth a combined HUF 360 billion, or approximately EUR 988 million.

The loans have a fixed annual interest rate of 3.25 per cent and a 15-year term, including a three-year grace period. The Hungarian government estimates that interest compensation connected to the arrangement will cost the state budget more than HUF 90 billion, or EUR 247 million.

The full amount is also covered by a Hungarian state guarantee, despite North Macedonia’s reportedly significant risk rating at Eximbank.

Authorities to decide whether further action is justified

The filing of the complaints does not establish criminal responsibility. Police and prosecutors must now assess the documents and determine whether formal investigations should be opened.

However, with the four transactions representing financing of more than EUR 2.7 billion, the outcome of the Eximbank investigations could have significant consequences for the management, oversight and future risk policies of Hungary’s state-owned financial institutions.

World.title: Hungary crypto regulation enters new phase as first central bank licence is granted
World.content:
Hungary crypto regulation has reached a turning point after the National Bank of Hungary granted its first domestic licence under the European Union’s Markets in Crypto Assets framework. CoinCash, once one of the country’s largest cryptocurrency brokers, can now prepare to restart services after months of suspension and regulatory uncertainty.

According to Hungarian business daily Világgazdaság, the central bank issued the crypto asset service provider, or CASP, licence to Tiwala Solutions Kft, the company operating CoinCash, on 20 July 2026. The decision makes it the first Hungarian-headquartered company authorised directly by the MNB under the EU’s MiCA rules.

The distinction is important: CoinCash is not necessarily the first licensed crypto platform accessible to Hungarian customers, as providers authorised elsewhere in the European Economic Area may operate across borders under the EU passporting system. It is, however, the first domestically established operator to complete the Hungarian central bank’s full licensing process.

What the licence allows CoinCash to offer

The authorisation covers six categories of crypto services: custody and administration, exchanging crypto assets for conventional currencies, exchanging one crypto asset for another, investment advice, portfolio management and crypto asset transfers.

This is considerably broader than CoinCash’s former core business of online currency conversion and Bitcoin ATMs. The company plans to restore its services gradually over the coming months, while introducing additional products covered by the new licence. Existing customers are expected to be informed directly about the reopening schedule, Világgazdaság reported.

CoinCash began operating in 2017 and later expanded through the acquisition of Hungarian crypto platform MrCoin. At its peak, it served tens of thousands of active customers and operated Hungary’s largest Bitcoin ATM network, according to the company information cited by the newspaper.

The company nevertheless suspended its exchange platform, ATM network and customer service on 18 December 2025, saying changes in the Hungarian regulatory environment made the temporary shutdown necessary. Its website continues to inform customers that services remain suspended while the company works to meet the applicable legal requirements.

Hungary crypto regulation goes beyond MiCA

For international readers, MiCA is the EU’s common regulatory system for crypto assets and companies providing related services. It introduces licensing, governance, consumer protection and capital requirements intended to bring the sector closer to the regulatory standards applied to conventional financial institutions.

The regulation also allows an authorised provider to offer services across the EU, subject to notification procedures. ESMA maintains a central register of authorised crypto asset service providers and has urged customers to verify whether the platform they use holds a valid MiCA licence.

Hungary has added another layer to the European framework. Crypto conversions targeting Hungarian customers must also be examined through an authorised validation system, which is supervised by the Supervisory Authority for Regulatory Affairs, known by its Hungarian abbreviation SZTFH.

The additional system requires a compliance statement for covered conversions between cryptocurrencies, or between crypto assets and conventional money. Legal analysts have described the Hungarian arrangement as unusual because it operates alongside the MNB’s licensing and supervisory powers under MiCA.

The lack of authorised validators contributed to serious uncertainty in late 2025. CoinCash, Revolut, eToro and other providers suspended or restricted their Hungarian crypto services as companies attempted to determine how the new requirements could be met.

That bottleneck has since begun to ease. The SZTFH’s public register currently lists two active crypto-conversion validation providers, Caduceus Zrt and Mikroháló Kft.

If you missed it – Revolut pulls the plug: Why Hungary just lost one of its biggest cryptocurrency gateways

A possible restart for the Hungarian crypto market

CoinCash’s licence demonstrates that a Hungarian-owned company can satisfy the MNB’s MiCA requirements, but it does not eliminate every obstacle facing the domestic market. Providers still need to integrate the separate validation process, maintain extensive customer identification systems and comply with anti-money-laundering and transaction-monitoring obligations.

For customers, stronger supervision could provide clearer complaint procedures and greater transparency about who controls their assets. A licence, however, does not remove the financial risks associated with cryptocurrencies, guarantee the value of investments or protect customers from market losses.

The development may also encourage other domestic companies to apply for authorisation rather than serving Hungary through foreign entities or leaving the market altogether. Competition will depend partly on how quickly CoinCash can restart and whether international platforms decide that complying with Hungary’s additional rules is commercially worthwhile.

The first MNB licence therefore does not mark a return to the lightly regulated crypto market of previous years. Instead, it signals the emergence of a smaller, more closely supervised sector in which operating legally requires substantially more capital, compliance expertise and institutional oversight.

For Hungary crypto regulation, the CoinCash decision is both a milestone and an experiment. It offers the clearest evidence so far that the country’s tightly controlled system can function, but the real test will be whether it can protect customers without driving competition and innovation out of the Hungarian market.
