World.title: Orbán dismisses pre-election funding scandal as political attack, yet even his supporters back asset recovery office
World.content:
The Fidesz asset recovery scandal is revealing a potential weakness in Viktor Orbán’s defence of decisions made before his party lost power. The former Hungarian prime minister continues to insist that public funds distributed under the Fidesz government were allocated legally and that the investigation into HUF 17 billion – approximately EUR 46.6 million – in cultural grants is a political attack. However, new polling indicates that even a significant minority of Fidesz supporters approve of the new government’s plan to establish an asset recovery office.

According to a Publicus Institute survey published by Népszava, 78 per cent of respondents support the creation of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Approval is almost universal among supporters of the governing Tisza party, but the proposal is also backed by 29 per cent of Fidesz voters.

That figure does not show that nearly one-third of Fidesz supporters believe Orbán or other former officials committed crimes. It does, however, suggest that Orbán’s description of asset recovery and corruption investigations as little more than political revenge is not being accepted automatically across his own political camp.

As we wrote yesterday, Fidesz support falls below 20% for the first time in 30 years, PM Magyar said.

Orbán focuses his NKA defence on the investigation

Orbán’s latest intervention came after investigators seized servers and databases used by Fidesz in connection with the National Cultural Fund, or NKA, investigation.

“The NKA case is a fabricated proceeding,” Orbán wrote in a Facebook post, claiming that its purpose was to make Fidesz unable to operate. He alleged that prosecutors had removed the party’s complete membership register, correspondence system and confidential personal information on political instructions.

At a press conference outside Fidesz headquarters, Orbán said the seized servers contained much of the party’s digital infrastructure, including membership and donation records. János Bóka, the party’s parliamentary group leader, said Fidesz was considering filing a criminal complaint over the authorities’ actions, according to Népszava’s report on the press conference.

Questions about whether the seizure was necessary and proportionate are legitimate. Party membership records and private correspondence contain sensitive information, and the authorities will need to explain why such extensive access was required.

However, concerns about the investigative procedure do not answer the separate question at the heart of the case: whether the NKA grants were awarded lawfully.

What prosecutors allege in the Fidesz asset recovery scandal

The Bács-Kiskun County Chief Prosecutor’s Office said there was reasonable suspicion that an NKA decision-making body had exceeded its authority and breached legal rules and internal regulations when approving 1,079 grants worth more than HUF 17 billion from December 2024 onwards.

Six people involved in assessing the applications were detained and questioned on suspicion of aggravated breach of trust. These are allegations, and no court has established the criminal responsibility of the officials or the recipients.

The case became politically explosive after it emerged that some beneficiaries were performers and organisations associated with Fidesz, including figures who supported the party’s election campaign.

By 29 June, recipients had returned HUF 2.38 billion, or approximately EUR 6.6 million, according to information obtained by 24.hu. Returning a grant does not itself prove that it was obtained or awarded unlawfully: some recipients reportedly cited cancelled programmes or concerns about reputational damage. Nevertheless, the repayments have increased pressure for a detailed examination of the original decisions.

The dispute is broader than one cultural fund

The NKA investigation is unfolding against the backdrop of wider post-election scrutiny of contracts, concessions and subsidies awarded during the Orbán governments.

In a separate case, the new government reported suspected misuse involving more than HUF 100 billion – around EUR 278 million – spent on educational software contracts to the police. That investigation is unrelated to the NKA grants, and the existence of a police report does not establish wrongdoing.

Orbán’s political strategy is to connect these cases into a single narrative: the Tisza government and the authorities are attempting to weaken or dismantle the largest opposition party. This allows him to shift attention from individual funding decisions to the methods and motives of investigators.

Why the Publicus findings matter

The proposed National Asset Recovery and Protection Office would be tasked with identifying public asset losses, unlawful enrichment and suspected corruption, while helping initiate proceedings to recover state property. The government says its purpose is to protect lawful and transparent management of public funds, according to the official consultation documents.

Public support alone does not guarantee that such an authority will operate independently. Its credibility will depend on transparent procedures, judicial oversight and equal treatment of government and opposition figures.

The Publicus survey, conducted among approximately 1,000 respondents between 16 and 21 July, was representative by age, education, gender, settlement type and region. As a single opinion poll, it should not be treated as a definitive measure of public judgement in the NKA case.

Its political message is nevertheless difficult for Orbán to ignore. His criticism of the seizure of Fidesz data may resonate with supporters concerned about due process. Yet when 29 per cent of Fidesz voters still welcome an institution designed to investigate and recover potentially misused public wealth, portraying every inquiry as political persecution may no longer be enough.

World.title: You can buy Hungarian PM Péter Magyar’s house near Lake Balaton
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s house in the picturesque Balaton Uplands – or, more precisely, the Hungarian prime minister’s former family home – has been placed on the market. The fully furnished property in Balatonhenye is available for HUF 299 million, approximately EUR 822,000.

According to Hungarian news portal Index, the house was built in 2017 by Magyar and his then-wife, former justice minister Judit Varga. The property passed to Varga following their divorce, meaning the prime minister is not its current owner.

What buyers get with Péter Magyar’s house

The property listing on ingatlan.com describes a 233-square-metre, two-storey home standing on a landscaped plot of more than 2,000 square metres.

The asking price works out at roughly HUF 1.28 million, or EUR 3,516, per square metre. The house contains four bedrooms, several bathrooms and a large open-plan kitchen and living area. It is being sold with its furniture and household contents, allowing the new owner to move in immediately.

The property combines traditional Balaton Uplands architecture with modern technology. Its white exterior, shuttered windows, stonework and regional architectural details are intended to reflect the historic character of the surrounding area.

Inside, the rooms have been designed in a French country style, with exposed beams, natural materials and furniture from Maisons du Monde. Two tiled stoves made by a craftsman from Herend are located in the living room and guest bedroom.

Swimming pool, smart technology and a large garden

Péter Magyar’s house also comes with a remotely controlled smart-home system. Heating and cooling, the alarm, cameras, electric gate and solar panels can reportedly be operated from a smartphone.

The home uses a heat pump for its underfloor and wall heating and cooling systems. There is no gas connection, while a two-kilowatt solar installation contributes to its energy supply.

Outside, the garden includes fruit trees, flower beds, a children’s tree house, an automated irrigation system and parking for three cars. A 60-square-metre terrace leads to an eight-metre-long swimming pool.

A neighbouring 8,018-square-metre agricultural plot is also available under a separate agreement, although its price has not been published.

A quiet village near Lake Balaton

Source: Ingatlan.com

For international readers, Balatonhenye is a small village in the Káli Basin, one of the most sought-after rural areas north of Lake Balaton. The region is known for volcanic hills, vineyards, traditional stone houses and increasingly expensive holiday properties.

The listing says the lake is approximately 11 kilometres away and can be reached by car in about 15 minutes. Balatonhenye also lies on a section of Hungary’s National Blue Trail, a long-distance hiking route crossing the country.

If you missed it: Where to buy property in Budapest: A district-by-district guide to the city’s best addresses

The property’s political history

The house was built while Magyar and Varga were married. They divorced in 2023 after 15 years, and the property became Varga’s as part of their financial settlement. Magyar announced in May 2025 that he had moved out permanently.

Since then, Magyar has become Hungary’s prime minister, a position confirmed by the Hungarian government’s official website and parliamentary records. The sale therefore gives the property a particularly unusual public profile, even though it is now a private asset associated primarily with Varga.

The house previously attracted political attention over a HUF 10 million – approximately EUR 27,500 – family housing subsidy used during its construction. Index reported that Varga repaid the amount in 2023 after questions arose about whether the property qualified under the programme’s rules.

For buyers with nearly EUR 1 million to spend, the listing offers more than a luxury country residence near Lake Balaton: it is also an opportunity to acquire a home closely connected to the private and political history of Hungary’s serving prime minister. Find the property listing on ingatlan.com.

World.title: Former PM Orbán at the White House? Report points to discreet Washington visit
World.content:
The prospect of Viktor Orbán at the White House has returned to the Hungarian political agenda after an American newspaper reported that the former prime minister visited both the White House and the US State Department during a recent trip to the United States. However, it remains unclear whether Orbán personally met President Donald Trump.

According to the American news outlet Washington Examiner, Orbán made an unannounced stop in Washington while in the United States for matches at the football World Cup. The American report said a source familiar with the visit had confirmed that Orbán entered both institutions.

What is known about Viktor Orbán at the White House

No official account of the reported visit has been published by the White House or the State Department. The identities of the people Orbán met and the subjects discussed have also not been disclosed.

Orbán, who remains president of Hungary’s Fidesz party, said after returning home that he had held important meetings during his American trip, including unofficial discussions. He declined to identify the participants, adding further uncertainty to reports of Viktor Orbán at the White House.

The claims follow contradictory statements from senior Fidesz figures. Zsolt Németh had said Orbán was expected to meet Trump. Bertalan Havasi, Fidesz’s communications director, subsequently denied that such a meeting was planned, insisting that Orbán’s trip was a private visit centred on the World Cup.

As we wrote earlier: Viktor Orbán under fire after declaring Hungarian democracy dead — then flying to the World Cup

The available reports therefore confirm neither a face-to-face Trump–Orbán meeting nor any formal negotiations. They indicate only that Orbán reportedly visited key US government buildings during his stay.

Orbán’s changed political position

The trip was Orbán’s first known visit to Washington since losing Hungary’s parliamentary election on 12 April 2026. Péter Magyar’s centre-right Tisza party won 141 of the National Assembly’s 199 seats, ending Orbán’s uninterrupted 16-year period as prime minister. Orbán was later re-elected as Fidesz president and is now the leader of Hungary’s largest opposition party.

For international readers, this change makes the reported White House visit particularly significant. Orbán no longer represents the Hungarian government, meaning any meetings would have involved the leader of an opposition party rather than the country’s serving prime minister.

A long history between Trump and Orbán

Trump and Orbán have maintained close political relations for several years. Trump received Orbán for an official bilateral meeting at the White House in May 2019, when the two leaders discussed NATO, trade, energy and security cooperation. Trump praised Orbán’s record and his approach to border protection during the public portion of the meeting.

Their relationship continued after Trump left office. Orbán visited Trump at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida in March 2024 and publicly supported his campaign to return to the presidency. The two met again in July 2024, following Orbán’s self-described Ukraine “peace mission”, and discussed possible ways of ending the war. A further Mar-a-Lago meeting took place in December 2024.

After Trump returned to the White House, he hosted Orbán for a bilateral lunch on 7 November 2025. Official White House photographs showed the two leaders meeting in the Oval Office and the Cabinet Room alongside senior members of the US administration.

Vice President JD Vance also appeared with Orbán in Budapest on 7 April 2026, just five days before the Hungarian election. The White House presented the visit as part of a broader US–Hungarian partnership covering energy, technology and security.

Many analysts believe that one of Orbán’s biggest mistakes was to assume that Hungarians were interested in the US Vice-President and Orbán’s battle against the EU. Voters sent a strong message in the election, and Viktor Orbán, who had been in power for 16 years, suffered a major defeat.

As we wrote a few days ago, Hungary lobbies Washington to avoid possible 100% US tariffs over Russian energy imports

Why the reported visit matters

Should the Washington Examiner report be officially confirmed, the visit would suggest that Orbán retains access to senior political circles in Washington despite his election defeat. His personal relationship with Trump could remain an important element of his international political influence and his domestic strategy as leader of the Hungarian opposition.

Until the White House, the State Department or Fidesz provides further details, however, the central question remains unanswered: Orbán may have entered the White House, but there is still no verified evidence that he met Donald Trump during this particular trip.

World.title: Hungary prescription drug VAT scrapped as government widens tax overhaul
World.content:
Hungary will abolish VAT on prescription medicines from 1 September, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Thursday. The Hungary prescription drug VAT decision is the latest element of a large tax overhaul launched since the new government and parliament took office in May 2026.

Prescription medicines are currently subject to Hungary’s reduced 5% VAT rate, compared with the country’s 27% standard rate. The government’s decision would bring the tax on prescription-only products down to zero, regardless of whether a medicine is subsidised by the Hungarian health insurance system.

Hungary prescription drug VAT to be abolished from September

The government expects the measure to reduce the amount patients pay for medicines, although the exact saving will depend on pricing rules, health insurance subsidies and whether the full tax reduction is reflected in retail prices.

The change could be particularly important for people living with chronic conditions, elderly patients taking several medicines and those using newer, more expensive treatments.

According to Forbes Hungary, the measure could reduce annual budget revenue by around HUF 7 billion, equivalent to approximately EUR 19.2 million at the Hungarian central bank’s exchange rate on 22 July.

The announcement gives the measure a firm implementation date. Detailed legislation will still determine precisely how the zero rate is applied and how pharmacies and pharmaceutical companies must account for the change.

Five smaller taxes and charges targeted for abolition

The prescription medicine decision follows a separate tax package announced by Magyar’s government on 17 July.

Under the proposal, five relatively minor taxes and charges would be abolished: the special municipal tax, the dog ownership contribution, the immigration surtax, the carbon-quota tax and the transaction charge linked to the carbon-quota tax.

As 24.hu reported, the special municipal tax can currently be imposed by local councils, although only 25 of Hungary’s more than 3,000 municipalities reportedly use it. The dog ownership contribution is levied in 16 municipalities, while the government says the immigration surtax has never generated revenue.

The package was announced as a government decision and prepared for submission to parliament. Until the legislation completes the parliamentary process and is promulgated, the exact dates on which the taxes disappear should be treated as provisional.

Pollution charges to rise despite carbon-tax abolition

Removing the carbon-quota tax does not mean that Hungary’s largest polluters will face lower environmental costs overall.

According to 24.hu, the government also plans to double the air-pollution charge paid by companies. It intends to review the environmental impact of large industrial operators, including their water consumption and the pollution of surface water, groundwater and soil.

Companies that fail to reduce their water use or harmful emissions could eventually face further increases in environmental taxes and charges. The details of these additional measures have not yet been published.

The carbon-quota tax itself had already come under legal pressure. In April, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that Hungary’s tax on carbon dioxide emission allowances was incompatible with EU law.

Corporate tax benefits and trust structures face tighter rules

The July package would also narrow selected corporate tax benefits used by large companies and certain asset-management foundations.

The government intends to end a provision under which companies could deduct three times the value of donations made to public-interest asset-management foundations from their corporate tax base.

It also plans to review tax practices connected with Hungarian private trusts, known as bizalmi vagyonkezelés. The government argues that these structures have sometimes been used to shelter large fortunes from taxation, although private trusts can also have legitimate roles in inheritance planning and the generational transfer of family businesses.

HVG said the government expects the tightening of corporate tax benefits and trust-related rules to generate tens of billions of forints in additional annual revenue. This remains a government estimate rather than an independently verified projection.

Wealth tax remains one of the largest planned changes

The most significant structural tax proposal is an annual wealth tax, but it has not yet been adopted.

The government’s current plan is based on a 1% annual tax on the portion of net wealth exceeding HUF 1 billion, approximately EUR 2.75 million. Property, investments, company shares and valuable movable assets could potentially form part of the tax base.

According to Portfolio, Magyar said the relevant legislation could be adopted by the end of October 2026, with the first revenue arriving in 2027. The government estimates potential annual receipts of HUF 300–600 billion, or approximately EUR 824 million–1.65 billion.

Important questions remain unresolved, particularly the valuation of privately owned companies, the treatment of debts and jointly owned family assets, and possible exemptions.

Other promised tax cuts have not yet been implemented

The government has also pledged to reduce VAT on fruit, vegetables and firewood and to introduce personal income tax relief for people earning below Hungary’s median wage.

One proposal would reduce the effective personal income tax burden on minimum-wage earners from the current 15% to 9%, using a tax rebate or credit. Smaller reductions would apply to earnings between the minimum and median wage.

These measures have not yet received the same firm implementation date as the Hungary prescription drug VAT change.

As Reuters reported, the government has also indicated that the special sectoral taxes imposed on banks, retailers, energy companies, telecommunications businesses and other industries will remain in place for the time being because they provide substantial budget revenue.

The emerging picture is therefore mixed: prescription medicines have received a clear starting date, several minor taxes are included in a proposed parliamentary package, while the wealth tax and broader personal income tax reforms remain under preparation.

World.title: Reformist PAS still tops preferences in Republic of Moldova but majority oppose union with Romania
World.content:
Moldovan president Maia Sandu's Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) remains at the top of voter preferences for the parliamentary elections, according to an IMAS poll conducted in June. The same survey showed that over half of the citizens of the Republic of Moldova would oppose unification with Romania in a referendum.

The reformist PAS has the trust of 20.6% of respondents, according to the survey, while 14.9% would vote for the Party of Socialists of the Republic of Moldova, and 10.2% for the "Democracy at Home" Party.

The pro-EU camp in Moldova does not enjoy a similar advantage when it comes to the next presidential elections. Roughly 13.9% of Moldovans say they would vote for pro-Russian Igor Dodon, the leader of the Party of Socialists of the Republic of Moldova (PSRM), for president, followed by Vasile Costiuc, president of the "Democracy at Home" Party - 9.9%, Renato Usatîi (Our Party) - 7.2%, Alexandr Stoianoglo - 6.6%, and Igor Grosu (PAS) - 6.5%.

Around a quarter of respondents, 24.1%, said they did not have an option for president. Maia Sandu cannot run a third time, according to the Moldovan constitution.

The IMAS poll also revealed that more than half of the citizens of the Republic of Moldova would oppose unification with Romania in a referendum. More exactly, the study showed that 54% of respondents would vote against unification, while only 33% would vote in favor of it.

Regarding a possible referendum on the Republic of Moldova's accession to the European Union, 48% of citizens would vote "for," while 34% would vote "against." By contrast, only 24% would support the country's accession to NATO, while 58% would vote against.

As for the direction of the Republic of Moldova's foreign policy, nearly half of those interviewed (49%) believe it should be "balanced, both with Russia and with the Europeans". Another 29% favor a pro-European orientation, while 12% would prefer a pro-Russia policy. Only 5% of citizens support a "pro-unification with Romania" policy.

At the same time, Russia's influence in the Republic of Moldova is perceived as "very strong" or "fairly strong" by 40% of respondents. By contrast, 52% consider Moscow's influence to be "very weak" or "fairly weak".

The poll was conducted between June 10 and 20, commissioned by Independent News, on a stratified, probabilistic, two-stage sample of 1,015 respondents aged 18 and over, representative of the adult population of the Republic of Moldova, excluding Transnistria. The interviews were conducted at respondents' homes by 33 operators from the IMAS network, in Romanian and Russian. The maximum margin of sampling error is ±3.1%.

World.title: US brokerage giant Interactive Brokers adds Bucharest Stock Exchange companies on its platform
World.content:
Interactive Brokers, the American brokerage giant with more than 5 million clients, USD 775 billion in assets, and more than 4 million trades processed daily across 170 markets, has added shares listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange to its platform, including Banca Transilvania, OMV Petrom, Romgaz, and Hidroelectrica.

Until now, a non-resident investor had to go through the bureaucracy of opening an account with a local broker. As such, few foreign investors placed their funds in Romanian companies. With the Interactive Brokers' addition, investors can buy Romanian shares directly from the same application used to trade Apple or Nvidia.

A similar decision was initially taken by NAGA, a broker that started in Romania and was listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange through a reverse merger. NAGA was the first international broker to offer direct access to the Romanian market at the beginning of 2025, but its scale is much smaller.

Only 22 Romanian companies appear in the Interactive Brokers "Market Screener," but all issuers on the BVB main market and some companies on the secondary AeRO market can be found. Funding the account in RON appears on the platform, but is not yet possible. The first orders have already been executed, although they were not of significant value, according to Termene.ro.

International investors can also gain exposure to seven of the nine ETFs listed on the local stock exchange, which are currently available only to professional clients. The two exceptions are the Globinvest Energy & Financials ETF Open-End Investment Fund and the BET BRK ETF Open-End Investment Fund.

The cost structure applied by Interactive Brokers for the Romanian market includes a variable trading commission of 0.28% of the order value, with a minimum threshold set at RON 10 and no maximum cap. In addition, there is an annual custody fee of 0.1% of the value of positions held in RON, calculated daily and directed to third-party entities responsible for settlement and custody.

The Bucharest Stock Exchange is currently seeing spectacular growth. According to an analysis by Croatian fund manager InterCapital ETF, the BET-TR index, which also includes reinvested dividends, delivered a total return of 758% in euros over the past decade.

The figure exceeds the returns delivered over the same period by markets such as Slovenia, Taiwan or even the US NASDAQ 100 index. Moreover, since the beginning of 2026, the BVB has ranked as the best-performing stock exchange in Europe, with a gain of almost 50% including dividends.

World.title: Western Romania: Restored Iosefin Water Tower to open to the public for Timișoara City Celebration
World.content:
The restoration and repurposing of the Water Tower in Timișoara’s Iosefin district have been completed, the Timișoara City Hall announced.

The edifice, which has been repurposed into a cultural center, will open to the public for the Timișoara City Celebration, scheduled to take place beginning July 31. It is the first time since the edifice was built, in 1914, that it opens to the general public.

"It is one of Timișoara's landmark buildings and a key element in our strategy to revive the historic Iosefin district. More than a century after it became operational, the tower has been given a new life as a spectacular, vertical cultural center. It was a complex project with many challenges. I'm glad that Timișoara has a new attraction on its cultural and tourism map," Timișoara mayor Dominic Fritz said.

Visitors will be able to climb to an observation deck located around 50 meters above the ground, offering panoramic views of the Iosefin district, the river Bega, and the city. They can also access a route through the interior of the former water tower, accessible by lift up to approximately 24 meters, after which the tour continues via staircases that wind through the building's original structural elements.

The tower's two original water tanks, preserved since 1914, have been incorporated into the visitor circuit and can also be used as exhibition spaces. The original technical staircase and exterior woodwork have been restored to preserve the monument's authenticity.

World.title: Sailor aboard gas tanker hit near Romanian waters dies in hospital
World.content:
One of the sailors injured following the explosion that occurred aboard the Gas Lisbon vessel while it was transiting the Black Sea near Romania’s territorial waters has died.

The sailor who died was one of the three crew members who were transported to hospital after the incident. He was hospitalized at the Tulcea County Emergency Hospital.

The three were brought to the hospital two days ago, after the vessel they were on was engulfed in flames.

"He suffered burns to the airways and had a pulmonary complication related to this burn, which caused his death," said Tudor-Ion Năstăsescu, the director of the medical unit, according to News.ro.

The other two injured sailors, both of Filipino origin, are hospitalized in the hospital's Intensive Care Unit.

"They are in a stable condition. They are hospitalized in Intensive Care, but there are no life-threatening issues. They do not require transfer to other medical units," he added.

Gas Lisbon, an LPG tanker flying the Liberian flag, had departed from the port of Alexandria (Egypt) and was heading to Reni (Ukraine), transiting Romania's Exclusive Economic Zone. It was approximately 20 nautical miles southeast of the town of Sfântu Gheorghe when it suffered major damage and a fire broke out on board.

Sources from the Lower Danube River Administration in Galati initially told Digi24 the ship was attacked by a naval drone. The sailors said they were woken up by powerful explosions. “When I woke up, I heard those explosions. It was like a bomb, like a missile,” one of the crew members recounted, according to TVRInfo. Several sailors stated that the vessel had allegedly been hit by three drones.

Romania’s acting defense minister, Radu Miruță, said on Wednesday, July 22, that the incident was yet another reminder that the country must be prepared for worst-case scenarios.

World.title: Romania appeals Brussels Court decision blocking ROMATSA funds over Pfizer dispute
World.content:
Romania’s Ministry of Finance has filed an appeal against the decision of the Brussels Court of First Instance by which Eurocontrol blocked the payment of amounts owed to the Romanian Air Traffic Services Administration (ROMATSA), as part of the enforcement proceedings requested by Pfizer against the Romanian state.

The Ministry of Finance's appeal will be examined on the same day as the one filed by ROMATSA, on July 28, but government sources said that it will be an administrative hearing, with the substantive hearing most likely expected in August. Both the Ministry of Finance and ROMATSA have hired separate legal teams, both specializing in Belgian law.

"Both ROMATSA and the Ministry of Finance have filed appeals. In Belgium, as in Romania, the courts are on holiday, but a hearing has been scheduled for July 28. We will see whether the case is discussed or not; at the moment it is not known," Mihai Diaconu, state secretary at the Ministry of Finance, told News.ro.

The Romanian Air Traffic Services Administration was notified by Eurocontrol on June 30, 2026, regarding the imposition of a precautionary enforcement garnishment measure, as part of enforcement proceedings initiated by Pfizer Romania against the Romanian state. The claimed amount is RON 3.42 billion, representing principal and interest, to which recovery costs of EUR 18.5 million are added.

Both the ROMATSA and the Ministry of Finance appeals seek the lifting of the garnishment imposed on the amounts managed through Eurocontrol.

According to the notification sent by Eurocontrol, the European organization is implementing its obligations as a garnishee third party and is temporarily freezing the amounts it collects for the en-route air navigation services provided by ROMATSA. Based on this notification, Eurocontrol is required to declare the amounts it holds or owes to the Romanian state and to temporarily freeze them, without being able to make payments to anyone other than the party requesting the garnishment until the dispute is resolved.

As early as July 10, ROMATSA warned that the situation could quickly affect the operation of the administration. Route charges collected through Eurocontrol represent the administration's main source of income (85% of total revenue), and the operating horizon based on its own resources is limited, measurable in weeks, not even months.

Frozen funds

The current situation is the third time that funds intended for ROMATSA have been affected through the collection mechanism managed by Eurocontrol, following the cases generated by the disputes between brothers Viorel and Ioan Micula and the Romanian state in 2015 and 2019.

At the beginning of April, a Belgian court ordered Poland and Romania to take delivery of a COVID-19 vaccine shipment with a combined value of EUR 1.9 billion produced by the American pharmaceutical company Pfizer. According to the court statement, Romania has to pay approximately EUR 600 million of the total sum, about 0.2% of its GDP. The sum poses a significant burden at a time when the government is attempting to reduce the fiscal deficit. In addition to the principal amount, interest charges continue to accumulate at a rate of approximately EUR 81,000 per day, equivalent to nearly EUR 2.5 million per month.

Romania’s Supreme Council of National Defence (CSAT) warned that a possible suspension of ROMATSA's activity would represent a major vulnerability for national security, affecting the surveillance of Romanian airspace and NATO missions on the eastern flank.

In this context, defence minister Radu Miruță said that authorities are also examining the possibility that responsibility for airspace control could, if necessary, be taken over by the structures of the Ministry of Defence.

World.title: Bucharest exhibitions: Pop art, photos by Cristian Mungiu at upcoming season of Art Safari
World.content:
The upcoming season of Art Safari will host exhibitions dedicated to pop art, the reality of climate change, and photography by filmmaker Cristian Mungiu, in addition to a show focused on Brâncuși, the organizers announced.

The exhibition Brâncuși and His Muses, curated by Doina Lemny, looks at the artist’s relationships with the women in his life: artists, writers, dancers and gallery owners who frequented his Paris studio. Among them are Baroness Renée Irana Frachon (the model for Sleeping Muse), Margit Pogány (the model for Mademoiselle Pogany), Lizica and Irina Codreanu, artist and writer Nancy Cunard, poet Mina Loy, dancers Marthe Lebherz, Florence Meyer and Marina Saliapin, as well as the sculptor's partner, British-born pianist Vera Moore.

The exhibition features a collection of photographs taken by Brâncuși, films, correspondence, posters, personal documents, and items that belonged to his muses, including dresses and jewelry.

The exhibition Pop Art. A World in Color traces the evolution of pop art, from its origins in post-war America to its global influence today.

The exhibition follows the movement through Andy Warhol's Factory, Roy Lichtenstein's comic book-inspired universe, and the visual languages of Keith Haring and Jean-Michel Basquiat. It also explores Nouveau Réalisme, the European response to pop art, and includes works by a new generation of artists who carried Warhol's legacy forward. “Works by internationally acclaimed contemporary artists, such as Takashi Murakami and Damien Hirst, demonstrate how pop art evolved into a global visual language in the 21st century,” a presentation of the show reads.

War and Peace, an exhibition presented in partnership with the National History Museum of Romania, explores “how violence has, for centuries, been invested with meaning, glory and necessity, while peace, though celebrated in ideology, has remained a fleeting and fragile exception in history.”

The New Climate. Are We Ready?, Art Safari’s interactive pavilion, challenges visitors to discover if they are ready to face the challenges brought on by extreme weather events. Once isolated occurrences, these are increasingly becoming part of everyday reality.

The temporary exhibitions pavilion will present Cristian Mungiu. Fjord – Photographs, with photos taken by the Romanian filmmaker during the research phase for the Palme d’Or-winning Fjord.

"Preparing a film is the happiest stage of the entire filmmaking process for me. It's a time when I'm allowed to wander through wonderful places and strike conversations with all kinds of people under the pretext that I'm working. During those periods I take many photographs, not only for the film that will eventually reach the screen, but also for the most wonderful film of all: of my life making films. I haven’t managed yet to tell that story properly, but I begin for now with these photographs taken while researching for Fjord,” the director explains.

The next season of Art Safari takes place from September 18 to December 20. The exhibition of photos by Mungiu is open from September 18 to November 2.

World.title: Romanian Irina Stoian appointed chief AI commercial officer at market research firm NielsenIQ
World.content:
Irina Stoian has been appointed chief AI commercial officer at NielsenIQ, one of the world's largest market research firms and a leader in the consumer intelligence segment, with operations in Romania.

The newly-created position is designed to accelerate NIQ’s enterprise AI commercial strategy and help clients turn the company’s AI capabilities into business impact and growth, according to the company press release.

Stoian will help align Product, Technology, Commercial, Partnerships, and Marketing around a unified AI growth strategy. Her remit includes shaping commercial AI offerings, strategic partnerships, pricing and business models, and deeper integration of NIQ capabilities into client workflows.

The appointment builds on NIQ’s broader AI strategy. The company’s AI portfolio includes ConnectAI, NIQ Optiq, and NIQ Cadence.

“AI is not a feature we are adding to NIQ; it is core to our product strategy,” said Jim Peck, Chief Executive Officer of NIQ. “Irina brings exactly the combination of commercial credibility and AI fluency we need to make that strategy land with clients.”

Stoian joins NIQ from Palantir Technologies, where she most recently served as Commercial AI Lead and spent nearly six years helping organizations deploy and scale AI-powered solutions. During her tenure, she held leadership roles spanning AI strategy, commercial operations, go-to-market execution, and enterprise transformation. Before Palantir, she worked at Barclays in analytics and commercialization-focused roles and was recognized by Forbes Romania’s 30 Under 30 program.

“I joined NIQ because it has the rare combination of trusted data, strong products, global scale, exceptional talent, and deep customer relationships needed to be a leader in this next era,” said Irina Stoian.

“As AI continues to evolve rapidly, we created the CAICO role to better connect product strategy, commercialization, and client needs,” said Troy Treangen, Chief AI & Product Officer at NIQ. “Irina will help connect strategy, product, commercial execution, and client needs to translate AI innovation into market impact.”

With operations in more than 90 countries, NIQ covers approximately 82% of the world’s population and more than USD 7.4 trillion in global consumer spend. NIQ has been active in Romania for more than 30 years and currently has more than 300 employees under the NIQ and GfK brands. The two local subsidiaries posted combined revenue of RON 116.7 million last year and a net profit of RON 9.73 million.

World.title: Five feature films, 26 shorts compete at Anonimul Festival in Romania’s Danube Delta
World.content:
A total of 26 short films will compete in the national and international short film competitions, while five feature films will vie for the Anonimul Trophy at the 23rd edition of the Anonimul International Independent Film Festival, set to take place from August 10 to August 16 in Sfântu Gheorghe, in Romania's Danube Delta, the organizers announced.

This year's program includes the feature film competition, national and international short film competitions, special screenings, and Q&A sessions with filmmakers and guests.

"We did not begin the selection process with a predetermined theme. Yet, as the five films came together, one question emerged to connect them: what happens when a person discovers they are living in a world already written for them, by family, authorities, tradition, history, the place where they were born, or even by their own fiction? This year's competition covers five distinct voices that question, challenge and, at times, surprise one another," Ludmila Cvikova, curator of the feature film competition, explained.

All five feature films will be screened in Sfântu Gheorghe after world premieres at major festivals including the one held in Venice, Sundance, Karlovy Vary, Warsaw, Busan, San Francisco and Palm Springs.

The feature film competition includes: Broken Voices, directed by Ondřej Provazník (Czech Republic, Slovakia); Kurak, directed by Emil Atageldiyev and Erke Dzhumakmatova (Kyrgyzstan); If I Go Will They Miss Me, directed by Walter Thompson-Hernandez (United States); The End of the World (Sfârșitul lumii), directed by Sebastian Pereanu (Romania); and Silent Rebellion, directed by Marie-Elsa Sgualdo (Switzerland, Belgium, France)

The winner of the Anonimul Trophy will be chosen by the festival public and will receive a EUR 3,000 prize.

The festival also includes Romanian and international short film competitions. From more than 150 submissions, film critic Ionuț Mareș selected 14 Romanian short films to compete for the EUR 1,000 Audience Award.

The Romanian competition includes: Ajutoare (Benefits), Bunicu doarme (Grandpa Is Sleeping), Cherry Master, Fursecuri și lapte (Cookies and Milk), Go Outside and Hug a Tree, Index, Interferențe (Interference), Lichior de mentă (Mint Liqueur), Mama (Mother), Proprietate privată (Private Property), Rosebuds, Tangent, Viitorul ți-l faci cu mâna ta, dar de ce să nu îl lași pe mâna unor specialiști? (You Shape Your Own Future, but Why Not Leave It to the Experts?), and Vizita (The Visit).

The international competition features 12 films selected from more than 200 entries from around the world. The EUR 1,000 Audience Award for Best International Short Film will be selected from the following entries: Ali (Bangladesh, Philippines); Class Photo (Lithuania); The Cow (Croatia, Montenegro); Dog and Wolf (Czech Republic); Hyena (United States, China); Mal de Madre (Spain); Nest (Switzerland); No Skate! (France); Norheimsund (Cuba, United States); Samba Infinito (Brazil); Someday, a Child (France, Lebanon, Romania); and These Voices Are Real (Iran).

"From troubled relationships to existential and artistic crises, from first sexual discoveries to the death of a family member, from unexpected encounters to life-changing decisions, this year's short film competition explores a wide range of subjects familiar to all of us through bold and engaging filmmaking styles. The international competition is a carousel of emotions and cinematic forms, as well as an audiovisual journey through different societies and cultures full of surprises," Mareș explained.

World.title: Albanian Protesters Clash With Police at Rally Outside Parliament
World.content:
Hundreds of protesters clashed with police in front of parliament on Thursday in the Albanian capital, Tirana, as MPs convened for their last session before the summer holiday.

The clash started when police tried to push a barricade forwards several metres to stop protesters from throwing eggs and tomatoes at MPs’ cars entering the parliaments building. When this attempt to move the protesters away failed, police used pepper spray and water cannon to disperse the rally.

At least one police officer and one protester were injured when stones were thrown. Dozens of protesters were affected by chemicals used in the water cannon; some required medical treatment.

Citizens.al, a local platform promoting civic journalism, said that one of its journalists, Vjolanda Peca, had been arrested while reporting on the protest. “Our editorial office condemns this act and calls on authorities to guarantee that journalists perform their duty freely, safely and without any pressure,” the platform said.

The protest in front of parliament was part of the ongoing rallies nicknamed the “Flamingo Revolution,” which started in opposition to planned tourist developments deemed threatening to bird life and the environment, including a project linked to Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. They have widened to include calls for Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation and an end to the rule of the two political parties that have governed the country for decades.

World.title: Financier-Turned-PM Plans Radical Cure for Moldova’s Ills
World.content:
Moldova’s President, Maia Sandu, rang Vasile Tofan in October last year to try to convince him to leave the private equity company Horizon Capital and become the country’s next prime minister. Tofan declined.

The businessman and economist Alexandru Munteanu took the job instead. When he then resigned on July 3, Sandu offered Tofan the job again. This time, he said yes.

“This time, I gave it a great deal of thought,” Tofan told media outlet Pro TV shortly after parliament approved his government lineup on Tuesday, with backing coming from Sandu’s ruling Action and Solidarity Party, PAS.

“My initial response was immediate: if the governing party believed I could serve my country, I was determined to do so,” he declared.

World.title: Closed Roads Leave Kosovo-Montenegro Mountain Region Cut Off
World.content:
Authorities in Kosovo have blamed the delays to the border demarcation on “technical issues”.

“Once these technical issues are resolved, the Ministry will work to facilitate border traffic,” the government said.

Montenegro’s interior ministry said “there is not a single problem” on its side of the border.

“Over the last decade, several initiatives have been sent to Kosovo authorities through diplomatic channels for the implementation of this Agreement, but there has been no response from their side,” the ministry told BIRN.

“The reasons for the non-implementation of the Agreement lie exclusively on the Kosovo side.”

The consequences, however, are felt on both sides.

Near Velika, a village on the slopes of Cakorr/Cakor mountain near the Lim River, an old military bunker stands as a ruined reminder that this was once a stronghold of the Yugoslav People’s Army, JNA.

“The troubled days are behind us, the years lived under the shadow of watchtowers and military outposts are gone, but we need to move freely,” said 56-year-old Vuksan Vuletic, who spends every summer with his family on Cakorr/Cakor mountain. He joined the road protest last month.

“The states must make a decision on this,” Vuletic told BIRN. “It would make a huge difference if this road were reopened for the entire Lim Valley and beyond.”

In Murino, another of the mountain villages, café owner Nedzad Cecunjanin said the city of Peja/Pec in Kosovo was “like a second mother” to people like him.

“We were educated there and relied on it for many of our needs,” he said. “During the war, it was where we found safety. We have many family ties and godparent relationships there. We even have our cemeteries there.”

“But all of that has gradually been disrupted because we have been cut off from Peja/Pec since 1999.”

“We appeal to the governments of Kosovo and Montenegro, as well as the EU and foreign embassies, to help reopen this road as soon as possible,” he said.

Not everyone agrees. Some villagers on the Montenegrin side fear the reopening of the road may lead to Kosovo seeking more land.

World.title: New Party Brings Fresh Hope – and Risks – for Turkey’s Embattled Opposition
World.content:
“We opened up a new road because they blocked all the others. We are opening up that road now. Are you ready to march to power? We will march to power.”

With these stirring words, Ozgur Ozel told his parliamentary group on July 21 he was leaving the main opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, to establish a new party.

Its name, logo and other details will be announced at a later date, after which various CHP MPs are expected to join it. An estimated 80 to 90 of the CHP’s 135 MPs are likely to switch sides.

Ozel, who was removed as CHP leader following a controversial court ruling in May, predicted that his new party would immediately become the largest opposition group in parliament.

World.title: Romanian City Holds Out Against Authorising LGBTQ+ Pride March
World.content:
Oradea’s unauthorised Pride March in 2025. Photo: Photo: Ovi D. Pop/Oradea Pride.

Just over 250 kilometres separate Romania’s western city of Oradea from Budapest in Hungary, but until recently the two cities shared another distinction: both had refused to allow Pride marches.

Hungary’s capital hosted a Pride event this year despite government opposition. Oradea is now the only major city in the European Union where local authorities continue to deny permission for a Pride march, after refusing to authorise the 2026 event on Wednesday.

“The City Hall has decided not to approve the event. All 115 possible routes proposed by the organisers are concentrated in the city’s central area … These routes are unavailable because they overlap with other authorised events, or are affected by major public infrastructure works,” municipal spokesperson Octavian Haragoș said, as quoted by the local news outlet ebihoreanul.ro.

The municipality did not explain why alternative routes outside the city centre could not be considered. The decision followed weeks of delays by the city council in ruling on the organisers’ request, where conservative councillors and religious groups dominated the debate.

Human rights groups condemned the decision, arguing that it violates the constitutional right to peaceful assembly.

“We consider this decision completely unacceptable because it effectively blocks people’s constitutional right to peaceful assembly,” Victor Ciobotaru, director of ACCEPT, Romania’s leading LGBTQ+ rights organisation, told BIRN.

“Under Romanian law, local authorities cannot ban a public march. Their role is to identify practical solutions to ensure that such events can take place safely and under appropriate conditions, not to prevent them altogether,” Ciobotaru added.

Citing the same legal argument, ARK Oradea, the organisation behind the city’s Pride Parade, said the march would go ahead on July 25 despite the municipality’s refusal to authorise it.

“Our march will take place … As a sign of solidarity and concern for the situation in Oradea, representatives of nine diplomatic missions accredited to Romania, as well as representatives of the Ombudsman Institution, will be present in Oradea to monitor the unfolding of events,” ARK said, adding that the presence of diplomats reflects growing international concern over restrictions on freedom of assembly and LGBTQ+ rights in Romania.

This marks the fourth consecutive year that Oradea’s authorities have refused to authorise the Pride Parade.

Last year, however, an unauthorised march was still held through the city centre, attended by several hundred mostly young people. There were brief scuffles between some participants and the police but the situation did not escalate.

Authorities later imposed fines totalling 19,800 lei (about 3,900 euros) on organisers and participants in the unauthorised march

Romania has made progress on LGBTQ+ rights since joining the European Union in 2007 but continues to rank among the bloc’s weakest performers in terms of legal protections and social acceptance.

Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 2001, but same-sex marriage and civil partnerships are not recognised, despite a 2023 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights requiring Romania to provide legal recognition and protection for same-sex couples.

Public attitudes toward LGBTQ+ people remain largely conservative, particularly outside major cities. Pride marches have been held annually in Bucharest for two decades, however, and in several other cities, generally under police protection and without major incidents.

Human rights organisations have urged Romania to strengthen anti-discrimination protections and fully implement European human rights standards, arguing that it is lagging behind in terms of the country’s commitments as an EU member.

World.title: EU, OSCE Missions Criticise Kosovo’s Demolition of Serb-Owned Villas
World.content:
Demolition of villas near Ujman/Gazivoda lake in north Kosovo on July 21, 2026. Photo: BIRN

International missions in Kosovo expressed concern on Wednesday over the police’s demolition of 11 villas belonging to local Serbs near Lake Ujman/Gazivoda in the Serb-majority north of the country.

Kosovo authorities said the houses were built illegally on land owned by the public water management company Iber-Lepenc, near the Ujman/Gazivode Lake. The operation began on June 26.

The European Union Office in Kosovo said that it regretted Tuesday’s demolitions, noting that, “the affected residents had already initiated court proceedings within the 15-day deadline provided in notices issued by the public enterprise Iber-Lepenc to vacate the land”.

The EU called for an “immediate halt to any further demolitions, forced removals or takeovers until concerns relating to due process, proportionality, property rights, human rights and effective remedies are adequately addressed.

“Irreversible enforcement measures in the context of pending proceedings and contested property claims raise serious rule-of-law concerns,” the statement added.

The OSCE Mission in Kosovo said that, “any action affecting property rights, including the demolition of illegally constructed buildings, must be carried out strictly within the applicable legal framework, with full respect for due process”.

The mission said affected individuals should be informed promptly and adequately of the legal basis for actions taken against their property. “The rule of law, transparency, and due process must be applied consistently and without distinction to all illegally constructed buildings across Kosovo,” it said.

It added that enforcement measures against unauthorised construction should follow the same legal standards and procedural safeguards for all communities. “Selective or uneven application of the law, whether real or perceived, risks undermining public confidence and negatively affect inter-community relations and trust,” it said.

Faruk Mujka, chief executive of the state-owned hydro-economic company Iber-Lepenci, wrote on Facebook on Tuesday that “11 illegally constructed villas had been removed during Tuesday’s operation”.

Mujka said the action was carried out by the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure with assistance from the police following a request from Iber-Lepenc to return the property to the company’s management.

Ujman/Gazivoda Lake is considered strategic infrastructure for Kosovo. It supplies drinking water to several cities, supports electricity generation and provides water for irrigation.

Fitore Pacolli, acting minister of the Ministry of Environment, Spatial Planning and Infrastructure, noted at the start of demolition work in June that the operation was being conducted to return illegally occupied property in northern Kosovo to the administration of Iber-Lepenc.

“The protection of our water resources remains our highest priority. For this reason, we will continue to protect them, manage them responsibly, and develop them as a vital asset for Kosovo,” Pacolli wrote.

But the Serbian government’s office for Kosovo condemned the operation as a “violent demolition” undertaken “without any court verdict”.

“The owners of the villas found out about the demolition of their property, which they had acquired for years, from the notices that were attached to their buildings, and when they asked for court decisions today, they did not receive them,” it said.

“All this indicates that these demolitions were not carried out with the aim of implementing some kind of law, but for a political reason,” it added.

NOTE: This article was amended on July 22, 2026 to clarify that Faruk Mujka is chief executive of the state-owned hydro-economic company Iber-Lepenci.

World.title: Serbia Indicts Six for Drug Trafficking Linked to North Macedonia
World.content:
Serbia’s Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime filed an indictment on Tuesday accusing six alleged members of an organised crime group of producing and trafficking drugs within Serbia and North Macedonia during 2025 until January 29, 2026.

The prosecution on Wednesday said the indictment was filed against Aleksandar Mijajlovic as the organiser, Ivan Dragnic as the co-organiser, and Nebojsa Spasojevic, Rade Spasojevic, Uros Mladenovski and Robert Zivkovic as members of the same crime group.

“The evidence collected … indicates that the organisers devised the group’s operational structure, established its hierarchy, assigned roles among its members in advance, and secured the financial resources necessary to carry out the criminal plan,” the prosecution said in a press release.

The group is suspected of transporting nearly five tonnes of marijuana from North Macedonia to Serbia and storing it in residential and commercial premises used by Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic in the village of Konjuh, near Krusevac, central Serbia, where the drugs were repackaged and prepared for distribution to end-buyers.

Spasojevic was a local official of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, at the time of the bust. Serbian Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic, himself from Krusevac, denied the party was involved and repeated that it was clear that there are “no protected individuals” in Serbia because they had arrested Spasojevic.

The suspects are charged with using the company Alfapharm Group, based in Skopje, as a legitimate business entity to cover the narcotics production.

The company held permits issued by the authorities in North Macedonia to cultivate and produce cannabis extracts for medical purposes.

“The company was misused to conceal the organisation of the procurement, storage, repackaging, and transportation of large quantities of the narcotic drug marijuana,” the press release said.

According to the prosecution, in November 2025, the group organised the procurement of 8,832 kilograms of dried cannabis flower from the supplier CBD Med Plant from Strumica, North Macedonia.

The drugs were stored at the premises of Alfapharm Group, weighed, repackaged and prepared for transportation. The group used documentation relating to the export of textile goods for this during international transport.

The indictment added that Robert Zivkovic is charged with managing storage of the drugs, supervising the packaging process, organising their transportation, and overseeing their unloading and storage in Serbia. Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic are alleged to have been responsible for receiving, storing, repackaging, and arranging the further transport of the drugs.

Serbian police arrested Uros Mladenovski at the end of January in Belgrade, when he collected around a hundred kilograms of marijuana from Spasojevic’s premises and transported it to the capital.

During searches of the residential and business premises used by the Spasojevic family, police discovered various arms, such as automatic firearms, ammunition, and a “Zolja” hand-held anti-tank rocket launcher.

Dragnic, Nebojsa and Rade Spasojevic and Mladenovski are in detention.

Zivkovic is a fugitive. A detention order has been issued for him, and both domestic and international arrest warrants have been sought.

Aleksandar Mihailovic was arrested in Austria on July 1 and a Serbian request for his extradition is pending.

The prosecution added that proceedings are being conducted before the North Macedonian authorities as well, and that both countries “continue to cooperate and exchange information within the framework of international legal assistance”.

Serbia’s authorities on January 29 seized five tons of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, which the Serbian prosecution then suggested may have originated from North Macedonia. A week later, North Macedonia police seized more than 40 tons of drugs.

The record-breaking seizures in both countries fuelled questions about whether North Macedonia’s legalisation of marijuana grown for medicinal purposes in 2016 has encouraged illegal production and smuggling.

World.title: North Macedonia’s Access-to-Information Agency Accused of Hindering Appeals
World.content:
North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information. Photo: BIRN.

Legal experts and transparency advocates have criticised North Macedonia’s Agency for the Protection of the Right to Free Access to Public Information after it began requiring electronic signatures on email appeals, arguing that this unlawfully restricts access to public information.

The Agency is the only institution responsible for deciding appeals when public bodies refuse or fail to provide information requested under the country’s freedom of information law.

Until recently, appeals could be submitted by email without additional formalities. However, the Agency has started rejecting emailed appeals unless they are certified with an electronic signature, which costs 2,000 to 4,000 denars (30 to 65 euros) annually.

Critics say the changes create an unnecessary financial and administrative obstacle to exercising a constitutionally guaranteed right.

“I believe they obstruct free access to public information in this country,” German Filkov, one of the authors of the Law on Free Access to Public Information and president of the Centre for Civil Communications, an anti-corruption and transparency watchdog, told BIRN.

Instead of creating new barriers, Filkov said, the Agency should focus on the growing number of state institutions that fail to respond to freedom of information requests.

The Agency has defended the new requirement by citing the 2015 Law on General Administrative Procedure, which it says obliges anyone communicating electronically with state institutions to use an electronic signature.

However, the State Administrative Inspectorate, which the Agency initially cited as the source of the guidance, told BIRN it had issued no written decision or instruction requiring such a practice.

One of the authors of the Law on General Administrative Procedure, which the Agency cites as the legal basis for its new practice, Skopje university law professor Borce Davitkovski, also questioned the Agency’s interpretation.

“They are not allowed to reject an appeal because it lacks an electronic signature,” Davitkovski told BIRN, noting that the law was designed to protect citizens rather than burden them with unnecessary bureaucracy.

Konstantin Bitrakov, an assistant professor at Skopje’s State Faculty of Law, argued that the Agency was misapplying the legislation and “setting a negative example for public institutions that hold information, whose decisions it is supposed to review on appeal”.

He said the legal provisions on electronic signatures apply to officials issuing administrative decisions, not to citizens filing appeals.

Lawyers told BIRN that citizens and organisations whose appeals have been rejected for lacking an electronic signature should challenge the Agency before the Administrative Court within 30 days.

The dispute comes amid concerns over access to public information.

A BIRN analysis found that the number of appeals filed with the Agency over administrative silence or incomplete responses had doubled last year, from over 300 filed in 2024 to over 600 in 2025.

The European Commission’s latest Rule of Law Report warned that some public institutions continue to reject information requests on arbitrary grounds or with significant delays.

In April, the new head of the Agency, Petar Gajdov, told BIRN in an interview: “As institutions, we are service-oriented towards citizens.”

World.title: Croatian Tourism Season Holding Steady as July Matches 2025’s Pace
World.content:
July the 23rd, 2026 – The Croatian tourism season is doing well as July this year is so far matching July 2025’s pace.

As Istrain.hr reports, the tourism industry remains on track for another strong year, with July performing at roughly the same level as last year’s record season, according to Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) Director Kristjan Staničić.

Speaking after a coordination meeting with tourist boards from Zadar County, Staničić revealed that the season has unfolded largely as expected. While June saw a slight dip compared to 2025, that followed a particularly strong May, leaving overall results for the first six months of the year virtually unchanged from last year. Early figures for July suggest that the trend is continuing. Staničić stressed that every single tourist season is influenced by different factors, including school holiday schedules, economic conditions in Croatia’s key source markets and major international events. Despite those variables, he believes Croatia has maintained a stable position in an increasingly competitive Mediterranean market.

“there’s no stagnation”

He also rejected suggestions that Croatian tourism has entered a period of stagnation, pointing instead to the country’s long-term strategy of growing outside the peak summer months. Rather than relying solely on July and August, Croatia is continuing to invest in pre-season and post-season tourism through health tourism, congress tourism, improved destination experiences and stronger air connectivity.

A key priority remains expanding flight connections. HTZ has increased funding for strategic partnerships with airlines and tour operators by around 30 percent this year, with the aim of improving access to Croatia, particularly during the shoulder seasons. Officials are also encouraging regional tourist boards to work more closely with airlines as they begin planning routes for next year.

new private accommodation rules cause a stir

Staničić also defended recent government measures affecting private accommodation landlords, arguing they should be viewed as part of a long-term strategy to improve quality and tackle the grey economy rather than as short-term restrictions.

He highlighted the “Your Host” quality label, which has helped participating properties achieve higher occupancy rates and greater visibility, while noting that future legislative changes will introduce stricter oversight of unregistered accommodation.

With visitor numbers broadly matching last year’s record-breaking performance despite a more challenging international environment, Croatia’s tourism authorities remain optimistic that the country is on course for another successful season.

World.title: Budget Fashion Chain Primark Set to Open Its First Store in Croatia
World.content:
July the 23rd, 2026 – Budget fashion chain Primark, which is extremely popular in every country in which it operates, is set to open its very first store in Croatia. Until now, the closest was in Ljubljana.

One of Europe’s most popular affordable fashion retailers by far is finally heading to Croatia. Primark, the Irish clothing giant known for its low prices and trend-driven collections, is preparing to open its first Croatian store, marking a long-awaited arrival for many local shoppers. Poslovni reports that for very many years, Croatian customers have travelled to neighbouring countries such as Slovenia, Austria and Italy to shop at Primark stores, often returning with suitcases full of clothing, accessories and homeware. Soon, they will be able to do so without leaving the country.

Primark has built an incredibly loyal following across Europe by offering fashionable clothing, footwear, beauty products and home goods at highly competitive prices. Its arrival in Croatia has been the subject of speculation for years, fuelled by strong demand from shoppers who regularly visit stores abroad. Social media has also played a role in the retailer’s popularity, with fashion influencers frequently showcasing Primark’s latest collections and seasonal bargains.

the first croatian primark store will be near zagreb

According to reports, the retailer is preparing to open its first Croatian location at Designer Outlet Croatia in Rugvica, just outside Zagreb. The shopping centre has increasingly attracted international brands, and Primark’s arrival is expected to further strengthen its position as one of Croatia’s leading retail destinations. While an official opening date has yet to be announced, preparations are reportedly underway.

Unlike many international fashion retailers, Primark focuses on offering the latest trends at prices that are often significantly lower than competitors. Its stores are known for having everything in stock, from everyday basics and seasonal fashion to children’s clothing, cosmetics, home decor and licensed merchandise from popular films and television series. The combination of wide product selection and low prices has made Primark one of Europe’s fastest-growing fashion retailers.

a much needed boost for croatia’s expensive retail sector (and for the public’s wallets)

Primark’s arrival reflects Croatia’s growing attractiveness to international retail brands. As consumer spending continues to evolve and modern shopping centres expand their offerings, more global retailers are viewing the Croatian market as an increasingly attractive destination. The opening is also expected to reduce the need for Croatian shoppers to travel abroad specifically for Primark purchases, keeping more retail spending within the country.

For thousands of Croatian fashion enthusiasts, the news ends years of waiting. Instead of planning shopping trips across the border, customers will soon have access to one of Europe’s best-known budget fashion brands much closer to home. If the first store proves successful, it could also pave the way for additional Primark locations in other Croatian cities in the years ahead.

World.title: Rolling Stone UK Recommends Croatian Špancirfest
World.content:
July the 23rd, 2026 – Rolling Stone UK has recommended the much-loved Croatian cultural festival Špancirfest as a great summer festival, spotlighting Croatia away from the beach.

It’s one of the best-loved Croatian cultural festivals, and now it has received international recognition after Rolling Stone UK included Špancirfest among its recommendations for unforgettable summer experiences in Croatia. Held each August, far from the sea in the historic streets of Varaždin, Špancirfest has built a reputation as one of the country’s most distinctive festivals, combining live music, street theatre, art, food, workshops and performances that transform the entire city into an open-air stage.

The inclusion by Rolling Stone UK places Špancirfest alongside some of Croatia’s best-known summer attractions, highlighting the country’s growing reputation not only for its coastline but also for its vibrant cultural scene.While Croatia is often associated internationally with beaches and islands, festivals like Špancirfest continue to attract visitors looking for authentic cultural experiences away from the Adriatic coast.

Unlike many music festivals held in a single venue, Špancirfest spreads throughout Varaždin’s picturesque Baroque old town. Historic squares, narrow streets and courtyards become performance spaces for musicians, artists, acrobats, comedians and street performers, creating an atmosphere that encourages visitors to wander through the city and discover something new around every corner. The programme traditionally includes concerts by Croatian and international artists, children’s entertainment, artisan markets, gourmet food stalls and interactive workshops, making it one of Croatia’s most family-friendly festivals.

showcasing northern croatia and a festival far from the coast and islands

For Varaždin, the recognition represents another opportunity to introduce international travellers to a region that is often overlooked by visitors heading directly to the Adriatic coast. Known for its elegant Baroque architecture, rich history and vibrant cultural calendar, the city has become one of Croatia’s leading destinations for cultural tourism. The beloved Špancirfest plays a central role in that reputation, drawing tens of thousands of visitors every year and providing a significant boost to local businesses, restaurants and accommodation providers.

International recognition from Rolling Stone UK also reflects a broader shift in how Croatia is being promoted abroad. Increasingly, international media are highlighting the country’s festivals, gastronomy, inland destinations and cultural heritage alongside its world-famous coastline. For travellers planning a summer trip, Špancirfest offers a chance to experience a different side of Croatia, one filled with music, creativity and historic charm in one of the country’s most beautiful continental towns. As Croatia continues to diversify its tourism offering, festivals like Špancirfest are helping demonstrate that some of the country’s most memorable summer experiences can be found far from the gentle waves of the Adriatic Sea.

World.title: Wizz Air Rules Out Zagreb Base for Now, Citing Market Conditions
World.content:
July the 23rd, 2026 – Despite things looking promising just days ago, Wizz Air has ruled out having a new Zagreb base for now, citing current market conditions.

Popular low-cost airline Wizz Air has confirmed that it has no immediate plans to establish operating bases in either Zagreb or Ljubljana, revealed the two capitals do not yet meet the commercial conditions required for such an expansion. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the announcement comes as both Croatia and Slovenia continue working to strengthen air connectivity, with regional airports competing to attract more airlines and new routes.

wizz air says no to a zagreb base – for now

Speaking about the company’s expansion strategy, Wizz Air representatives said that neither Zagreb nor Ljubljana currently offers the market conditions needed to justify opening a permanent base. While the airline continues to operate flights to both cities, establishing a base would require a larger and more sustainable level of passenger demand, route opportunities and long-term profitability. For now, the carrier says it remains focused on markets where it sees stronger growth potential.

An airline base is far more significant than simply operating flights to an airport. It typically involves stationing aircraft and crews permanently at a location, allowing airlines to launch more routes, increase flight frequencies and offer earlier departures and better connections. For airports, securing a carrier’s base often leads to increased passenger numbers, more tourism and the creation of new jobs linked to aviation and airport services. Without a local base, airlines generally have less flexibility to rapidly expand operations.

competition is hotting up

Airports across Central and Southeast Europe are increasingly competing to attract low-cost carriers, offering incentives and investing in infrastructure to encourage airlines to establish long-term operations. Zagreb Airport has continued to dramatically expand its route network in recent years, welcoming new airlines and destinations while strengthening connections across Europe. However, competition remains intense, particularly as neighbouring airports also seek to position themselves as regional aviation hubs.

Despite Wizz Air’s decision, Croatia’s aviation sector continues to see significant changes. Several airlines have announced new seasonal routes this year, while airports including Zagreb, Split, Dubrovnik and Zadar continue to record strong passenger numbers during the summer season. At the same time, Croatia is working to improve domestic connectivity, with seasonal flights linking Osijek to several Adriatic destinations and ongoing discussions about further strengthening regional air links.

looking to the future…

Although Wizz Air has ruled out a new Zagreb base for now, the airline has not closed the door permanently. Should passenger demand continue to grow and market conditions improve, both capitals could once again be considered for future expansion. For the moment, however, travellers can expect Wizz Air to maintain its existing network rather than significantly increasing its presence through locally based aircraft.
