World.title: IN NUMBERS: Does mentioning priority legislation in SONA guarantee enactment?
World.content:
Rappler looked into the priority bills mentioned during SONAs and how past presidents fared in making sure they became law

Once the priorities are set, the president selects a few of the discussed legislation to mention during his or her annual address. Then during the SONA, the president calls for Congress to expedite passage of these bills.

According to the former director of the Senate Economic Planning Office, this is where the LEDAC discusses legislation aimed at boosting the countryâs socioeconomic development and ironing out differences between the executive mechanism and legislative branches of government.

Professor Jean S. Encinas-Franco of the University of the Philippines Dilimanâs Department of Political Science said that these bills or policies undergo a series of consultations with both houses for finalization before presidents deliver their SONA .

But it was not until 1992, through Republic Act No. 7640 , that former president Fidel V. Ramos institutionalized the process through the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (LEDAC).

Legislative priorities are bills or policies recommended for national, regional, provincial, or local development planning.

Hereâs a review of the past and present administrations and their performance in terms of enacted legislation.

Which of the past administrations were clear about their legislative priorities and which saw them through actual enactment into law?

But these priorities can change, depending on the current political climate and public interest. Some legislation are stalled, diverted, or long forgotten in the gutters.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.âs fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on July 27, 2026, will once again report on the past yearâs accomplishments, ongoing efforts, and priorities looking forward.

Passing rate of SONA priority legislation This graph shows a comparison of the last three presidencies. Enacted Unpassed Benigno S. Aquino III Rodrigo R. Duterte Ferdinand Marcos Jr.* * Note: Marcos Jr. has yet to finish his term and only includes four SONAs. Sources: SONA Transcriptions, Senate Bills, and LawPhil Project

All three administrations saw that more than half of the priority legislation did not become law. According to Cagayan Vice Governor Manuel Mamba, who served as chief of the Presidential Legislative Liaison Office from 2012-2015, some legislation were never meant to be passed and only served to make an administration look good. âWhen it doesn't fit the interest of those in power and those in the legislature and the politicians, it's just there to die a natural death. And that is why sana hindi nila pina-prioritize kung alam naman nilang hindi napapasa. So fina-file lang âyan basically because it is not meant to pass.â (And that is why they shouldnât prioritize it if they know it will not be enacted. Theyâre just filing it because it is not meant to pass.) Either the House of Representatives or the Senate can introduce or refile a bill. Both can also file identical or companion bills, which can place importance or urgency on the issue being sought to be addressed.

Yearly count of legislation brought up during SONA This graph shows the annual number of legislation mentioned by each president. Replay Timeline Source: SONA Transcriptions

In 2011, former president Benigno S. Aquino III did not call on Congress to pass any legislation during his SONA. The most number Aquino mentioned was 10 in 2013. Mamba noted that the Aquino administration was âproactiveâ in introducing pieces of legislation, including those that were never entertained or prioritized before. But during the administration of former president Rodrigo Duterte, the number skyrocketed. At the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Duterte called for the passage of 21 priority bills. Among these were government agencies focused on disease prevention, control, and virology. The pandemic also struck the nationâs wealth at the time, prompting the enactment of legislation targeted at economic recovery. A year prior, in 2019, Duterte had 19. Mamba pointed out that Duterteâs term was âreactiveâ and focused on addressing the pandemic. He also said that the Marcos administration had to be reactive in the wake of the UniTeam division. The Marcos-Sara Duterte tandem crumbled in 2024 after a series of conflicting events, including different political stances, Cabinet resignation, open hostility, and, eventually, the impeachment trial of the Vice President. âThey could have done so much in the first three years if only they were together, if only there was no division,â Mamba mentioned. âThat is why this is more now dictated on the survival of the administration and to keep them acceptable to the people.â The current administrationâs count dipped coming into his third year. Marcosâ focus began to pivot from wishlist bills to those that could address current issues that affect Filipinos. âIf you look at the Marcos priorities now, para sa akin, it's not really institutional in nature,â Mamba mentioned. (For me, if you look at Marcosâ priorities now, itâs not really institutional in nature.) âIt's more of the immediate impact that they are after, for just to sustain themselves in power,â he added. Marcosâ midyear performance contradicts the previous two administrations, which saw an increase in the number of measures introduced. Encinas-Franco explained that an administration may be pressured to come up with defining âlegacyâ measures, given itâs halfway through its term. âPriorityâ legislation Despite its label, less than half of each presidentâs list passed and eventually enacted, whether within the same year or later.

Priority bills enacted into law across administrations This graph shows the rate of passage of each legislation mentioned by the last three presidents. * Note: Marcos Jr. has yet to finish his term and only includes four SONAs. Sources: SONA Transcriptions, Senate Bills, and LawPhil Project

Overall, Aquino had the fewest number of bills mentioned during his SONA and passed into law. Only eight of the total 23 mentioned during his presidency were enacted. The two other administrations saw similar percentages in terms of unpassed legislation. However, Duterte had a larger sample size during his term. But Encinas-Franco cautioned against being rigid in interpreting priority legislation, as its label does not guarantee passage. She noted that all legislative measures take a long time to be enacted due to different factors. âYou are also competing with the rest of the other proposed measures in the legislative mill,â she said. âAlso, if there's a lot of pushback from civil society movements, from business interests, then it also becomes quite challenging to have it passed.â These groups and public opinion can also pressure Congress to refile revised bills that were not enacted in the previous legislative period. Unexpected events may push back these priorities as well â such as, according to Encinas-Franco, the recent call to revisit the minimum age of criminal liability, following the school shooting in Tacloban City. Budget is also another factor why some legislation are stalled, said Encinas-Franco. In 2022, Marcos vetoed the creation of a transportation safety board due to redundancies with the functions of the Department of Transportation, the Philippine National Police, and the National Bureau of Investigation. The argument was that adding another government body would require funds to sustain operations. âIf the government is in a tight fiscal situation, then of course, people and even legislators would be sensitive to creating a program or an organization that will be perceived by the public as a waste of public funds,â she noted. Mamba added another factor: the interests of members of Congress. âProfit of the capitalist dictates the norm,â he said. âMost of our politicians are politicians of vested interests, especially of the money of our country. And most of them are supported also by the oligarchs of this country, and most of them are members of the oligarchy.â Setting own agenda Not all measures mentioned are consulted with LEDAC. The president is also a major agenda-setter of legislation, according to Encinas-Franco.

Inclusion in the Common Legislative Agenda This graph shows the number of bills that are included in and not included in the Common Legislative Agenda (CLA). View by President Part of CLA Not Part of CLA Sources: SONA Transcriptions and LEDAC

World.title: Housing provided, but schools for settlers’ children often overlooked
World.content:
EDCOM 2 urges the Department of Education to address the lack of school facilities in resettlement projects, and prioritize the construction of classrooms in areas with severe congestion and multiple shifts

MANILA, Philippines – Housing projects without planned education facilities are compounding the severe shortage of classrooms and contributing to the poor quality of learning in the country, according to the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2).

During a Senate basic education committee hearing on Thursday, July 23, EDCOM 2 Executive Director Karol Mark Yee reported that there are 58 housing projects by the National Housing Authority (NHA) that do not have planned school facilities.

Yee was citing Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD) data submitted to EDCOM 2.

The 58 NHA housing projects, representing over 167,000 units, are located in Bulacan, Rizal, Cavite, Laguna, Pampanga, and Metro Manila.

Under the 2008 implementing rules and regulations of Batas Pambansa Blg. 220, education facilities are only required for low-cost developments with 1,500 units and above.

“Policies are silent about the cumulative challenges faced by schools when multiple housing sites are set but without any schools to go to,” Yee told senators.

He described what the commission found in Naic, Cavite: At least 48 low-cost NHA housing sites there have generated more than 12,000 students that existing schools cannot accommodate. In Yee’s presentation, he said that many live beyond the schools’ two-kilometer catchment area.

Play Video

Yee noted that EDCOM 2 has raised the issue since 2024, with the Department of Education (DepEd) and DHSUD signing a memorandum of understanding to address the matter in July 2025. However, this MOU was only for forthcoming housing projects.

Without government action, schools in Naic saw a spike in enrollment figures by 5,405 students between the end of school year 2025-2026 in March and the start of SY 2026-2027 in June. This increase meant the town needed at least 135 additional classrooms to comply with the 1:40 classroom ratio.

“Ang tanong po no’ng mayor: ‘Saan po kami kukuha ng espasyo at lugar na pagdadalhan ng lahat ng estudyante?’” the EDCOM 2 executive director said.

(The mayor asked: Where will we get the space to put all of these students?)

DepEd urged to address issue

During the hearing, NHA Region IV Manager Roderick Ibañez said they have sent a list to the DepEd of housing sites that need funds for school facilities.

“The NHA only needs P2.8 billion to complete the backlog of classrooms in Region III and in Region IV, which are the priority regions of DepEd. We have been waiting for the budget for two years,” Ibañez said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Yee appealed to the DepEd and the DHSUD to immediately address the lack of school facilities in NHA resettlement areas, and to clarify agency roles and coordination mechanisms for school site development.

“Consistent with the National Education Plan, we would like to urge DepEd to prioritize construction in areas with the most severe congestion and with triple, multi-shifts, because we saw in the data that these are also the areas with high rates of bullying and school violence,” he said in a mix of English and Filipino.

While the DepEd vowed to solve the issue, funding to set up schools in housing projects might not be released this year, and may be considered in 2027 yet.

Progress in classroom construction

The issue was brought up as Senator Bam Aquino, chairman of the Senate basic education committee, conducted the hearing to get updates regarding classroom construction in 2026.

The Philippines is confronted with a 166,000-classroom backlog. As of Wednesday, July 22, over P23 billion out of the P67.9-billion 2026 budget for classroom construction has been released to the DepEd, said Education Undersecretary Filemon Javier.

Two other construction modes — local government units (LGUs) and public-private partnerships (PPPs) — were introduced in a bid to plug the gap, as well as move away from depending entirely on the corruption-mired Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).

The DPWH promised to complete 5,000 classrooms this year using previous budgets. Under the 2026 budget, it targets to start building an additional 6,000 classrooms.

Over 200 LGUs have so far signed a memorandum of agreement (MOA) with the DepEd for LGU-led classroom construction. However, the release of funds to LGUs will only be done once there is a resolution to award the first tranche.

Not all LGUs are expected to sign MOAs with the education department this year to build classrooms.

Meanwhile, the DepEd hopes to issue a notice of award for the winning bidder to set up 3,000 classrooms under the PPP modality by October.

At least two companies have shown interest in this project under the PPP for School Infrastructure Project Phase III. – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines: No permission-seeking in 2024 Ayungin ‘understanding’ with China
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) The DFA pushes back after China’s envoy claims the Philippines agreed not to construct on the BRP Sierra Madre in a 2024 temporary deal

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Thursday, July 23, that a temporary deal with China in 2024 does not mean Filipinos seek permission for resupply missions, allow the boarding or inspections of Philippine ships, “concede the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction” in Ayungin Shoal in the West Philippine Sea.

“As stated from the outset, the Provisional Understanding is a set of principles and approaches observed by both sides in order to avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation in the conduct of the Philippines’ routine rotation and resupply (RORE) missions for daily necessities to the BRP Sierra Madre in Ayungin Shoal,” said the DFA in a statement.

The provisional understanding, sometimes called a provisional agreement, was made between the two countries in 2024 a month after China Coast Guard (CCG) personnel harassed Filipino soldiers who were already moored by the BRP Sierra Madre, a warship that serves as a makeshift outpost in Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal in the West Philippine Sea. That 2024 incident resulted in one soldier losing his thumb and Philippine Navy equipment destroyed as the CCG intervened in a RORE mission to the Sierra Madre.

It’s a deal that’s made headlines recently after a July 20, 2026 confrontation between the CCG and Philippine soldiers, the first in two years. CCG personnel entered Ayungin Shoal and sailed around the BRP Sierra Madre, taking photos and videos, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan, speaking to media on Tuesday, July 21, said the CCG were reportedly inspecting the warship to check on reported construction activities as proof of the Philippines bringing in supplies — a supposed violation of the agreement, according to the ambassador.

Play Video

Much has been said about the provisional agreement — many of it rooted in speculation, no thanks to its secrecy.

The exact details of the understanding have never been made public. Ironically, its secrecy is one of the few things made public about the agreement.

“The Philippines’ legal position, grounded in [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea] and vindicated by the Arbitral Tribunal, remains unchanged and non-negotiable,” said the DFA.

By stating that the agreement “does not concede the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction,” the DFA is indirectly addressing Jing’s claims.

Ayungin Shoal, as affirmed by the 2016 Arbitral Award, is a low-tide elevation that is part of the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone where it should enjoy exclusive rights to exploit and protect resources. That means the Philippines should not be restrictied from activities in those waters, to include building or strengthening structures such as the BRP Sierra Madre.

“The Philippines continues to conduct rotation and resupply missions, including normal shipboard activities in BRP Sierra Madre, as a matter of routine government function within Philippine jurisdiction and in the exercise of its sovereign rights under international law particularly UNCLOS and the 2016 Arbitral Award, and will continue to do so for as long as necessary in line with the national interest,” said the DFA.

The agreement was made under former foreign affairs secretary Enrique Manalo, although the current Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro was then the undersecretary that led efforts to speak to China.

“There is no mention of that undertaking in the provisional understanding,” Lazaro said in a press briefing following the ASEAN foreign ministers meeting on Thursday, referring to Jing’s claim that construction and construction materials were not permitted. – Rappler.com

World.title: SEA Games champion Dines Dumaan seeks financial help after road crash
World.content:
STANDOUT. Pencak silat athlete Dines Dumaan of the Philippines during the 2017 Southeast Asian Games.

MANILA, Philippines – Pencak silat standout Dines Dumaan, who delivered medals for the country on the international stage, needs financial help for a head surgery following a motorcycle accident.

According to the Philsilat Sports Association, the 31-year-old pride of Panitan, Capiz, underwent operation on Thursday, July 23.

“Dines needs financial assistance. He was brought to Capiz Doctors’ Hospital yesterday morning,” the Philsilat Sports Association told Rappler on Thursday.

No official report has been released but a video circulating online shows Dumaan riding a motorcycle before he crashed into a roadside structure at around 4:25 am on Wednesday, July 22, his helmet falling off after the impact.

“At this time, only Dines knows exactly what happened, as the family was informed only after he had already been brought to the hospital yesterday morning,” the Philsilat Sports Association said.

In one of the biggest feats of his career, Dumaan captured the Philippines’ lone gold medal in pencak silat in the 2017 Southeast Asian Games in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

That ended the country’s 12-year drought for a pencak silat gold in the SEA Games, or since Marniel Dimla ruled in the 2005 edition hosted by the Philippines.

A year later, Dumaan bagged bronze in the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, Indonesia.

His other accolades include a gold in the 2017 Asian Pencak Silat Championship in Chungju, South Korea, and a bronze in the Philippines’ hosting of the 2019 SEA Games.

Fellow pencak silat athlete Ian Christopher Calo appealed for help for his “brother,” saying Dumaan needs approximately P100,000 as downpayment for his surgery.

Dines Dumaan. Papart Ian Facebook page

“Dines is a Filipino athlete who wholeheartedly brought honor to our country through the medals he won. Now, he is the one who needs our support in the most important battle of his life,” Calo wrote on his Facebook page in Filipino.

“Any amount or help you can give will be a great help to him and his family.”

Rappler reached out to Dumaan’s family members but has yet to get a response. – Rappler.com

World.title: Army recovers guns, explosives after clash with Maguindanao terrorists
World.content:
COTABATO CITY, BARMM, Philippines — Government forces clashed with combined armed groups composed of Dawlah Islamiya (DI) Hassan Group, Bangsamoro Islamic Freedom Fighters (BIFF), and Panenekelan criminal gang in Maguindanao del Sur early Thursday morning.

Two local terrorists were also arrested during intensified law enforcement operation in Maguindanao del Sur.

Article continues after this 

Soldiers of the Army’s 38th Infantry Battalion, led by its battalion commander, Lt. Col. Erwin Felongco, engaged the combined forces of DI-BIFF-Panenekelan groups in a firefight beginning at 5:30 a.m. on July 23 in Barangay Inaladan, Shariff Saydona Mustapha town.

The firefight lasted for about 30 minutes until the gunmen retreated.

Brig. Gen. Edgar Catu, commander of the Army’s 601st Infantry Brigade, said pursuing government forces recovered two high-powered firearms near the clash site, including an M16 rifle and an M1 Garand rifle.

READ: Army links fresh Maguindanao attacks to antiterror operations

The military noted that the armed group’s strength had already been significantly weakened following the death of Esmael Abubakar, alias “Commander Bungos,” leader of the BIFF-Bungos Faction, during a military operation in Sultan Kudarat, Maguindanao del Norte on July 5, 2026, and the arrest of Muslimin Amilil, one of the leaders of the Panenekelan group and an alleged bomb maker for the BIFF and Dawlah Islamiyah, in Barangay Tukanalipao, Mamasapano on July 21.

Article continues after this 

READ: Alleged bomb expert, wife nabbed in Maguindanao del Sur

Catu said these setbacks forced the remaining members of the armed groups to consolidate their forces.

Article continues after this 

He said the ongoing military campaign was launched following the ambush of police personnel in Shariff Aguak in March and was followed by armed encounters in Datu Hoffer Ampatuan and Mamasapano towns.

“The death of Esmael Abubakar, alias ‘Bungos,’ and the arrest of Muslimin Amilil dealt a major blow to the group, prompting its remaining members to unite,” Catu said.

“We will continue clearing our areas of responsibility to ensure that the first-ever BARMM Parliamentary Elections will be conducted in a peaceful and secure environment,” Catu said.

On July 22, two alleged members of the Panenekelan criminal gang, including a 20-year-old student, were arrested during a joint police and military operation Tuesday afternoon in Barangay Tukanalipao, Mamasapano, Maguindanao del Sur.

Police Capt. Steffi Salanguit, spokesperson for Police Regional Office-Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, identified the arrested suspects as Alias Saidemn, 20, a student, and Alias Razid, an adult, both residents of Tukanalipao village.

They were believed to be members of the Panenekelan criminal gang, an armed group allied with Dawlah Islamiyah and BIFF operating in the so-called “SPMS box,” an Army term for the adjoining towns of Shariff Aguak, Datu Saudi Ampatuan (formerly Pagatin), Mamasapano and Shariff Saydona Mustapha.

Police said the two were arrested following the arrest of Muslimin Amilil, former BIFF member and known bomb maker linked to the March 28, 2026 ambush in Shariff Aguak that left five police officers killed.

The arrested suspects were associates of Amilil. Police recovered from them a .45-caliber pistol, ammunition, and two hand grenades.

Maj. Gen. Jose Vladimir Cagara, commander of the 6th Infantry Division, commended the troops for their successful operation.

“Every firearm we recover represents lives saved from violence. The dismantling of their leadership and the voluntary surrender of members of violent extremist groups are clear indications that their organization is steadily weakening,” he said.

World.title: Over 1,000 ha of farms get year-round irrigation in Palawan town
World.content:
ABORLAN, PALAWAN, Philippines — President Marcos led the inauguration ceremony and turnover of the Ibato-Iraan Small Reservoir Irrigation Project (SRIP) in Barangay Sagpangan, here on Thursday, July 23, marking the start of a new significant chapter in agricultural development in the town.

The Ibato-Iraan SRIP, the first reservoir-type irrigation system in the province, is considered the largest project of the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) in the province of Palawan, worth P866.2 million with a capability of providing steady and year-round water supply to some 1,072 hectares of agricultural land across three barangays: Iraan, Isaub and Sagpangan here.

Article continues after this 

The project, which was turned over to the Ibato-Iraan Farmer’s Irrigators Association, Inc., is expected to benefit some 425 member-farmers and their families, where Marcos said he sees a steady increase in productivity with improved crop yields and higher incomes.

READ: Marcos opens dam in Sultan Kudarat, gives aid in South Cotabato

He said for so many years, farmers in the area have relied solely on unpredictable rainfall, making every planting season uncertain. With the completion of the irrigation system, they can now plan their cropping seasons with greater confidence, improve farm productivity, and achieve more stable harvests and higher incomes.

READ: Marcos pushes climate-smart farming as Bohol irrigation project opens

The project’s inauguration officially marks the beginning of its operation, providing a reliable water supply that will benefit farming communities and strengthen agricultural productivity for generations to come.

Article continues after this 

“We expect an increase in harvest and better quality of products for a higher income for our farmers,” he said.

“More than that, this project also brings peace of mind to farmers with a steady supply of water for a better future for every family who depends on farming,” he added.

Article continues after this 

After the inauguration, Marcos flew back to Puerto Princesa City to also lead the ceremonial distribution of 10-kilogram rice subsidies to 1,000 beneficiary families under the Local Government Support Fund, which he said intends to ensure that vulnerable families will have food on their tables as part of his administration’s commitment to address hunger and improve food security.

He said through the LGSF, the national government aims to continuously provide assistance to low-income families as support to programs of local government units in addressing food security. /cb

World.title: Iloilo City raises Blue Alert as TD Kiyapo threatens Western Visayas
World.content:
ILOILO CITY, Philippines — The Iloilo City Government has placed the city under Blue Alert and activated its Emergency Operations Center (EOC) as Tropical Depression Kiyapo is expected to bring heavy rains and possible flooding over Western Visayas in the coming days.

Mayor Raisa S. Treñas, chairperson of the Iloilo City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (ICDRRMC), signed the directive on July 23 ordering disaster response clusters, district councils, barangay disaster committees, and concerned government agencies to heighten preparedness measures ahead of the weather disturbance.

Article continues after this 

The order takes effect beginning 12 noon on July 24 and will remain in force until lifted.

READ: Kiyapo to make possible landfall in Babuyan Islands on Friday

According to the memorandum, the decision was based on monitoring by the Iloilo City Operations Center and the latest forecast issued by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), which placed the center of Tropical Depression Kiyapo east of Northern Luzon as of 11 a.m. Thursday. The cyclone was packing maximum sustained winds of 45 kilometers per hour, gusts of up to 55 km/h, and moving northwestward at 25 km/h.

READ: Kiyapo putting 6,947 barangays at risk of landslides, floods — OCD

Pagasa also warned of heavy rainfall associated with both Kiyapo and the southwest monsoon, with Iloilo expected to receive 50 to 100 millimeters of rain from Friday noon until Saturday noon. Rainfall may be heavier in mountainous and elevated areas, increasing the risk of flooding and rain-induced landslides.

Article continues after this 

Under the Blue Alert, all ICDRRMC vice chairpersons, cluster leads, and members have been directed to remain on standby for possible deployment, closely monitor weather conditions, and immediately report incidents to their assigned response clusters to ensure rapid coordination among concerned offices.

The memorandum also instructs all District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Councils (DDRRMCs) and Barangay Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committees (BDRRMCs) to activate their respective emergency operations centers, raise their own alert status to Blue Alert, and implement disaster preparedness measures to protect residents.

Article continues after this 

Barangays, district councils, key offices, and partner agencies have likewise been ordered to regularly submit situational reports to the Iloilo City Emergency Operations Center as weather conditions continue to develop.

The city government urged residents to stay updated on official weather advisories, monitor local announcements, and prepare for possible heavy rains and related hazards over the next two days. /cb

World.title: P50,000 reward offered for info on village councilor’s slay in Isabela
World.content:
ECHAGUE, ISABELA, Philippines — Local government officials have earmarked P50,000 as reward money for informants who can lead to the arrest of the killers of a former village chair and incumbent councilor in Barangay Malibago here.

Police Colonel Manuel Bringas, Isabela police director, hoped that the reward money would help to arrest the motorcycle-riding gunmen who shot and killed village councilor Lito Publico, 61, inside his farm resort compound on July 17.

Article continues after this 

READ: Gunmen on motorcyle kill village councilor in Isabela

Bringas said they have formed the Special Investigation Task Group-Publico (SITG-Publico) with assigned team members for intelligence gathering, manhunt operations, and follow-up investigation.

READ: Cop, village chair among 4 killed in Isabela shooting

Probers have released screenshots of the killers from a closed-circuit television camera in the area.

“We condemn the dastardly act … We will not stop until the killers will be identified, arrested, and charged,” he said. /cb

World.title: Marcos urged to include Site Blocking Bill in legislative priorities
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

MANILA, Philippines — As President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona), a consumer advocacy group has urged his administration to include the Site Blocking Bill in one of its legislative priorities to provide a safe and secure digital economy for the country.

CitizenWatch PH co-convenor and former lawmaker Atty. Kit Belmonte said that the government’s demonstration of site blocking through Shared Blocking Management Database is a success. He explained that the database is a portal that enables regulators to work with Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center and the National Telecommunications Commission in prohibiting illegal online activities.

With this, Belmonte said that the institutionalization of the site blocking will allow the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) to swiftly crack down on pirated and illegal websites.

Article continues after this 

READ: Blocking of sites with pirated content pushed

“What is needed now is to complete the legal framework by extending the same capability to intellectual property enforcement. The Site Blocking Bill will empower the Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines to act more swiftly against piracy websites that continue to exploit creators, investors and consumers,” Belmonte said in a press release on Wednesday.

While Belmonte acknowledged the IPOPHL’s progress in strengthening intellectual property enforcement, he said that its site-blocking capability still needs to have explicit statutory authority.

READ: Senate asked to urgently pass bills to protect creative sector

He then emphasized that the proposed bill is aligned with Marcos’ administration agenda to innovate and strengthen the digital economy and transformation.

Article continues after this 

“The administration has consistently championed digital transformation, ease of doing business, and a more competitive economy. Supporting the passage of the Site Blocking Bill would be a logical extension of that vision. It will strengthen online consumer protection, encourage innovation, protect our creative industries and reinforce the rule of law in the digital space,” he added.

He also said that the passage of the bill will provide confidence to investors, inventors, software developers, researchers and creative professionals that their ideas will be protected by the law. /cb

World.title: No official info yet that Atong Ang has already left PH, says NBI
World.content:
Fugitive businessman Charlie “Atong” Ang — File photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) has no official information yet that fugitive businessman Atong Ang, the alleged mastermind in the disappearances of cockfighting enthusiasts (sabungeros), has already left the country.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag said this on Thursday when asked about reports that Ang had fled the country amid arrest orders against him over the alleged kidnapping and killing of at least 34 cockfighting enthusiasts between 2021 and 2022.

“That is yet to be verified. We have no official information at the moment,” Matibag told reporters in an ambush interview.

Article continues after this 

READ: PNP checking reports Atong Ang has left country

When asked about what information the NBI has been receiving regarding Ang’s location, Matibag said, “Other than the open source intel that we have and that we saw in the report, that’s all.”

READ: Remulla: Atong Ang moving around Calabarzon every 2 days to evade arrest

Meanwhile, when further asked, the NBI director refused to disclose the locations the bureau visited to track the gambling tycoon, explaining that “we may still go back to those areas.”

The NBI, as well as the Philippine National Police, is currently tracking Ang after the Laguna and Batangas courts recently issued arrest orders in connection with multiple criminal complaints against him regarding the missing sabungeros. /cb

World.title: NBI: There’s ‘person of interest’ in Hontiveros’ online death threats
World.content:
Sen. Risa Hontiveros —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) Director Melvin Matibag said on Thursday that there’s a “person of interest” behind the online death threats against Senator Risa Hontiveros.

Matibag confirmed this after saying that the bureau is already in the process of investigating Hontiveros’ online death threats, adding that he had spoken with the senator’s chief of staff regarding the case.

Hontiveros earlier released a statement, saying that she herself had become a target of what she described as the “wave of death threats” and “pro-killing” remarks that circulated on social media following the recent killing of vlogger Alicia Lipata, mostly known as Mima Alicia.

Article continues after this 

READ: Hontiveros seeks NBI help over online death threats against her

“There is a (person of interest). It is in the social media post itself. And we are submitting it to the Forensic Laboratory at the Cybercrime Division for proper disposition,” Matibag said in an ambush interview on Thursday.

READ: PNP: 2 nabbed over pro-Marcos vlogger slay

According to Matibag, the NBI will conduct a case buildup on the matter, noting that “after the case buildup, if we feel that it’s enough for us to file a case, we will file one with the DOJ (Department of Justice.)”

The NBI director then pointed out that the cases of death threats nowadays are “very alarming” and have already become “a norm” on social media.

Article continues after this 

“So we need to stop this. It’s very alarming because even our high-ranking government officials receive death threats. That’s why I say that our national security will be under attack right now,” Matibag said.

READ: Cops to be sanctioned if photojournalists’ ‘harassment’ is proven

Article continues after this 

When asked about his warning to the individuals behind the circulation of death threats, the NBI director said, “As law enforcement, we will do our law. We will do our mandate. As to the law and order, if we need to go after you, we will go after you.”

“But make no mistake that this will be political or personal. We will base our actions on evidence and according to the process and to the law,” said Matibag. /cb

World.title: Police file raps vs Negros Occ board member linked to e-sabong
World.content:
BACOLOD CITY – The Police Regional Office Negros Island Region (PRO NIR) has filed criminal and administrative complaints against Negros Occidental 3rd District Board Member Andrew Gerard Montelibano before the Office of the Ombudsman.

The complaints were filed on July 20, by the Regional Special Operations Group (RSOG), the PRO NIR confirmed in a press statement on Thursday, July 23.

Article continues after this 

READ: E-sabong ops busted in Negros town; link to provincial board member eyed

The regional police command did not specify the charges it lodged against Montelibano who was tagged for alleged links to an illegal online sabong operation in a property his family corporation owned in Barangay Alicante of E.B. Magalona town.

The illegal activity was discovered following an arrest operation against a wanted person in Negros Occidental on July 8.

Montelibano on Thursday told the Inquirer he could not give a comment yet about the RSOG charges as he was not aware of the filing of the complaints.

The PRO NIR emphasized that the filing and receipt of these complaints are part of the legal process and should not be construed as a determination of guilt.

Article continues after this 

The PRO NIR refrained from discussing the specific details, evidence, and allegations contained in the complaints, as these are now under the jurisdiction of the Office of the Ombudsman and remain subject to its evaluation.

The police command said any further disclosure may unduly affect the proceedings and, as such, will defer to the proper legal process.

Article continues after this 

“The Police Regional Office Negros Island Region remains steadfast in its commitment to uphold the rule of law through professional, impartial, and evidence-based law enforcement, while respecting the independence of the Office of the Ombudsman in the disposition of the complaints,” the PRO NIR said.

Brig. Gen. Romano Cardiño, PRO NIR director, at a press conference on July 9, said Montelibano has been named a “person of interest” following the discovery of a multi-million peso illegal online cockfighting (e-sabong) operation located on his property in E.B. Magalona town

A police manhunt operation for a person wanted for murder and frustrated murder, led to the discovery of the alleged e-sabong operations and the arrest of four individuals in Hacienda Pilar, Barangay Alicante.

Montelibano said he was not aware that e-sabong operations were happening on his property and he is not part of that business.

World.title: Kazakhstan Temporarily Reduces Oil Production Amid CPC Export Suspension
World.content:
98357

ASTANA — Kazakhstan has temporarily reduced oil production following the suspension of loading operations at the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal in the Black Sea, the Energy Ministry said on July 23.

Loading operations at the CPC marine terminal have been temporarily suspended to ensure the safety of vessels, crews and the environment in the Black Sea. All production and technical facilities of the consortium remain fully operational and are ready to resume crude oil shipments as soon as conditions normalize.

“Due to restrictions on oil intake into the pipeline system, oil-producing companies have made a controlled adjustment to daily production levels to prevent storage facilities from reaching capacity. The temporary reduction in oil output is a technological measure aimed at maintaining stable production processes,” reads the ministry’s statement.

The ministry said it is in contact with CPC management, major shippers, shipowners and relevant government agencies. Consultations are ongoing to ensure safe navigation and facilitate the prompt resumption of stable exports of Kazakh oil to global markets.

Reuters reported earlier that Kazakhstan’s oil production had declined following the closure of a Black Sea terminal serving as the country’s main export route for crude oil, which was recently targeted by drone attacks. According to industry sources cited by Reuters, the decline has been notably sharp at the Chevron-led Tengiz field, Kazakhstan’s largest oilfield.

Kazakhstan condemned the drone attacks on civilian vessels transporting oil through the CPC infrastructure on July 17 and 19, describing them as threats to international energy security.

World.title: Kazakhstan Allocates Over $22 Million for KazSat-3R Communications Satellite
World.content:
105302

ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government has allocated 10.4 billion tenge (US$22.3 million) to begin developing the KazSat-3R communications satellite, which will replace the existing KazSat-3 spacecraft and ensure the uninterrupted operation of the country’s national satellite communications system.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov signed the corresponding resolution as part of the implementation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s directive to strengthen Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure and expand access to modern telecommunications services, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on July 23.

KazSat-3R will replace the current KazSat-3 satellite, whose planned operational life expires in 2029. The new spacecraft is intended to ensure continuity of national satellite communications services while supporting the long-term development of Kazakhstan’s telecommunications sector.

The project is expected to enhance the reliability of satellite communications and television broadcasting networks, expand internet access in sparsely populated and remote areas, strengthen information security and reinforce the country’s technological sovereignty.

The KazSat satellite system currently provides television broadcasting, data transmission, mobile communications and internet services. It is used by 19 domestic telecommunications operators and government agencies, serving more than two million television subscribers.

The satellite project forms part of broader efforts to modernize Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure. Over the past two years, high-speed internet coverage has reached 99% of the population, including more than 4,500 rural settlements. Other initiatives include expanding fiber-optic networks in rural areas, implementing the Last Mile project, rolling out 5G, extending mobile coverage along highways and deploying modern satellite technologies.

More than 90% of public services are now available online, while the launch of national supercomputing capacity and the unified QazTech digital platform is intended to support the development of artificial intelligence and the digital economy.

According to the government, KazSat-3R, together with new Earth observation satellite projects, will strengthen Kazakhstan’s space industry and expand its technological capabilities.

World.title: IOC Recognizes Kazakhstan’s Olympic Team Preparation Model as International Best Practice
World.content:
79320

ASTANA – The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has recognized the National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Kazakhstan’s system for preparing Olympic delegations as a Best Practice and recommended it to other National Olympic Committees.

The IOC highlighted Kazakhstan’s Athlete and Team Official Agreements (ATOA), developed by the NOC to complement the IOC’s standard Conditions of Participation (CoP). The agreements are tailored to Kazakhstan’s national legislation and cover a broad range of legal, organizational and operational matters related to participation in the Olympic and Youth Olympic Games, the NOC said on July 22.

The IOC noted the introduction of four separate agreements for athletes, coaches and medical staff, media representatives, and other team officials. The documents establish standardized provisions governing the code of conduct, compliance with IOC regulations, financial terms, the use of personal social media during the Games, official uniform requirements and dispute resolution procedures.

According to the IOC, the agreements also reflect a multidisciplinary approach, drawing on the experience of previous Kazakh Olympic delegation leaders (Chefs de Mission) and contributions from the NOC’s sports, international relations, media, marketing and legal departments.

The IOC described Kazakhstan’s model as an effective example of integrating international standards and the Olympic Charter into national practice. It recommended it for adoption by other National Olympic Committees, recognizing Kazakhstan’s approach as an international best practice.

World.title: Kazakhstan Forms 82 Overseas Polling Stations for Kurultai Elections in August
World.content:
87861

ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry has announced on July 22 the composition of election commissions established at the country’s diplomatic missions abroad to organize voting in the elections of deputies to the Kurultai, scheduled for Aug. 23.

A total of 82 overseas polling stations have been formed at Kazakh embassies, consulates and permanent missions across Europe, Asia, the Middle East, North and South America, Africa and Oceania to ensure voting access for Kazakh citizens residing or staying abroad.

The ministry said the commissions were established in accordance with the Constitutional Law on Elections, the presidential decree calling the elections, and the Central Election Commission’s calendar plan for election preparations.

The published list includes the chairpersons, deputy chairpersons, secretaries and members of all precinct election commissions operating at Kazakhstan’s foreign missions. The measure is aimed at ensuring the openness, transparency and accessibility of the electoral process for citizens outside the country.

World.title: Kazakhstan Dominates Central Asia’s FDI Stock as Uzbekistan Gains Ground
World.content:
684362

ASTANA – Central Asia’s foreign direct investment (FDI) stock rose 3.6% to $235.5 billion in 2025, with Kazakhstan retaining roughly two thirds of the region’s total, according to the latest World Investment Report released by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD).

Kazakhstan accounted for nearly 66% of Central Asia’s total, solidifying its position as the region’s largest destination for foreign investment. The nation’s FDI stock, which refers to the accumulated value of FDI held in a country, stood at $156.4 billion as of 2025. It went up a little bit from $155.1 billion in 2024. In 2010, the figure was just $82.6 billion.

Uzbekistan, meanwhile, recorded the strongest annual increase from $20.5 billion in 2024 to $26 billion in 2025.

Kazakhstan was a major destination for newly announced large-scale investment projects. One of them relates to a non-ferrous metals project worth more than $12 billion announced by China’s East Hope Group. The report ranks it among the 10 largest greenfield projects announced in developing Asia during the year.

FDI inflows

In terms of FDI inflows, Central Asia received $4.97 billion in 2025, up 12.1% from $4.43 billion in 2024. This is a substantial fall compared to $9.8 billion that the region recorded in 2022.

According to the report, Uzbekistan drove Central Asia’s foreign investment recovery in 2025, attracting nearly $4.4 billion as inflows into Kazakhstan turned negative. Kazakhstan recorded net FDI outflows of $861 million in 2025, compared with net inflows of $227 million a year earlier.

The Kyrgyz Republic posted the region’s fastest percentage increase, with inflows more than doubling to $642 million. Tajikistan’s FDI inflows fell to $86 million, down 70% from $291 million.

According to the report, resource and infrastructure projects in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan featured prominently in the region’s investment activity and project pipeline.

“Investment activity was concentrated in metals and metal products, which together accounted for approximately 45% of total greenfield project activity in the region, followed by energy, transport and storage, chemicals, food processing, and ICT,” reads the report.

Global trends

While global FDI increased by 6% to $1.6 trillion in 2025, this recovery has been uneven and fragile. When excluding financial flows routed through Europe’s largest investment hubs, the increase narrows to 4%.

FDI inflows in developed economies increased by 11% to $723 billion, whereas developing economies received $901 billion in FDI, an increase of 2%.

The largest FDI destination in 2025 was the United States, which received $277 billion. It was also the largest source of FDI last year, followed by Japan and China.

The report indicates that investment activity is becoming more concentrated across regions and sectors.

“Semiconductors, electronics, AI infrastructure, data centres, renewable energy and battery supply chains continued to drive large projects. Project activity was concentrated in China, India, Kazakhstan, Malaysia and the United Arab Emirates, mainly in electronics, digital infrastructure and construction,” it said.

These industries accounted for 44% of global greenfield investment last year, growing from 16% in 2020. Kazakhstan is positioning itself to benefit from the same shift, with major investment plans spanning renewable energy, battery materials, data centers, AI infrastructure and advanced processing of metals and critical minerals, instead of relying solely on extractive industries.

Changing model

Expert Sultan Valikhanov echoes this point in his piece for the EconomyKZ analytical website, cautioning that the rise in global FDI should not be read automatically as a boom in new factories.

“For three decades, the formula was simple: production moved to where labor was cheaper and costs were lower. That allowed dozens of developing countries to join global supply chains and attract factories, logistics hubs and industrial clusters. Capital followed efficiency. The cheaper it was to produce, the greater the chance of attracting an investor,” Valikhanov wrote.

This model is now breaking down. He explained that part of last year’s increase came from intracorporate flows, restructuring and capital routed through international financial centers rather than the expansion of productive capacity.

“What matters, therefore, is not how much capital crossed borders, but where exactly it went,” Valikhanov added.

Stronger domestic capacity

“If most investment is flowing into digital infrastructure and advanced manufacturing, the decisive advantage becomes a country’s ability to support such projects through reliable energy, transport links, engineering talent and a digital ecosystem built around production,” Valikhanov wrote.

That is particularly relevant to Kazakhstan. The headline figures tell only part of the story. What is important is whether that capital went to industries that are capable of generating local value, technology transfer and skilled employment.

UNCTAD also emphasized that countries need to make “deliberate national policy choices,” which among others include “realistic entry points” into changing value chains, and coordinating investment, jobs, supplier policies and infrastructure.

“This will also require renewed international cooperation, with partnerships that balance the resilience that investing countries expect with the development that recipient countries need,” said UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno.

Kazakhstan has increasingly treated trade and investment diplomacy as an instrument of industrial policy, not merely foreign relations. High-level diplomatic visits secure capital, technology, logistics links and access to new value chains. This logic shapes Kazakhstan’s ties with long-established strategic partners such as China and its engagement with newer partners.

“Today, investment follows strategic calculation and industrial policy marked by subsidies, economic security and technological advantage. Governments are competing with new investment policy measures, at a record high in 2025,” said Pedro Manuel Moreno.

He noted that the reshaping of global supply chains is creating opportunities for developing economies to become manufacturing bases, critical-mineral processing hubs and gateways to regional markets. In this context, Kazakhstan is trying to position itself in all three areas by developing transcontinental transport routes, expanding domestic processing of critical raw materials and investing in industrial, technological and skills capacity.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Use Digital Tenge Across Government Spending This August
World.content:
118899

ALMATY – Kazakhstan to begin using the digital tenge in public procurement from August after completing the integration of the digital currency platform with the Finance Ministry’s information systems, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on July 22.

The announcement followed a government meeting chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, where officials reviewed progress on pilot projects testing the central bank digital currency and discussed challenges to its wider implementation.

According to the ministry, the legal status of the digital tenge platform and its operating procedures have now been established. A total of 340 billion digital tenge (US$626 million) has been issued, with 20 pilot projects completed, 10 underway, and 50 more in preparation.

Beginning in August, the digital tenge will be used for public procurement of goods, including medicines, fuel and lubricants, and other material supplies. Pilot projects cover infrastructure construction, budget lending and subsidies, grant financing, government support measures, public procurement, tax administration, as well as procurement by the National Bank and quasi-state entities.

The government has also introduced mandatory use of the digital tenge for eight categories of budget expenditures covering projects worth more than 100 million tenge (US$184,000).

Officials identified end-to-end traceability of public funds as one of the main challenges to expanding the project. According to the government, while digital tenge transactions can already be tracked from budget allocation to the main contractor, many subcontractors are not yet prepared to conclude smart contracts because current legislation does not require their use.

To address the issue, the ministry has prepared amendments to existing legislation that would establish the legal framework necessary for wider adoption of smart contracts and improve transparency throughout the public spending chain.

World.title: Almaty to Host Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in September
World.content:
163853

ALMATY – The Central Asia Fintech Summit (CAFS) 2026 will take place in Almaty on Sept. 11, bringing together financial institutions, fintech companies, regulators, investors and technology leaders to discuss the future of digital finance in Central Asia.

Organized by the National Payment Corporation of Kazakhstan and the National Bank of Kazakhstan, the summit will take place at Tselinny Center of Contemporary Culture from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.

The event is expected to serve as one of the region’s leading platforms for dialogue on financial technologies, digital assets and the development of modern financial infrastructure.

The summit will bring together representatives of the banking sector, fintech firms, international organizations, technology companies, regulators, investors and industry experts to discuss emerging trends and opportunities shaping the regional financial ecosystem.

Building on the momentum of the 2025 edition, organizers say this year’s summit aims to further strengthen cooperation across the industry. Last year’s event marked a shift from a discussion platform to a mechanism for coordinating the fintech sector, resulting in the launch of digital asset initiatives and the signing of strategic industry agreements, including those related to QR payment infrastructure.

The 2025 summit attracted more than 4,000 participants, featured over 80 speakers, and welcomed delegates from more than 30 countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan Reports Record Ice Cream Production in June
World.content:
143524

ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s ice cream production more than doubled in June compared to the same month last year, reaching nearly 20,100 tons, according to new data released by the Bureau of National Statistics. The surge comes as the country’s dairy industry continues to expand, with ice cream among the fastest-growing product categories in the first half of 2026.

The latest figures complement the bureau’s earlier report showing that Kazakhstan’s overall dairy manufacturing output increased by 11.9% in the first six months of the year, driven primarily by strong growth in cheese, butter and ice cream production.

June’s production was 116% higher than a year earlier and almost doubled compared to May. It also exceeded the previous June average of the past five years by 2.5 times and surpassed the previous monthly record of 10,800 tons, set in July 2016, by 85%.

The sharpest increase was recorded in plombir ice cream, a rich, high-butterfat vanilla ice cream, with production reaching 10,200 tons, 3.6 times higher than in June 2025 and nearly three times more than in May. Cream ice cream production also expanded, rising 75% year-on-year and 57% month-on-month to 7,500 tons.

The value of production also increased sharply. Enterprises engaged in ice cream manufacturing produced goods worth 24.3 billion tenge (US$45.4 million) in June, approximately doubling both year-on-year and month-on-month.

The sector has maintained strong momentum since late 2024. Production volumes have recorded annual growth every month since then, averaging 32% year-on-year throughout 2025 and accelerating to around 60% so far in 2026.

According to the Agriculture Ministry, Kazakhstan also became a net exporter of ice cream for the first time in its history last year, with exports exceeding imports.

World.title: Russia’s state Duma passes law targeting citizens abroad, restricting property rights and passport renewals
World.content:
Russia Passes Law Targeting Citizens Who Left the Country

Russian Embassy in Lisbon, Portugal. Photo: Antonio Pedro Santos / EPA

On July 22, Russia’s State Duma approved, in its second and third readings, a bill introducing what it calls “temporary restrictive measures.” The legislation targets people living outside Russia who are deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties.

The restrictions will apply to anyone convicted under any article of Russia’s Criminal Code. They will also affect people facing a range of administrative charges — many of them based on provisions that Russian authorities have increasingly used to prosecute political opponents and dissenters.

The law will take effect once it is officially published.

This article is based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe.

What restrictions would the law introduce?

Authorities would be able to impose the following measures on people entered into the special registry:

freeze bank accounts and other assets;

block access to banking apps and online accounts;

redirect a person’s income into a special ruble-denominated account;

prohibit the sale of real estate and vehicles;

block the registration of property and automobiles;

suspend licenses, permits and accreditations;

bar individuals from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers;

restrict driving privileges;

deny access to government and consular services;

prohibit notarial services and transactions carried out through a power of attorney.

Before the vote, State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said that Russians living abroad should be thinking about how to appear before a court.

“We are talking about people who are harming our country — extremists, traitors to our homeland. People who have spent years trying to do everything possible to destroy our state,” Volodin said.

How the registry will work

The government will create a state registry of people who are outside Russia and deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties. The registry will be maintained by the Justice Ministry, which already administers the country’s lists of “foreign agents” and “extremists.”

Information will be supplied to the Justice Ministry by the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Federal Bailiff Service and other government agencies.

To be entered into the registry, a person must meet three criteria:

have a criminal conviction or administrative penalty that has entered into legal force;

be officially deemed to be “evading” enforcement of that sentence or penalty;

be outside Russia.

The law, however, does not specify how authorities will determine whether someone is “evading” enforcement.

An interagency commission will be established to coordinate information sharing between the Justice Ministry and law enforcement bodies. It will also decide whether to impose the restrictions.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov said he expects the registry to expand regularly, much like Russia’s list of “foreign agents.”

“I believe the mechanism will closely resemble the weekly expansion of the ‘foreign agents’ register. It will become a show of intimidation through the constant addition of new names,” he told Novaya Gazeta Europe.

Who could be affected?

Formally, the law applies to anyone outside Russia who has been convicted of a crime or an administrative offense and is deemed to be evading enforcement of the resulting sentence or penalty. The specific article under which a person was convicted does not matter.

In practice, however, those most at risk are people prosecuted for political reasons. According to lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov, this primarily includes journalists, politicians, human rights defenders and civic activists.

The law also applies to people facing administrative charges under six specific provisions:

failure to comply with Russia’s “foreign agents” law;

violations of regulations governing the activities of a “foreign agent”;

calls to violate Russia’s territorial integrity;

“discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces;

calls for sanctions against Russia;

participation in the activities of an “undesirable organization.”

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova said the legislation is primarily intended to intimidate Russians living abroad. Since the state cannot physically detain them, she argued, it is instead restricting their civil and property rights.

In her view, the authorities also aim to silence opponents of the war and spread fear among Russians who have left the country.

What happens to a person’s money and property?

The law allows authorities to freeze a person’s funds and other assets. Formally, this does not amount to confiscation, since ownership does not transfer to the state. In practice, however, it would make it much more difficult for people to manage or dispose of their property.

All payments, including pensions, would be redirected to a special ruble-denominated account. The rules governing access to and use of those funds will be determined later by the Central Bank of Russia. Court costs and other financial penalties could also be deducted directly from the same account.

People included in the registry would be barred from selling real estate or vehicles. They would also be unable to register ownership of newly acquired property or register a vehicle.

In addition, banks would block their access to mobile banking apps and online accounts, making routine bank transfers impossible. Banks would also be allowed to deny them loans and other forms of credit.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina described the measures as a tool of financial pressure.

“It creates a paradoxical situation. A person is deprived of access to the very financial tools needed to fulfill the obligations that led to their inclusion in the registry,” she said.

Restrictions on business and employment

People included in the registry would be barred from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers.

If their profession requires a license, authorities would refuse to issue a new one. Existing licenses could also be suspended until the individual is removed from the registry.

The government would also be able to suspend permits and accreditations that have already been granted.

Driver’s licenses would not be revoked outright. However, the right to drive would be suspended until the person is removed from the registry.

Ban on powers of attorney and access to government services

People included in the registry would no longer be able to use an enhanced qualified electronic signature. Existing certificates could be revoked, and new ones would not be issued.

They would also lose access to Russia’s Gosuslugi online government services portal, making it impossible to submit applications, process official documents, or access federal and regional public services online.

Before carrying out any notarial act, Russian notaries would be required to check the registry. If a person’s name appears on the list, the notary would be obligated to refuse service.

The law would also prohibit anyone from carrying out transactions on behalf of a listed individual under a power of attorney. In practice, this would deprive Russians living abroad of one of the main ways to manage their property and handle legal matters in Russia remotely.

Which consular services would be denied?

One of the law’s most significant restrictions concerns Russian consulates abroad. People included in the registry would lose access to nearly all consular services.

They would no longer be able to:

obtain a new international passport;

notarize a power of attorney;

certify copies of documents or authenticate signatures;

obtain notarized consent required for legal transactions;

register a marriage or a legal name change through a consulate;

receive consular assistance if detained abroad;

rely on Russia for emergency consular assistance while overseas.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina said the most consequential provisions are the ban on representation through a power of attorney and the restrictions on consular services. Those are the mechanisms that allow Russians living abroad to handle most legal matters remotely.

At present, even people held administratively liable can still obtain a new international passport through a Russian consulate. Those charged with or convicted of criminal offenses also retain access to some consular services.

Once the law takes effect, however, obtaining official documents without returning to Russia will become significantly more difficult.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov described the initiative as a form of de facto deprivation of citizenship.

“Citizenship technically remains, but a person is no longer able to exercise the rights that come with being a citizen,” he said.

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova agreed with that assessment. In her view, the law would leave affected individuals in a situation approaching statelessness, as the Russian state would effectively cease providing them with documentation and legal assistance.

What is the “humanitarian allowance”?

The law provides for what it calls a humanitarian allowance. The payment may be granted if a person included in the registry has close relatives who are financially dependent on them.

Eligible relatives include parents, a spouse, or children who have no independent source of income. The allowance would be paid monthly using the person’s own frozen funds.

The decision to grant the payment would be made by the interagency commission, while the amount would be set by the Russian government in coordination with the Central Bank.

When would the restrictions take effect?

The restrictions would come into force the day after a person’s name is added to the registry.

In theory, a person could be removed from the registry in several circumstances:

if a court overturns or revises the underlying decision;

if the person begins serving their sentence or complies with the penalty;

if the person returns to Russia;

if the person dies.

If the Justice Ministry fails to remove someone from the registry without justification, that person may file a request for review. The ministry must issue a decision within 20 working days, and its refusal can be challenged in court.

In practice, however, not all penalties can be served remotely. For example, a prison sentence cannot be served from abroad. As a result, anyone convicted and sentenced to imprisonment would have no realistic way to be removed from the registry without returning to Russia.

Administrative penalties present a different paradox. A person on the registry would face restrictions on banking services while also being barred from appointing a representative under a power of attorney. It therefore remains unclear how they would be able to pay an administrative fine and secure their removal from the registry.

What do lawyers recommend for those at risk?

The law will take effect once it is officially published. Lawyers advise people who could potentially be affected to resolve key property and documentation issues before it comes into force.

In particular, they recommend:

settling matters related to real estate and vehicles in Russia in advance;

obtaining notarized copies of Russian documents;

securing apostilles for school certificates, university diplomas, and civil status documents;

renewing international passports while they can still obtain long-validity documents;

withdrawing funds from Russian bank accounts and deposits;

obtaining apostilled certificates confirming the absence of a criminal record and their driving history.

Once a person is added to the registry, many of these steps would no longer be possible.

exchange

World.title: ‘Unsolved crimes are being passed off as suicides’: Armenian soldier’s death sparks questions
World.content:
Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

A serviceman has died at an Armenian military base. Investigators found the body of 20-year-old conscript Narek Torosyan on July 21. The Investigative Committee released only limited information after the incident. It said authorities had opened a criminal case and launched an investigation.

The committee later charged two of Torosyan’s fellow servicemen with driving him to suicide through negligence. One is a junior sergeant and the other a private. Authorities have placed both men under arrest.

The Ministry of Defence has made no public statement about the soldier’s death. Human rights activists and politicians have condemned the ministry’s silence.

Among them was human rights defender Zhanna Aleksanyan, who regularly raises concerns about human rights violations in the armed forces. She wrote on social media that Defence Minister Suren Papikyan ultimately bears responsibility for the lives of servicemen.

“The minister remains strikingly detached when soldiers die. At the end of each year, he tries to downplay the numbers, but no genuine effort exists to reduce the death toll,” she said.

According to official figures, eight servicemen have died since the beginning of 2026.

What we know so far

Armenian media report that Narek came from the town of Charentsavan and was a fourth-year student at the Russian-Armenian University. He hoped to become a sports journalist. The army drafted him in January 2026. Shortly before the incident, he had gone home on leave and visited his family. Reports also identify Chambarak as his duty station.

Authorities have not disclosed where the incident took place or what exactly happened.

According to a version published by several local media outlets, other servicemen severely beat the soldier before he took his own life.

Charentsavan Mayor Hakob Shahgeldyan also told reporters that, according to the information available to him, Narek had died by suicide. However, the mayor provided no further details.

Comments

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan wrote:

“The Ministry of Defence remains silent about the death of 20-year-old serviceman Narek Torosyan.

The minister has still offered no explanation or clarification. Did he visit the military unit to find out what happened and why? I am certain he did not. He bears responsibility for the life of every serviceman, and he is accountable to both their families and society.

I cannot accept the ‘suicide’ version circulating in the media. Journalists may learn that a serviceman has died, but they cannot know the circumstances of his death. Law enforcement agencies often leak such versions to the press. They later use those same reports to support their own conclusion that it was ‘suicide.’

And in the army, most ‘suicides’ are in fact unsolved murders.”

Tigran Abrahamyan, an opposition MP from the I Have Honour alliance, wrote on social media:

“Soldier Narek Torosyan, who died following the incident at the Chambarak military base, was my student. […]

Narek was a kind, gentle person with outstanding personal qualities. Both students and lecturers respected and cared for him.

Given the sensitivity of the case, I do not want to comment on the different versions or discuss the information available to me.

One thing is clear, however. The state has failed to ensure proper discipline, maintain a healthy psychological environment in military units, and provide effective oversight. That failure ultimately leads to incidents like this.

The authorities must carry out an objective and comprehensive investigation and take steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.”

Mané Tandilyan, founder of the Country to Live party, said:

“Do not say that incidents like this are inevitable in the army. We must not accept such an attitude. After so many losses, it is unacceptable that we continue to lose our young people in peacetime.

How do officers demonstrate accountability? How has violence and cruelty become so deeply rooted among 18- to 20-year-olds that it repeatedly leads to deaths? What is the army doing to foster mutual respect, discipline and responsibility?

What is especially alarming is that intolerance and aggression are becoming increasingly visible in society. And yes, much of the responsibility lies with the country’s top leadership, which speaks to society in a language that fuels division, hostility and hatred. That atmosphere eventually seeps into people’s everyday relationships.

We must overcome this nightmare. Let us each begin with the people around us.”

Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

World.title: Historic home of Abkhaz literary patriarch Dmitry Gulia destroyed in Abkhazia
World.content:
Dmitry Gulia’s dacha destroyed in Abkhazia

An outcry has erupted in Abkhazia after reports emerged that a businessman had seized and demolished historic seaside dachas belonging to Dmitry Gulia, regarded as the patriarch of Abkhaz literature, and Konstantin Simonov, the renowned Soviet writer.

The two properties were located in the coastal settlement of Agudzera. According to reports circulating on social media, the owner of a neighbouring beachfront plot decided to expand his estate by taking over the writers’ properties. The buildings were demolished, and the entire site was levelled with heavy machinery.

The dacha was built in 1957 by the prominent Soviet writer Georgy Gulia for his father, Dmitry Gulia, the founder of Abkhaz literature.

According to Dmitry Gulia’s granddaughter, Tatyana Gulia, he was already elderly and in poor health, and doctors advised him to live by the sea. Dmitry Gulia spent the last three years of his life in the modest single-storey house, which had a veranda and three rooms. He also died there.

Agudzera, Abkhazia. Family members and guests of writer Georgy Gulia at the family dacha, 1970s. Photo from the Gulia House Museum’s Instagram account.

The public outcry forced the Abkhaz authorities to state that “a mistake had been made and there was no threat of the land being seized.”

Next to the Gulia house stood the dacha of another prominent Soviet writer, Konstantin Simonov, who was a close friend of Georgy Gulia. Before his death in 1979, Simonov bequeathed the property to the Gulia family.

During the 1992–93 Georgian-Abkhaz war, both writers’ dachas were looted and partially destroyed. After the war, staff from the Dmitry Gulia Museum helped maintain the two buildings.

Tatyana Gulia discovered that the land had been taken over while visiting the cemetery in Gulripsh, where her grandmother is buried. She wrote on social media:

“We suddenly saw a bulldozer driving across our property, leveling everything to the ground, despite the memorial plaque that had been installed there by the Dmitry Gulia Museum.”

After public outrage mounted, Aslan Ankvab, the head of the Agudzera village administration, called the Gulia family to say that officials had reviewed all the documents and confirmed that both the land and the house remained the property of the Gulia family.

“The remains of the house have been destroyed, but the land itself has been preserved. The authorities have decided to describe what happened as a misunderstanding,” Tatyana Gulia later wrote.
