World.title: The Belarus factor: Belarusians fighting for Ukraine on Lukashenko’s rule, the threat of war and Russian manipulation
World.content:
Belarusians serving in Ukraine’s Armed Forces

Svytiaz / hromadske

How realistic is the prospect of a new Russian offensive launched from Belarusian territory? Would Alexander Lukashenko send the Belarusian army into Ukraine? Should Kyiv strike Belarusian oil refineries that help sustain Russia’s war effort? And what do Belarusians serving in Ukraine’s Armed Forces think?

hromadske spoke with fighters from the Kastus Kalinouski Regiment. One serviceman, who goes by the call sign Hetman, speaks Ukrainian because he comes from a family of ethnic Ukrainians from the Brest region. Three of his comrades speak Belarusian.

The fighters do not disclose their names or any identifying details that could allow the Belarusian authorities to identify them. Their relatives remain in Belarus, where security officers have already carried out searches of their homes, threatened family members and subjected them to questioning.

All of those interviewed know firsthand what Belarusian prisons and pretrial detention centers are like. Some have been held there, while others narrowly avoided imprisonment. For them, joining the Kastus Kalinouski Regiment became a continuation of their struggle against Alexander Lukashenko’s regime.

An hromadske report.

A country of political prisoners

According to a fighter with the call sign Salam, meaningful political and civic activism in Belarus has become virtually impossible because of the regime’s pervasive control.

“Lukashenko seems to have taken inspiration from Orwell’s 1984. Any attempt by people to organize independently is crushed,” he says.

Since 2020, around half a million people have left Belarus. Between 40,000 and 60,000 Belarusians have been subjected to political repression, according to Salam. That has included arbitrary detention, torture, sexual violence and lengthy prison sentences.

According to Salam, people released from prison are often forced into exile. Independent civil society organizations have been dismantled, while independent media outlets have been designated as “extremist organizations.” Even subscribing to an independent Telegram channel, he says, can result in 30 days of detention and torture.

Salam also claims that simply speaking Belarusian in public can lead to punishment, as the authorities may interpret it as an act of political protest.

Salam on the Bakhmut front, 2023. Photo from Salam’s personal archive

According to Algerd, more than 5,000 opponents of the Lukashenko regime have been imprisoned on politically motivated charges. The regiment has also documented around 400 cases of people persecuted for supporting Ukraine. The reasons include donating to Ukraine’s Armed Forces and having links to the Belarusian Hajun monitoring project, which tracked the deployment and movement of Russian troops.

He says prison sentences have become somewhat less severe than they were in 2020 and during the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Even so, those convicted still face terms of 10 to 15 years. People accused of sabotaging railways or taking part in the attack on the Machulishchy air base have received sentences of 20 years or more.

Hetman sums up the situation succinctly: “The screws have been tightened. The authorities control everything—and Russia controls the authorities.”

Algerd near Bakhmut, September 2023. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive

What the Belarusian opposition can do

During the 2020 protests, some Ukrainians mocked the largely peaceful nature of the demonstrations in Belarus. Algerd believes that perception tells only part of the story.

“Television showed you white socks, but not the violent clashes with the security forces,” he says. “In Pinsk, for example, protesters fought back against OMON riot police. Across the country, up to a million people took part in the protests.”

According to Algerd, the Belarusian protest movement unfolded under very different conditions from Ukraine’s Maidan.

“Ukraine had a genuine political opposition and relatively democratic institutions. By 2020, Lukashenko had already consolidated control over the KGB, the army and the rest of the security apparatus,” he says.

In the aftermath of the protests, the regime carried out another sweeping crackdown on its political opponents. Some opposition figures remain behind bars, others have gone into exile, and many have abandoned public political activity altogether.

“Six years have passed since the last mass protests. The Belarusian opposition is fragmented and lacks unity,” Hetman says.

According to Algerd, the Belarusian protest movement unfolded under very different conditions from Ukraine’s Maidan.

“Ukraine had a genuine political opposition and relatively democratic institutions. By 2020, Lukashenko had already consolidated control over the KGB, the army and the rest of the security apparatus,” he says.

In the aftermath of the protests, the regime carried out another sweeping crackdown on its political opponents. Some opposition figures remain behind bars, others have gone into exile, and many have abandoned public political activity altogether.

“Six years have passed since the last mass protests. The Belarusian opposition is fragmented and lacks unity,” Hetman says.

Algerd near Kupiansk, October 2023. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive.

Algerd sees the Belarusian opposition’s value in a different light. In his view, Western governments recognize Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya as the legitimate representative of democratic Belarus, and that international standing should be put to use.

Svytiaz, however, criticizes the Ukrainian authorities for the warm reception Tsikhanouskaya received in Kyiv. He notes that Belarusian volunteers—who have been fighting and suffering losses in Ukraine for years—have never been received at such a high official level.

“In 2020, people voted for Tsikhanouskaya above all because they wanted Lukashenko out. She did not have a fully developed political platform, and it remains unclear what her government would actually look like if she came to power. Yet Ukraine welcomed her at the highest official level, while Belarusian volunteers have never received such recognition. That is a serious miscalculation by the Ukrainian authorities,” Svytiaz says.

In his view, Kyiv should develop a separate strategy for engaging with Belarusian volunteers fighting on Ukraine’s side.

Salam near Zaporizhzhia, 2026. Photo from Salam’s personal archive.

Will the Belarusian army attack Ukraine?

Five years into the war, Ukraine continues to fortify its border with Belarus. Kyiv has not ruled out the possibility that Russia could once again use Belarusian territory to launch an offensive.

Svytiaz believes such a scenario remains possible because “anything can be expected from Moscow.” At the same time, he says Alexander Lukashenko is likely to avoid direct involvement if he can. Yet Belarus’s dependence on the Kremlin means Russia could ultimately force his hand.

Algerd, however, argues that it is not currently in Moscow’s interest to draw Belarus directly into the fighting.

“Russia is already using Belarusian factories to produce and repair military equipment,” he says. “It also tests military hardware there and trains mobilized troops.”

Algerd with fellow soldiers near Kupiansk, December 2023. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive

Salam views the issue primarily through a political lens. In his opinion, direct participation in the war would be politically suicidal for Alexander Lukashenko. For decades, his propaganda has been built around a single promise: that he would keep Belarus out of war.

“In 2015, Lukashenko told Belarusians: If you want a war like the one in Ukraine, vote for the opposition. After Russia’s full-scale invasion, he repeated that the war was the consequence of Ukraine’s pro-European course,” Salam says.

He also argues that in February 2022, Lukashenko believed Russia would quickly defeat Ukraine and capture Kyiv within three days. Today, however, Salam believes he no longer has the same confidence in Russia’s military strength. “That’s why Lukashenko has no desire to join a losing war,” he says.

Algerd on Christmas Eve 2024, Zaporizhzhia front. Photo from Algerd’s personal archive.

The fighters point to three additional factors they believe make direct Belarusian involvement less likely: Vladimir Putin’s distrust of Belarusians, widespread anti-war sentiment within Belarusian society, and the army’s limited combat capability.

According to Algerd, in 2022 Russian commanders did not allow Belarusian doctors to treat wounded Russian soldiers. Instead, medical personnel were brought in from Russia.

He also argues that Putin did not insist on deploying the Belarusian army during the invasion because he understood how limited Lukashenko’s support was inside Belarus.

Salam in the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, April 2022. Photo from Salam’s personal archive

Salam believes that most Belarusians do not want war and are unwilling to fight for Lukashenko. While part of society has embraced Russian propaganda, he argues that the risk of widespread resistance would remain high if Belarus were drawn directly into the conflict.

Hetman offers another reason why Lukashenko may hesitate: arming large numbers of people could ultimately threaten his own rule if those weapons were turned against the regime.

The fighters also give a bleak assessment of the Belarusian military, describing its combat readiness as extremely poor.

Hetman near Pokrovsk. Photo from Hetman’s personal archive

“One out of ten,” Hetman says, rating the Belarusian army’s combat capability on a ten-point scale.

Salam adds that the military has virtually no real combat experience.

Nor, the fighters note, has Ukraine encountered the latest Belarusian weapons that Minsk periodically claims to have developed. It is also unclear whether the Belarusian army is prepared for modern warfare, where drones play a central role on the battlefield.

Belarus is estimated to have a theoretical mobilization reserve of around 400,000 people. Svytiaz, however, doubts that the authorities could actually send them to the front.

“They would either leave the country or protest,” he says. “Forcing them to fight would require another wave of repression. That would be costly and difficult—and Belarusian prisons are already overcrowded.”

Could Ukraine strike Belarus?

Belarusian oil refineries continue to supply petroleum products to Russia. Russian troops use Belarusian military training grounds, and Moscow also relies on Belarusian infrastructure to help guide attack drones toward Ukraine.

That raises the question of whether Ukraine would be justified in targeting such facilities.

Hetman considers Belarus a co-aggressor alongside Russia since 2022. In his view, Ukraine would have the right to strike if Belarusian territory were once again used to launch a ground offensive or missile attacks.

For now, however, he says no such aggression is taking place. As a result, he sees no legal or military justification for Ukrainian strikes on Belarusian oil refineries.

Salam near Zaporizhzhia, 2025. From Salam’s personal archive

Salam also warns against deploying Ukrainian ground forces into Belarus. Such an operation, he argues, would require diverting troops from other sections of the front, while holding captured territory would create major logistical challenges.

He also points to China’s position. Beijing has invested heavily in Belarus and views the country as a key link in its overland trade corridor to Europe. China, he says, has little interest in seeing that route disrupted by war.

At the same time, Salam says Ukraine could justify limited strikes against facilities that directly support Russia’s military operations — for example, communication relay stations used to guide or coordinate drone attacks.

Sviatsiaz believes Ukraine has the technical capability to destroy the oil refineries in Mazyr and Navapolatsk.

But doing so, he argues, would deprive Belarus of fuel for its domestic market and deepen the country’s dependence on Russia. The Kremlin could then use fuel supplies as another lever of pressure on Minsk.

“Ukraine must act wisely,” Sviatsiaz says.

Salam, for his part, hopes Ukrainian strikes on Belarus never become necessary. He does not want to see the war spread onto the territory of his own country.

Fighters from the Kalinouski Regiment in a dugout near Bakhmut, 2022. From Salam’s personal archive.

When could the Kalinouski regiment return to Belarus?

In March 2022, Alhierd was told that the Belarusian unit would fight for Ukraine first. One day, he says, it might also fight for Belarus.

For now, however, he believes such an operation would be pointless. Belarus, in his view, remains firmly under Russia’s control.

He argues that if Moscow is defeated, one condition of any capitulation should be the withdrawal of Russian forces from Belarus. Only then, he says, could Alyaksandr Lukashenka be presented with an ultimatum: hand over power peacefully or face the dismantling of his regime by force. In that scenario, the Kalinouski Regiment could play a role.

Salam identifies two circumstances under which the regiment might enter Belarus. The first would be the outbreak of new mass anti-government protests requiring armed support. The second would be Belarus’s direct entry into the war against Ukraine.

Sviatsiaz says the prospects for a peaceful transfer of power ultimately depend on developments in Russia. Lukashenka’s government, he argues, survives primarily because of Moscow’s backing.

“Belarusians are fighting Russia in Ukraine to weaken it and bring Belarus’s liberation closer,” he says.

Alhierd believes there is little Ukraine can realistically do inside Belarus at this stage. From Alhierd’s personal archive

Why they keep fighting

According to the interviewees, the Kalinouski Regiment has not recorded a single case of unauthorized abandonment of duty. Its fighters, they say, understood exactly what they were signing up for and why they chose to fight.

If a Belarusian volunteer is killed, however, the soldier’s family is not eligible for Ukraine’s standard compensation payment of 15 million hryvnias.

Capture or disappearance creates additional risks. Relatives who remain in Belarus cannot report a missing family member to the authorities or provide DNA samples for identification, as doing so could expose their connection to a volunteer fighting for Ukraine.

Despite those risks, the regiment’s fighters continue to serve. They also raise money to support veterans of the unit, many of whom struggle to obtain state assistance.

“Would I still fight for Ukraine if I received no combat pay and no compensation for being wounded? I think I would. Money does not change the purpose of this struggle. I have a duty to help liberate Ukraine from Russian occupation.

For Belarus, this is of fundamental importance, because it too remains under Russian occupation and must become free,” Hetman says.

He believes many Belarusians take pride in the Kalinouski Regiment’s fighters. If a historic opportunity to return to Belarus ever emerges, he says, the unit would have the backing of a significant share of the country’s population.

This article was produced with the support of the Media Network.

exchange

World.title: Armenian rights lawyer files ECHR complaint over Ruben Vardanyan’s 20-year jail sentence in Baku
World.content:
ECHR complaint over Vardanyan case

Human rights lawyer Siranush Sahakyan has filed a complaint with the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) over the case of Ruben Vardanyan, the former state minister of the former unrecognised Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. She said she would represent Vardanyan before the court. Sahakyan has represented Armenian detainees at the ECHR for many years.

“The application sets out in detail violations of eight articles of the European Convention on Human Rights, supported by comprehensive legal and factual arguments,” Sahakyan said in a statement shared with the media and posted on social media.

Vardanyan is one of 19 Armenians still held in Azerbaijani prisons. In February 2026, a military court in Baku sentenced him to 20 years in prison.

According to Sahakyan, the defence was only recently able to obtain the court’s written judgment, which was required before an application could be submitted to the ECHR. She said Azerbaijan had withheld the ruling until then, which is why the complaint was filed only on 19 July.

The court found Vardanyan guilty of a number of serious offences, including waging war, financing terrorism and deportation.

Armenian rights groups, however, have described the trial in Baku as “political rather than legal”. Vardanyan himself called the proceedings “a farce” and “a mockery of justice”. During the hearings, he instructed his lawyer not to present arguments in his defence.

“It is impossible to protect rights in a system that fundamentally denies the right to a fair trial. That is why Ruben Vardanyan decided to continue his fight for justice through international legal mechanisms,” Sahakyan said.

Details of Vardanyan case

In her statement, Sahakyan disclosed further details of the case. She said the military court in Baku did not read out the full verdict. Now that Vardanyan’s family has passed the written judgment to his lawyers, it has become clear that he was convicted on 41 counts under 21 articles of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code.

According to Sahakyan, the judgment does not substantiate Vardanyan’s personal criminal responsibility with facts or evidence.

“Instead, the court concluded that the ‘criminal organisation’ – the leadership of the self-proclaimed Republic of Artsakh – had been operating in Nagorno-Karabakh since 1988. It also found that Vardanyan joined this ‘organisation’ in December 2020, although he was living in Moscow at the time.”

She also said the court treated Vardanyan’s appointment to a civilian administrative post as a violent seizure of power. His commercial and charitable activities were classified as illegal entrepreneurship and financing terrorism, while his entry into Nagorno-Karabakh via the Lachin Corridor was deemed an illegal crossing of Azerbaijan‘s state border.

Sahakyan said Vardanyan had not appealed against the verdict because he regarded the trial as staged and pre-planned, and considered all domestic legal remedies ineffective.

Background

On 17 February, a military court in Baku sentenced Russian-Armenian businessman, billionaire and philanthropist Ruben Vardanyan to 20 years in prison. His case was heard separately from those of the former leadership of Nagorno-Karabakh.

A month after the verdict, Vardanyan’s family said he had tried to raise concerns with Azerbaijan’s Human Rights Commissioner, Sabina Aliyeva, during a phone call with relatives, but the call was cut off.

The family has repeatedly appealed to the international community, saying that neither Vardanyan nor the other Armenian detainees in Azerbaijan have access to institutional protection. They argue that the country lacks independent human rights protection mechanisms. They have also noted that the International Committee of the Red Cross, which had facilitated contact between detainees and their families, has ceased operations in Azerbaijan.

On 5 February, two weeks before Vardanyan’s sentence was announced, an Azerbaijani court handed life sentences to several other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders, including former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, his deputy Davit Manukyan, former parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and former Foreign Minister Davit Babayan. Former presidents Arkady Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison.

All of the detainees faced a range of serious charges, including terrorism and genocide. Ghukasyan and Sahakyan received lighter sentences because they are over 65, and Azerbaijani law does not allow life imprisonment for people above that age.

Independent media and human rights observers were not allowed to attend the trials. Information about the proceedings was published by Azerbaijani state and pro-government media.

World.title: One minor killed, three injured in shooting in central Tbilisi
World.content:
Shooting in central Tbilisi

Late on July 22, four people, including two minors, were injured in a shooting on Vera, a central street in Tbilisi. All were taken to hospital. One of the minors died shortly after being admitted, Irakli Pirtskhalaishvili, a doctor at the clinic, told reporters.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry confirmed the incident, saying one person had been arrested in connection with it. The suspect has been charged with using a firearm and wounding four people.

He attempted to flee the scene but was detained after a police chase. According to the ministry, the suspect resisted arrest with a weapon and “sustained finger injuries during the arrest.”

The investigation is being conducted under Articles 19 and 109 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (attempted murder), which carry a penalty of up to 20 years in prison or life imprisonment.

Many witnesses to the shooting: what they say

The shooting took place in central Tbilisi, at the intersection of Akaki Shanidze and Akaki Khorava streets. The area was crowded at the time of the incident.

Eyewitness Elene Koridze wrote on social media that three young men sitting in a car “were shot simply because they were laughing.”

“About an hour ago, right outside my home, a man opened fire on three 17- and 18-year-old boys sitting in a car simply because they were laughing. He then also shot a woman who was nearby. He was quickly apprehended.

It was clear this was neither a premeditated attack nor an act of personal revenge. This is not just an isolated serious crime to which the police responded quickly, but a direct reflection of the reality we live in,” Koridze wrote.

Another eyewitness, Tiko Kvaliashvili, said:

“I was walking home when I saw a crowd on Shanidze Street and went over. Two patrol cars arrived, people started shouting, and someone was running. One boy was unconscious in the car, while two others were in shock. I gave them first aid as best I could. One had been shot in the arm, the other in the shoulder. I don’t know why they were shot.”

The son of journalist Eka Kvesitadze also witnessed the incident. She said it happened near their home while her son was out walking the dog.

“Someone had shot several minors. They were lying there covered in blood,” another witness wrote.

Witnesses also told reporters that a nearby parked red Alfa Romeo had around a dozen bullet holes.

As of now, Interior Ministry has not released any additional details.

World.title: Pro-EU protester Onise Okriashvili attacked in Tbilisi after disinformation campaign
World.content:
Georgia protester Onise Okriashvili beaten

Stand-up comedian Onise Okriashvili, an active participant in Georgia’s pro-European protests that have been ongoing for nearly two years, was brutally beaten by three people late on July 22 outside his home in Tbilisi’s Vake district.

Before the attack, Okriashvili had become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government media. Based on the context of the attack, this appears to have been the reason behind the assault.

A video of the attack, recorded by eyewitnesses, has spread on social media.

The footage shows three young men brutally beating Onise. “You insulted Nodar Dumbadze (a classic of Georgian literature), how dare you, bastard?” the attackers are heard saying to him.

Onise Okriashvili can be heard calling for help. Several people are nearby, but they do not dare approach him. The desperate screams of a woman trying to stop the attackers can also be heard.

Who is Onise Okriashvili and why did he become a target of propaganda?

Onise Okriashvili is known for his criticism of the ruling Georgian Dream party on social media. He also regularly organises solo protests aimed at drawing public attention — appearing with relevant posters in places where large numbers of people gather, including on public transport.

“Only their children study in Europe” — reads the sign held by Onise Okriashvili during one of his solo protests. Photo from the activist’s social media page

In recent days, the activist has become the target of a disinformation campaign by pro-government TV channels. They have repeatedly aired a fragment from a comedy show Punchline Therapy, in which he uses a vulgar expression while referring to Nodar Dumbadze, a classic of Georgian literature.

The fragment was shown without context, making it appear as if Okriashvili was directly insulting the writer.

On July 19, the comedian recorded a video in which he said:

“I apologise that in this video I am not talking about more important events in the country. Young people my age are dying every day because of drug use; there are political prisoners in the country; emigration is sharply increasing, and these emigrants have been deprived of the right to vote in elections, along with many other problems.

But for the third day now, Georgian Dream’s propaganda machine has been using all its resources to turn people against me. Here is an example of the video they are using to try to discredit me.“

The conversation in the video excerpt goes:

‘Is there someone you cannot stand?’ ‘What if I say Nodar Dumbadze? (vulgar expression) I will only name our government, no one else.’

“During a performance, we speak hypothetically and can say the most absurd thing that comes to mind at that moment.

This video clearly shows that I am, of course, not insulting (Nodar Dumbadze), but speaking only hypothetically, deliberately using the most absurd example that came to mind at that moment. Comedy often works exactly this way — it uses unexpected twists. That is why the audience laughs at that moment.”

“Just today we were discussing filing a lawsuit against the propaganda media for spreading defamatory claims, and today Onise was attacked,” his wife, Mariam Samushia, told journalists.

She said she heard shouting in the street in the evening. Since Onise had become a target of a propaganda campaign in recent days, she called him to warn him. Only later did she realise that her husband had been attacked.

“This is artificially created hatred,” she said.

The Interior Ministry said a criminal case had been opened over the attack on Onise Okriashvili under Article 126 of Georgia’s Criminal Code (violence). According to reports, one of the attackers has been taken to a police station and is being questioned.

News in Georgia

World.title: Chechnya’s recruitment machine: How Kadyrov sustains his forces by enlisting civilians
World.content:
Kadyrov’s Forces in Ukraine

An investigation by Novaya Gazeta Europe shows how the war has reshaped the system of power in Chechnya.

Ramzan Kadyrov has significantly expanded the number of armed units under his control. But his most loyal formations are largely kept away from the front lines.

Instead, combat losses are replenished with ordinary residents of the republic, who are often pressured into signing military contracts.

For the investigation, journalists interviewed 178 Chechen families who lost relatives in the war, as well as current and former servicemen. Their reporting examines how Chechnya’s recruitment system operates and reveals the true scale of its wartime losses.

Kadyrov’s forces

Over the course of the war, five new regiments and five battalions have been established in Chechnya. Formally, they are part of Russia’s Defense Ministry and the National Guard. In practice, however, Kadyrov determines key personnel appointments, where the units are deployed and how extensively they are involved in combat.

According to figures provided by Kadyrov, the number of security personnel in Chechnya has grown from 4,800 in 2003 to 36,243 today. At the start of 2022, before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, those forces numbered roughly 16,000 to 18,000. That means Chechnya’s security apparatus has approximately doubled in size over the course of the three-year war.

The human rights group Memorial argues that the expansion amounts to the strengthening of Kadyrov’s personal army. But a source in Chechnya’s regional office of the Federal Security Service offered a different explanation. According to the source, Kadyrov became trapped by the image of being “Putin’s chief foot soldier.” While he continued to create new units, he also sought to shield his most loyal security personnel from frontline combat.

At first, the authorities attracted recruits with high salaries. They then began actively recruiting people from other parts of Russia. Later, military service was opened to unemployed residents of Chechnya. As the flow of volunteers dwindled, the authorities increasingly turned to coercion.

The safe rear ended in the Kursk region

In 2023, Kadyrov secured the deployment of several Chechen units to the Russian border regions of Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod. At the time, these areas were considered relatively safe rear positions, allowing Kadyrov’s forces to be pulled back from the most intense sections of the front.

That changed on Aug. 6, 2024, when Ukrainian troops crossed into the Kursk region. The Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment, which had been guarding the border, offered little visible resistance. Its personnel abandoned their positions, and some were surrounded and taken prisoner.

The border regions subsequently became the scene of heavy fighting involving the Akhmat special forces, the West Akhmat Battalion and the Akhmat-Chechnya Regiment. One Akhmat commander claimed that Apti Alaudinov’s unit alone suffered more than 1,500 killed and wounded.

Security forces are shielded, civilians sent to the front

After the fighting in the Kursk region, Kadyrov moved to reduce the involvement of key National Guard units in the war. Much of the burden was shifted instead to formations under Russia’s Defense Ministry.

Sources interviewed by the publication say the decision was driven by the need to preserve the foundations of Kadyrov’s rule. His grip on power depends on the loyalty of the republic’s security forces. A prolonged war depletes that resource faster than the Chechen leadership can replace it.

A telling example is the National Guard’s Baysangur Benoevsky Battalion. It is overseen by Adam Kadyrov, the 18-year-old son and presumed heir of the Chechen leader. The battalion has been equipped with modern weapons, its own training ground and a well-funded infrastructure. Its personnel signed contracts that предусматривают service in the war. Yet the unit has remained almost entirely in Chechnya, where it focuses on training.

Another National Guard unit, the Sheikh Mansur Battalion, was deployed to the front in December 2023 and has been engaged in combat ever since.

According to the investigation, the Baysangur Battalion is effectively financed with federal funds allocated for the war while serving as the Kadyrov family’s personal security reserve.

Coerced recruitment

Since the autumn of 2024, the Chechen authorities have carried out a large-scale campaign of forced recruitment. Kadyrov publicly proposed sending what he called “troubled youth” to the front. District police departments were then assigned monthly recruitment quotas of between 25 and 50 people.

Those detained are taken to collection centers in Sernovodsk and at the Khankala military base. According to testimonies from recruits and their relatives, they are held under guard, given inadequate food and receive little to no military training. Some are sent without proper uniforms or equipment, receiving weapons only after they reach the front.

People can be sent to the front for reasons as minor as a street fight, a traffic violation, driving without insurance, tinted car windows or unpaid utility bills. Others are detained for subscribing to opposition channels or for political posts found on their phones. In some cases, relatives are offered the chance to pay for a detainee’s release or to find other “volunteers” to take their place.

According to the journalists’ estimates, 67 such raids were carried out across Chechnya between October 2024 and May 2025.

Hidden casualties

The Chechen authorities prohibit the publication of information about those killed in the war. Families are often instructed to bury relatives at night and to forgo the traditional multi-day mourning rituals. As a result, publicly available casualty lists capture only a fraction of the true death toll.

Officially, around 500 residents of Chechnya have been confirmed killed. But a source in the republic’s government told the investigators that more than 2,300 deaths have been verified internally. Another roughly 1,000 people are listed as missing in action.

Of the 183 fatalities documented by the journalists, 113 were sent to the war after October 2024. Of those, 97 had signed military contracts under coercion. The average time between deployment and death was about two months. Only 84 of the 178 families interviewed were able to recover and bury the bodies of their relatives.

The investigation identifies a fundamental shift in Kadyrov’s approach. At the start of the war, he deployed members of the security forces while portraying those forcibly recruited as volunteers. Now, his most loyal units are kept inside Chechnya, while civilians are openly treated as expendable manpower.

The authors argue that this marks a troubling precedent. Repressive practices first tested in Chechnya have often, over time, spread to the rest of Russia.

World.title: Origin breach could fuel wave of AI-powered scams, cyber experts warn
World.content:
Personal details stolen in the Origin Energy data breach could give scammers the opportunity to launch highly targeted attacks, cyber security experts warn, with artificial intelligence (AI) making it easier to impersonate victims, clone voices and build detailed personal profiles.

They say the information could be used to create convincing phishing emails, phone calls and text messages, pass identity checks for online accounts, and help criminals impersonate victims to authorise fraudulent transactions.

The warning comes after Origin confirmed on Thursday there had been unauthorised access to and disclosure of some customers's data.

Origin Energy confirms hack Energy company Origin has confirmed that there has been unauthorised access and disclosure of some customers' data, a day after it announced it was investigating a "potential" breach.

The information included names, dates of birth, phone numbers, home addresses and email addresses, as well as the last four digits of some credit cards and the last three digits of some bank account numbers.

Origin is Australia's largest energy retailer with more than 4.8 million customers. The company said it was still working to determine the total number of people affected and would notify impacted customers once their details had been confirmed.

While there is no indication full payment card details were compromised, experts say the stolen information remains highly valuable and are urging affected customers to remain cautious about unsolicited emails, text messages and phone calls long after the breach.

Scams pretending to help you

Professor Richard Buckler, a cyber security expert at the University of New South Wales (UNSW), said the greatest risk for most customers is not the breach itself, but opportunistic scammers exploiting anxiety surrounding the breach.

"The secondary attacks tend to catch more people than the original attack and cause more damage," he said.

"They can appear to be trying to help you ... 'Your data's been stolen, just verify yourself to us and we'll fix it for you' or ask you to log into a website."

His advice was for customers to "be alert but not alarmed" and avoid clicking links in unsolicited emails or text messages.

This fake Netflix email is an example of a phishing scam. Experts warn criminals could use stolen Origin customer data to create even more convincing messages. (Supplied: consumer.ftc.gov)

Rahat Masood, a senior lecturer in cyber security at UNSW's School of Computer Science and Engineering, said criminals no longer needed bank details to launch convincing attacks.

"People think data is only sensitive if it includes credit card details or bank details," she said. "But that's not the case anymore."

The anatomy of a phishing scam Phishing is the most commonly reported scam in Australia, with scammers harvesting tens of millions of dollars every year from unsuspecting victims.

Dr Masood said names, phone numbers, email addresses and home addresses could be combined with information from social media and other public sources to create highly personalised phishing emails, text messages and phone calls.

"They can actually build a whole lot of scenarios where they ... pretend to be a friend, family member or bank representative, asking you to share sensitive information, make a transaction or transfer money."

She said AI had dramatically accelerated that process, allowing criminals to rapidly search public information, build detailed profiles of victims and generate personalised scam messages "in seconds".

"If they know your profile, they can send you a very promising job link or pretend to be someone you trust," Dr Masood said.

"And you never know what's behind that link. It could be malware and lead to further breaches."

Identity theft in the AI era

Professor Daswin De Silva, director of the Centre for Data Analytics and Cognition at La Trobe University, said if the combination of personal information is exposed, then the breach could also allow criminals to impersonate customers and bypass some identity checks.

"The last four digits of a credit card are often used to verify someone's identity," he said.

"Cyber criminals can now use this information to launch impersonation attacks by pretending to be Origin customers."

Professor De Silva said many online retailers already stored customers' payment details, meaning criminals might only need enough information to satisfy identity checks before attempting purchases.

"You don't always need the full card number," he said.

"Some organisations authenticate customers using the last four digits before allowing a transaction."

Richard Buckler says fraudulent Origin utility bills could be used as proof of identity, increasing the risk of identity theft after the breach. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

He said the stolen information could also be merged with data from previous breaches, such as the Qantas cyber attack, allowing AI tools to rapidly build increasingly detailed profiles of victims.

"Once this information is out there, it tends to stay out there," he said.

" What usually happens is the data ends up on the dark web, then it gets traded, and given the richness of the [Origin] data, this would probably attract a lot of interest. "

Qantas customers' data leaked to dark web after cyber attack Hackers have released personal data from Qantas customers onto the dark web, following a cyber attack in July.

Professor Buckler said one aspect of the breach that concerned him was Origin's ability to issue utility bills, which can be used as proof of identity.

"If there's enough information to make a bill look legitimate, people with disinformation could print bills that appear to come from Origin," he said.

"That counts for 20 points under Australia's 100-point identity check, so there's potentially slightly more risk of identity theft in this case."

Dr Masood said AI had also lowered the barrier for more sophisticated impersonation scams.

"If you have a video online or you've spoken publicly, they can use five or 10 seconds of your voice and clone it," she said.

"They can then send a WhatsApp voice message or make a phone call pretending to be you. With AI, they can do almost anything now."

How to protect yourself

All three cyber security experts say affected customers should remain cautious in the weeks and months ahead, warning scammers are likely to exploit public awareness of the breach.

World.title: Interest rates don't just hit households. Small business is feeling the pinch
World.content:
Nestled between Longreach and Yeppoon in central Queensland's vast red expanses sits the hamlet of Barcaldine.

Tourists are drawn to the Garden City of the West because of its historic roots at the start of the Labor movement and its lush, leafy streets drinking from the Great Artesian Basin below.

Jeff Bowman owns the local tourist shop and cafe and says when war broke out a world away in Iran in March, they seriously considered closing up shop for the entire six-month dry season.

Jeff and Kerry-Ann Bowman run retail stores Barcaldine and Beyond and Barcaldine Country Rumours. (Supplied)

With petrol prices skyrocketing, he said the "fear factor" kept tourists away, who grimaced at the hours-long road journey to take in the region's vistas.

"As soon as they mentioned the word fuel rationing [tourism] completely stopped. It was just phenomenal. People were frightened," he said.

"We were 42 per cent down, which is quite dramatic for us."

Mr Bowman is one of the many small and medium business owners around the country bracing for the end of the fuel excise in August and worried what the re-escalation of hostilities in the Middle East will mean for their business.

For the small operation, it is not just the loss of income that has hit them; it is also the rise in costs, including electricity to run cafe equipment and, most importantly, freight to their remote location.

How much will fuel prices increase? With the price of oil rising and the fuel excise cut due to end, drivers are facing twin threats when it comes to the price of fuel.

"We cannot buy from [some suppliers] because of the freight costs," he said.

It has been a particularly tough year for small to medium-sized enterprises around the country with a combination of oil prices, interest rates and inflation all twisting the screws on operators.

That has been on top of new or imminent regulatory reforms like payday super, changes to credit card surcharges and wage decisions like the abolition of junior pay rates.

It comes as consumer sentiment tanks and businesses deal with the usual bill increases such as rents and wages.

Small bank lender signals SME stress

Fears about the plight of small businesses came to a head in June with a profit downgrade from small-to-medium enterprise lender Judo Bank.

It was on the back of three troubled loans adding up to about $75 million, including one to a Sydney window manufacturer, a Canberra financial planner and a Victorian construction industry business.

Judo Bank specialises in lending to small to medium-sized businesses. (Supplied)

Insiders told the ABC each of the three loans had unique issues, but the profit downgrade and needing to put $20 million aside to cover the bad debts was enough to worry the market.

Judo's shares dived 46 per cent, wiping $700 million off its share market valuation in minutes.

Credit agency Equifax said overall the SME sector is resilient, but there are pockets of distress.

Small businesses struggling amid rising costs Small businesses struggling with rising costs say a recent wage increase was the final straw.

While starting from a low base, small business insolvency rates are starting to tick upward with a 13 per cent increase in the number of businesses going bust in the six months to May 2026 compared to the same period last year.

More businesses are also pulling up stumps, with business exit rates up 37 per cent in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the same quarter in 2025.

And businesses are taking longer to pay suppliers, with the number of firms taking 31–60 days to pay growing to 9.5 per cent in May 2026 compared with 8.3 per cent at the same time last year.

Credit shopping is up

Equifax's Brad Walters says there has been an increase in credit shopping among high-risk small to medium businesses, meaning owners are having trouble getting loans.

Brad Walters says there are pockets of distress in the small business sector. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

This includes businesses in the construction, manufacturing, transport and logistics industries, or those with low liquidity.

"For the high-risk small business community we've seen that trending up, and that's now at four times the rate that it is for their low-risk counterparts. That's really problematic," he said.

"It can signify those businesses are approaching multiple funders or credit providers at the same time and can signal that they're finding it difficult to get ready access to finance," Mr Walters said.

Small businesses were also moving away from plans to expand, particularly in Victoria.

"For smaller businesses we're actually seeing a flat line of their credit appetite. In fact, we're seeing a bit of a pullback in their interest around growth capital," he said.

"That's really a reflection of their cautiousness in the current market, but also their concern around immediate cash flow given the pressures they're facing."

Interest rates hurt businesses too

For Victorian steel manufacturer Solidity, it is interest rate rises that really test their mettle.

The company makes helical piles, also known as screw piles, which are part of the foundation systems in residential and commercial builds, and even transmission and renewable energy projects.

Steel manufacturer Solidity says it has a large bank loan and every interest rate rise hurts. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"We're a debt company business so we have a pretty significant bank loan that allows us to operate the business, and that's at a variable rate," managing director Brodie Houghton said.

" Every time the RBA increases the interest rate our cost of business increases pretty significantly. "

Solidity employs about 40 people, and its construction division also feels the impact of fuel price rises.

"During April, when fuel pricing was at its highest, we saw an increase to the base cost of running that part of the business [by] about 30 per cent," he said.

They are about to expand to a much larger site, but Mr Houghton said any support to SMEs like his was missing the mark.

Solidity makes screw pile shafts and employs around 40 people. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

The rising price of steel is adding to costs at the same time as competition with cheap overseas imports heats up.

"We've seen steel price increases about 4 per cent every two months," he said.

"There's imported fabricated products coming into Australia at between 15 to 50 per cent lower prices than the lowest local bid."

He said the loan rules for the government's Economic Resilience Program (ERP) were too tight and his company does not get priority on state-run building projects.

The ERP was announced to give businesses access to zero interest loans to help those impacted by the fuel shock and other market disruptions.

"We're really expecting there's going to be a real pinch over the coming months," he said.

" The current period right now, it feels a lot like 2020. There's a lot of uncertainty. "

Instant asset write-off help

Council of Small Business Organisations of Australia chief executive Skye Cappuccio said there were things the government could do, like raising the tax threshold for the instant asset write-off.

Skye Cappuccio would like more federal government support for SME owners. (ABC News: Timothy Sweeney)

"Currently the threshold for that for small businesses to access is set at $20,000, where we know that to really support small businesses to invest in the equipment and the tools that they really need to drive their productivity it needs to be much higher," she said.

"Small businesses across the country are resilient, but times are tight and the pressures are really high. A lot depends on what happens over the next six months."

Small Business Minister Anne Aly said in a statement the government was offering practical support including tax breaks, removing nuisance tariffs and free access to mandatory standards.

"We're delivering over $3.8 billion in new measures that lower taxes for businesses and start ups," she said.

Payday superannuation changes Payday super takes effect from next week, but some businesses are still unaware of the changes.

She said reforms like payday super would benefit everyone, including 8.9 million workers, and made payroll management smoother with fewer liabilities accruing.

"Good workers are critical to any successful business, and fair wages and super help businesses attract and retain the people they need," Ms Aly said.

Jeff Bowman said he would just like to see remote businesses given more support to overcome the tyranny of distance.

"We'd just like to be considered more. We need tourism in outback Queensland to continue growing," he said.

World.title: Gippsland CFA volunteers seek compensation as cancer cluster cases grow
World.content:
For decades, the Nar Nar Goon Fire Brigade in Victoria's south-east has answered the call during some of the state's biggest fires.

Now, the brigade is facing a battle of its own, with growing concerns about its members' health and the future of its aging station.

According to its captain, Justin Seddon, the brigade had recorded 22 cancer cases among long-serving members, including three deaths.

In January this year, he sent a letter detailing the brigade's cancer cases to state ministers, including State Emergency Services Minister Vicki Ward, and Eastern Victoria MP Harriet Shing.

He said since then the number of cases had grown.

The letter sent by the Nar Nar Goon brigade to state ministers in January 2026. (Supplied)

"This isn't new … the only new thing that comes is the list keeps getting longer," Mr Seddon said.

"Every single one of those people on that list is a volunteer. They've given up their own time to go and support their community."

Mr Seddon said the cause of the cancer cluster remained unknown.

"Is it the exposure to the types of fires we're going to?" he said.

"Is it something local to here? We're just not sure what that is.

" I don't want to see another member get sick here at Nar Nar Goon. "

Seven of the brigade members who have experienced cancer were not covered by the state's presumptive rights legislation. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Compensation 'minefield'

Although compensation for firefighters diagnosed with cancer exists, almost half of the brigade's 22 members fighting cancer, past and present, do not meet the eligibility requirements.

State presumptive rights legislation recognises certain cancers as being linked to firefighting, relieving firefighters of having to prove their illness was caused by their work.

In Victoria, presumptive protections only apply to people with specific types of cancer, who have a certain role, who meet a certain length of service, who received their cancer diagnosis on or after June 1, 2016 and apply for compensation within 10 years of stopping volunteering.

Mr Seddon said "gaps" in the legislation leave some members to navigate a "minefield" of administrative work, all while dealing with the stress of cancer.

"[Members who aren't covered have] got to go through different avenues to try and get support, and that can be quite difficult," Mr Seddon said.

"Anyone who puts the uniform on should be covered."

A firefighter's personal battle

Kevin Chisholm has been a volunteer firefighter for more than 40 years. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Kevin Chisholm is a volunteer at the brigade and has been with the Country Fire Authority (CFA) for more than 40 years.

He was diagnosed with aggressive prostate cancer shortly after his 70th birthday last year.

Mr Chisholm underwent surgery, but the cancer spread to other parts of his body, requiring six weeks of radiation treatment, five days a week.

His daughter, Carlie Chisholm, said he was supported through the WorkCover process by the brigade, but the paperwork, appointments and administrative tasks added another layer of stress during an already difficult time.

Ms Chisholm, a registered nurse and CFA volunteer firefighter of more than 20 years, said the diagnosis had taken a heavy toll on the family.

"His normalcy is taken away from him," she said.

"It's logistically a bit of a nightmare, but you get through it."

Carlie Chisholm says her dad's cancer diagnosis took a toll on the family. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Mr Chisholm qualified for compensation under Victoria's presumptive rights legislation and said he was grateful the support existed.

But Mr Chisholm said Victoria's laws should be expanded for other members.

Other jurisdictions have broader protections for firefighters, and Mr Chisholm said frontline volunteers deserved consistent support.

"We serve in the community, the minimum thing would be, we get looked after," he said.

Barriers to compensation

Ross Sottile, a lawyer at Maurice Blackburn, said proving a link between firefighting exposure and cancer without presumptive coverage placed a significant legal and medical burden on sick firefighters.

Lawyer Ross Sottile says many firefighters face a significant legal and medical burden if they are not covered by presumptive legislation. (Supplied)

"Cancer does not observe legislative boundaries.

"They're receiving chemo, and they're also fighting a WorkCover claim to try and just get basic entitlements," he said.

"They're dealing with the financial stress of having no income coming in."

Advocate calls for expansion of presumptive legislation

Tracie Lund, a former councillor and emergency services advocate, is pushing for the laws to be expanded.

Fighting a battle on two fronts This CFA worker helped battle fires for 25 years before facing the biggest battle of his life.

"Exposure doesn't discriminate, and we shouldn't be discriminating based on roles and cancers either," she said.

Ms Lund became an advocate after her husband Simon's experience navigating the system following his terminal cancer diagnosis.

"One of the mantras that you hear a lot through emergency services is, 'We work as one,'" Ms Lund said.

" But they're not covered as one, they're not seen as equal under the legislation. "

Ms Lund is Labor's candidate for the seat of Morwell in the upcoming state election.

A Victorian government spokesperson said the government has expanded the scheme since the legislation was introduced and is "always [looking] at ways to further prioritise firefighter health and safety".

Tip of the iceberg

For Mr Seddon, gaps in presumptive legislation were only part of a larger issue in the lack of support for firefighters at the brigade.

He pointed to an aging station with only one toilet for 35 members, no showers to wash off carcinogens, trucks that could not fit properly in the building, and a meeting room too small for the entire brigade.

He said the brigade has had to spend thousands of dollars of its own funds on measures to reduce risks, but moving into a new building was key.

The CFA said it had taken all necessary steps to confirm that the existing station was safe.

The Nar Nar Goon CFA brigade hopes to be moved to a new facility. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

In this year's state budget, money was allocated to acquire land for a new brigade building, but Mr Seddon said there had been no timeline on when this would happen.

"What we need is money to build the fire station and get us out of here," he said.

The ABC understands the CFA has identified two prospective sites which are currently undergoing suitability checks.

Mr Seddon said he wondered whether growing health issues in his brigade could be widespread.

"There's 1,200 CFA brigades out there," he said.

"Are we just the tip of the iceberg?"

World.title: How China won the car wars
World.content:
In June, China sounded an ominous warning to its global rivals on, of all places, the Melbourne docks.

Decked out in shiny red and white livery, an impressive-looking, purpose-built LNG-powered bulk carrier pulled into the Port of Melbourne on its first voyage to Australia.

On board the BYD Zhengzhou was a cargo of 5,000 newly built electric vehicles.

The largest-ever single EV shipment to Australia illustrated a changing of the guard in the automobile industry, here and globally.

Australia acts is something of an international auto industry litmus test.

With no domestic industry since its demise a decade ago and little in the way of trade barriers, Australia has become a valuable gauge of consumer taste for an industry in the midst of its greatest upheaval in more than a century.

The BYD Zhengzhou, seen here in 2025, sends a message to the auto industry. (Facebook: BYD Malaysia)

The shipment came after a period of lingering pandemic-era disruptions that left frustrated customers waiting more than a year for new cars.

Momentum for EVs was building, with Tesla in the driver's seat, but Australians had remained sceptical about the design and build quality of Chinese-made automobiles.

That's no longer the case.

In the space of just a year, BYD, the Chinese automobile giant, has quickly narrowed the sales gap with leader Toyota, and is on the cusp of becoming the country's most popular vehicle brand.

"I'm driving one right now," says Riz Akhtar, the founder of research group carloop, mid-journey from Bendigo to Melbourne.

"It costs around $40,000. It's quiet, it's comfortable, drives well and is loaded with technology."

The equivalent Japanese or European built vehicle would be more than 25 per cent more expensive, he says.

" Consumers aren't stupid. They're not going to spend money they don't need to. "

From green warriors to cost worries

In the decades following World War II, Australians drove locally made American cars.

General Motors, Ford and Chrysler dominated the field with high-end European vehicles holding the luxury end.

And then Japanese cars, led by Toyota, captured the Australian passenger car market.

Toyota and Mazda still stand tall over the Australian motoring landscape when measured by total sales.

But their positions are crumbling, with both losing ground as Chinese EVs — cheap and loaded with technology — bound ahead.

China's EV domination In China, you can swap an empty electric vehicle battery in about four minutes. It is part of how China has come to dominate the EV industry.

Spurred on by the onset of a once-in-a-generation fuel crisis, there is now a sudden widespread consumer acceptance of battery-powered vehicles, here and elsewhere.

But the world's automobile establishment has been caught napping.

Japan, Europe and especially America have dabbled with the new technology, mistakenly believing they could slowly transition towards an electric future.

In America's case, it has reversed course back to its gas guzzling past, a decision that threatens to undermine its long-term future.

A quick look at the most recent Australian sales figures illustrates the undeniable trend.

In the first half this year, sales for every major Japanese auto manufacturer bar Honda sank.

Mazda shed 17 per cent compared with the same period last year, Toyota was down 21 per cent, Subaru and Mitsubishi dropped 25 per cent each and Nissan was off 32 per cent.

Each of the Chinese suppliers, meanwhile, notched up spectacular gains.

All were off a much smaller base, which exaggerates the percentage gain. But there's no denying the trend.

BYDs from the consignment of 5,000 delivered to Melbourne. (ABC News: Lachlan Bennett)

BYD sales jumped 124 per cent, Chery leapt 77 per cent and Geely soared 495 per cent.

The dramatic decline in Japanese vehicle domination has been coupled with a sudden shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars.

Last month, almost a quarter of all cars sold in Australia were fully electric. A year ago, it was just 7 per cent. Add in hybrids, and EVs are now neck and neck with petrol and diesel fuelled automobiles.

According to Pitcher Partners' Steve Bragg, the Iran war has helped shift the dial.

"Five years ago, most people who wanted to drive an EV were doing it for environmental reasons," he says.

"Now it's financial reasons."

Japan, South Korea and Europe roll over

The global auto industry is suddenly in a panic.

Toyota vice-chairman Koji Sato has called for greater cooperation between Japanese producers in a desperate bid to streamline production and lower costs.

"Unless things change, we will not survive," he told an annual supplier meeting in March.

But it's too little too late, according to Akhtar, especially in Australia.

"They have no product in the pipeline," he says.

Most Japanese manufacturers, he explains, are scrambling to deliver EVs, but most of the new models are underpinned by Chinese manufacturers and components and, some cases, are simply rebadged Chinese-made cars.

"Japan had the lead on EVs," he says.

"The very first EV I drove was a Mitsubishi i-MiEV back in 2010, but they lost that lead because they were too busy propping up their internal combustion engine cars, hybrids and hydrogen-fuelled models."

In Europe, meanwhile, Volkswagen chief Oliver Blume has foreshadowed staff lay-offs of up to 100,000 workers after years of turmoil which has seen VW drop the ball on technology.

VW's share price has halved since his predecessor was brutally axed four years ago as it strains under the weight of Donald Trump's tariffs and China's rapid march to auto industry dominance.

That's prompted asset sales and massive new investments in China with VW determined to produce cars for the hotly contested Chinese market.

China's EV dominance is no accident.

Loading...

It forged a strategic policy as far back as 2000, poured cash and financial incentives into the project in 2009 and encouraged battery firms such as BYD and others to shift into automobiles.

Driving the initiative was a desire to reduce China's reliance on imported oil, which made it captive to foreign powers, and reduce pollution.

It simultaneously embarked on a strategy of dominating the refining and production of almost all industrial metals.

In addition to steel, China dominates minerals crucial to battery production, such as lithium, cobalt, manganese and graphite. And it churns out almost all the world's anode and cathode production.

South Korea once went head to head with China on batteries but concentrated on the more expensive nickel-magnesium-cobalt option while China opted for the cheaper lithium-iron-phosphate version.

China won.

Loading...

It now accounts for 90 per cent of the world's battery production, giving Chinese auto producers a competitive edge.

But like many of its programs, China's EV strategy has been almost too successful. It now produces far more cars than it can consume, which has tightened profit margins at home and forced producers to aggressively shift into export markets.

Tariffs bring the Detroit Three undone

The opening line read: "Well, this is awkward."

The review on specialist website MotorTrend was for a spanking new American built EV, a van from Detroit Big Three stalwart Chevrolet, which appeared late last year.

The magazine delivered thumbs up all round for the machine.

There was just one problem.

According to a New York Times investigation into the demise of American-built EVs under the Trump administration, in the fortnight between the time the marketing team had dropped the van off for review and its publication, the BrightDrop had been binned.

Major manufacturers that scrapped EV projects have taken a bath. "2026e" denotes BloombergNEF's forecast for this year. (BloombergNEF)

It wasn't the only one.

In the past two years, Ford, Buick, Dodge, Jeep, Honda, Nissan and Acura have scrapped a series of US-built SUVs, pick-ups and passenger cars. Volvo junked an entire all electric line-up.

The Trump government's removal of Biden-era tax credits and tailpipe emissions standards are the root cause. Almost all have retreated back to thirsty ICE pick-ups and SUVs.

US pulls back from buying EVs as rest of the world accelerates High petrol prices are driving EV sales around the world, with the leading international authority predicting 30 per cent of all new cars sold this year will be electric.

The losses were staggering. The write-downs on the scrapped projects cost between the Detroit Three close to $US50 billion.

And while the Trump administration's tariffs have built a protective wall around the US auto industry, helping juice margins and boosting profits, they've cordoned off the rapidly evolving electric revolution and stifled domestic innovation.

"America is now sandwiched since both Mexico and Canada have relaxed tariffs and are importing Chinese made EVs," Akhtar says.

That's made cars on either side of the border significantly cheaper than in the US.

In the mid-'60s, American auto manufacturers accounted for about 95 per cent of all cars sold around the world. By 2015, that had shrunk to less than half as Japan ate into market share.

All indications are that EV production and demand has suddenly reached a global tipping point, as witnessed in Australia.

But America has all but abandoned them, now building less than 5 per cent of global EVs, while China accounts for more than 75 per cent.

Given the pioneering role that Elon Musk's Tesla played in building high-end EVs, the shift has been nothing short of remarkable.

Tesla still holds an exalted place in the world of electric cars. But the technological edge that stood it apart from the competition is narrowing, while the cost of buying one has widened considerably.

World.title: Charli xcx follows Brat with her most reflective album yet
World.content:
Charli xcx isn't afraid to turn the lens on herself, bringing her existence as an artist, performer and human into sharp focus.

But on her new album Music, Fashion, Film, her gaze extends beyond her own image. Instead, the British artist dissects and discusses the enduring legacy of art and artists, and how creative figures are remembered long after their moment has passed.

The 33-year-old star has been inescapable for the past few years. After a lauded performance at the 2023 Coachella Festival, she then dabbled in composing for films, including Bottoms, Bodies Bodies Bodies, and Barbie.

Loading Instagram content

Then came Brat summer.

Her seventh album Brat would see Charli become a household name.

She broke audience records at the taste-making Boiler Room club and live stream.

The video for single 360 assembled a cross-generational council of "It Girls" like Julia Fox, Chloë Sevigny, Gabbriette, Rachel Sennott, Emma Chamberlain, Alex Consani, Hari Nef, Chloe Cherry and Richie Shazam.

Hear and read more from triple j triple j brings you the best new music from Australia and around the world. Discover your next favourite artist here.

A deluxe version of Brat with carefully curated remixes, collaborations and features saw the acid-green album achieve critical acclaim.

Even 2024 US presidential candidate Kamala Harris got on board.

Brat cemented Charli's party girl legacy set in the concrete floors and bathroom doors of nightclubs across the globe.

"I think the Charli of 2007 would just be really grateful that I was making my eighth record," Charli xcx tells triple j Breakfast's Abby and Tyrone.

"I think when I started I never really had the intention of kind of like 'I'm gonna make eight records'.

"I didn't know much about the music industry at all when I first started making music, I just wanted to do it.

"I had a real passion for making music, but I wasn't having the foresight of a long career."

In the afterglow of Brat, Charli's work in the film industry blossomed. She produced her own mockumentary-style film, The Moment, and starred in indie films like Erupcja and 100 Nights of Hero.

Her collaboration with John Cale of The Velvet Underground on gothic industrial song House was the lead single for Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights, helping set the tone for the film. It also established that Charli knows game when it comes to art and its creators.

It laid the foundations for her next body of work.

Creating without distraction

The visual world of her new album Music, Fashion, Film was introduced with the black and white film clip for Rock Music, a stark difference to the high-saturation visuals of Charli's previous work.

She wanted the focus on the art form, without the distractions of bright lights and rich colours, and made the intentional move to be more offline while producing the album.

Charli xcx poses on the red carpet at the 2025 Grammy Awards, where she was nominated for eight awards and won three. (Reuters: Daniel Cole)

"I think historically, I've been a very online artist," she says.

"So, I think when I say this, I understand that some people don't believe me, but I have this year been trying to take a bit more of a step off the internet.

"That doesn't always work, you know? Sometimes I am still googling myself. This year I have been a lot more offline than in previous times and that's really nice and good for anyone.

"I want to do things that fulfil me as an artist and a person. And I think sometimes it's hard to follow that inner voice. There are a lot of distractions around."

Lasting legacies

Charli's recognition of the greats and their legacies permeate through the album.

From the cover art featuring John Cale, Marc Jacobs and Martin Scorsese, three legends of their craft representing the three titular art forms, to a recorded conversation with David Cronenberg closing out final song No One Lasts Forever.

The front cover of Charli xcx's new album features John Cale, Marc Jacobs and Martin Scorsese. (Supplied: Atlantic Records)

The conversation is the only feature on the record, shifting away from the collaboration-heavy, all-in approach of Brat.

But how does the It Girl of experimental pop music link up with the seminal originator of film's body horror genre?

"I went to Toronto to sit down with him and record him, and we spoke for like an hour," she said.

"We recorded [the] conversation and chose the parts that felt most related to the song. But the entire conversation itself is so interesting. He's such an interesting person and smart and kind. I could listen to him talk forever.

"I think he has a really interesting perspective on legacy and on art and artist, so I really wanted him to be a part of this song because I knew that he would just speak so effortlessly about it."

Seeing a lime green square everywhere? Hear the album behind the meme Our take on the zeitgeist-dominating Brat from Charli xcx.

The result, the closing moment of her eighth album, is like the finishing touch on a director's cut.

Cronenberg's thoughts marry with the track seamlessly, as if he had a click track in his ear during the conversation. Turns out he was just incredibly in sync with Charli's work.

"What's really crazy is he actually spoke in tune of the song," Charli says.

"We didn't record with the song underneath, we were just having a conversation that we recorded.

"When we got the vocal and went to the studio, we were like, 'Oh my God, he's actually totally in tune with the song without ever even having like heard it the day that we wrote it'.

"I was like, 'OK, he is a genius.'"

What's next for Charli xcx?

Looking ahead, Charli xcx has plans to extend her own legacy.

She might be thinking about future projects — "an album called Best Friends and all the songs [are] about my friends" — but after the relentless past few years, she knows she desperately needs to pause.

Loading Instagram content

When she makes it back to Australia, Charli xcx has made it clear that she wants to have another swing at triple j's Like A Version.

"I remember when I did that last time I had a busted hairstyle and it still really haunts me," she said.

"Sometimes I'll see videos of me doing that and my fringe is kind of like … up. Like, I look insane. Maybe we need a redo where I look hotter."

Charli xcx's eighth studio album Music, Fashion, Film is out now.

Hear Abby and Tyrone on triple j Breakfast weekday mornings from 6am.
