World.title: Adolescence creator swaps therapy for chains in new movie
World.content:
Welcome to the ABC Arts July film wrap.

This month sees the continuation of two very different franchises: the latest gorefest in The Evil Dead series and the potentially last edition of mind-blowingly stupid stunts from the Jackass crew.

Plus, a ginkgo tree observes the ebbs and flows of life in Silent Friend, Adolescence's Stephen Graham approaches teen behavioural problems in a very different way in The Good Boy and propaganda gets put under the microscope in The Wizard of the Kremlin.

Happy watching!

Evil Dead Burn

French director Sébastien Vanicek turns the gore up to 11 in Evil Dead Burn. (Supplied: Sony Pictures)

Say the words "evil dead" out loud, as if foolishly reading from the blood-stained Necronomicon, and images of horror director Sam Raimi and his chainsaw-wielding star, Bruce Campbell, will likely appear.

Fast facts about Evil Dead Burn Starring: Souheila Yacoub, George Pullar, Maude Davey, Tandi Wright Director: Sébastien Vanicek Where: In cinemas now

But just like the demonic Deadites that possess the living and the dead alike, the diabolical franchise that first manifested in 1981 can assume many forms.

Irish filmmaker Lee Cronin cast Aussie stars Lily Sullivan and Alyssa Sutherland in the 2023 reboot, Evil Dead Rise, which cleverly swapped the creepy cabin in the woods/medieval castle for a condemned apartment tower.

French director Sébastien Vanicek ups the gore with his Aotearoa-shot, bone-breaking and skin-frying follow-up, Evil Dead Burn. Coming in hot off Infested — Attack the Block, but spiders — he brings his co-writer Florent Bernard along.

Swiss star Souheila Yacoub plays Alice, who's feeling confused after the death, in a spookily manipulated car accident, of her violent husband, Will. He's played by Aussie George Pullar, with countrywoman Maude Davey as his dementia-afflicted gran, and Kiwi Tandi Wright as her daughter. The in-laws shoot icy glares Alice's way at the wake.

That's the least of her troubles. Turns out the family has an arcane dagger in the attic that can slay the Deadites. Cue a gross-out assault on their crumbling home with evil dead even weaponising a dishwasher door.

There are nervous chuckles to be had during the unrelentingly gruesome kills that follow. But the lack of time spent establishing care-factor may have you summoning the goofball wit of Campbell's sadly absent Ash Williams.

Stephen A Russell

The Good Boy

Tommy (Anson Boon) experiences a very unique kind of teen rehab in The Good Boy. (Supplied: Skpoia Film)

The Good Boy, not to be confused with Good Boy — the 2025 horror film that unfolds from the perspective of a dog — catapults us directly into the strobe-lit, alcohol-soaked, drug-coated reality of Tommy (Anson Boon).

Fast facts about The Good Boy Starring: Stephen Graham, Andrea Riseborough, Anson Boon, Kit Rakusen Director: Jan Komasa Where: In cinemas now

He's always raring for a fight, cruel and lecherous to friends and strangers alike, and completely impervious to the consequences of his action.

That is, until he's abducted by Chris (an always excellent Stephen Graham), kept captive in a rural family manor and subjected to a rehabilitation program that involves being chained by the neck in a dungeon and indoctrinated with an endless stream of his own TikToks and motivational infomercials proselytising about the ills of substance abuse.

It becomes increasingly clear, if Chris's kidnapping doesn't already make evident, that there's something uncanny transpiring in this household. Chris's wife Kathryn (a serpentine Andrea Riseborough) looks like a reanimated corpse and is almost catatonic with an unspoken grief, while their homeschooled son Jonathan (a suitably jittery Kit Rakusen) is too eager to please and perennially on the verge of tears.

But Tommy isn't being abused, at least not in the traditional sense. He's fed well, provided reading materials and celebrated on his birthday. Through intricate levers of gradually loosened controls, he graduates through a series of hoops, attaining more freedom as he's judged to be more reformed.

The film derives tension from the chasm between Tommy's possible transformation and inclusion in this new family unit and his desire to still enact harm, with Boon excellent as a man undergoing a metamorphosis that is neither desired nor always welcomed.

Bolstered by its star power, The Good Boy interrogates the ethics of forced rehabilitation, the psychology of Stockholm Syndrome and the prison of the nuclear family. The film suffers from an ending that's too pat to truly do its outlandish premise, eerie suppositions and the questions it poses justice, but it's an intriguing watch nonetheless.

Sonia Nair

Jackass: Best and Last

Johnny Knoxville and the rest of the Jackass crew are in theatres for what could be their last feature film. (Supplied: Paramount Pictures)

There are two types of people in this world: those who enjoy seeing someone catapulted into the air inside a used portable toilet, and those who lack taste.

Fast facts about Jackass: Best and Last Starring: Johnny Knoxville, Steve O, Jason Acuña, Poopies Director: Jeff Tremaine Where: In cinemas now

Of course, pranks and extreme high-concept endurance tests are hardly in short supply online. But beyond exploiting the frailty of the human body for entertainment, the Jackass series — almost in Richard Linklater style — has evolved into a touching celebration of male friendship enduring through 25 years.

This (allegedly) final film is largely comprised of the team's former stunts and pranks, opening with an infamous stunt so dangerous and easily replicated it was never allowed to air on TV. The pre-existing clips, particularly on the big screen, are still potent enough to induce hysterical laughter, dread and nausea; the new material doesn't exactly raise the bar, but still finds ways to take prostate exams and electrical shocks to spectacular new extremes.

Jackass's journey to infamy For more than 25 years, prank franchise Jackass has been delighting teens and terrifying parents. Now the gang is heading to the cinemas for what could be their last ride.

As a send-off to one of gen X's finest cultural achievements, Best and Last could've afforded to spend more time with its cast when they aren't engaged in shenanigans. Occasional behind-the-scenes insights help detail their commitment to the bit, like watching frontman Johnny Knoxville demand to be struck by a large bull for a second time after being dissatisfied with the first take.

Across the Jackass movies, there's always been something very pure about watching a group of men explore each other's bodies with so much aplomb. Eternally childish as they may be, they embody a type of joyful, carefree masculinity that's been sorely missing.

Jamie Tram

Penny Lane is Dead

Kat is a victim of Angus's influence and her own bad decisions. (Supplied: Umbrella Entertainment)

Kat isn't like other girls: she's worse. Much, MUCH worse. Blazing onto the screen with dyed red hair and a skimpy 80s goth wardrobe, Kat, played with glee by Sophia Wright-Mendelsohn (yes, THAT Mendelsohn), is baking some fatally spiked cupcakes to the tune of Am I Ever Gonna See Your Face Again by The Angels. The intended consumer of said cupcakes? Penny Lane, of course.

Fast facts about Penny Lane Is Dead Starring: Sophia Wright-Mendelsohn, Bailey Spalding, Tahlee Faraday, Alexandra Jensen Directed by: Mia'Kate Russell Where: In cinemas now

Penny, after all, is the perfect girl: pretty, blonde, rich and smart. So, when Penny 'accidentally' invites her cousin Kat to her girls-only getaway at the family beach house, it's up to her closeted girlfriend Toni and wallflower BFF Amy to try to keep her out of trouble.

As the title suggests, things go south pretty quickly, and the girls soon find themselves dealing with three party-crashing criminals who are cursed with oh-so-very itchy trigger fingers.

New Ozploitation horror is like Puberty Blues from hell After spending years in special effects and make-up, filmmaker Mia'Kate Russell's ocker nightmare Penny Lane Is Dead has made it to the silver screen.

It's a cracker of an opening sequence: a source of intrigue, an indicator of the black-as-tar comedic tone, and a bangin' needle drop. From titles to credits, Mia Kate Russell's throwback horror Penny Lane is Dead throttles along at breakneck pace, equally evoking Quentin Tarantino's Death Proof and the tricks and tropes of Ozploitation.

The characters are intriguingly layered — particularly Kat — and each new nail-biting development tests them in ways that get at those layers adeptly. The soundtrack picks are fun, era-appropriate and always well earned by the stacking and release of tension.

Penny Lane is Dead is an Aussie indie that really goes the distance. Check it out.

Silvi Vann-Wall

Silent Friend

Tony Leung Chiu-wai plays a neuroscientist captivated by a ginkgo tree in Silent Friend. (Supplied)

Delicate and meditative, Silent Friend is a film about relationships — between people, and between people and the natural world. Set across three generations at a university in Germany, the silent friend of the title is an ancient ginkgo biloba tree that is a witness to the lives of the students and faculty.

Fast facts about Silent Friend Starring: Tony Leung Chiu-wai, Luna Wedler, Enzo Brumm Directed by: Ildikó Enyedi Where: In cinemas now

Tony Leung Chiu-wai is captivating in a largely silent role as Tony, a visiting neuroscientist in the near future who turns his attention to the tree when COVID leaves him isolated on campus. In the past, Luna Wedler plays Grete, the first female student to be permitted to study at the university: brilliant, driven, and unique. And in between them, in the era of counterculture, is Enzo Brumm as Hannes, a literature student with a crush on his neighbour and a growing enthusiasm for her geranium.

Each develops a relationship with the natural world that calls into question how we see nature and how it in turn reacts to us.

The cinematography, by Gergely Pálos, is stunning. Each timeline has its own distinct look, with different film stock and colour grading; and while the film moves between its stories without any narrative markers, the visual style of each scene makes it immediately clear which era the viewer is watching.

And across those eras, outside the human politics and personal dramas, the tree, the only one of its kind on campus, grows and watches. That isolation is, perhaps, a reflection of the challenge each character faces, but this isn't a film that belabours such metaphors. The director and writer, Ildikó Enyedi, has done a masterful job of creating these worlds and of making them feel real. This is the stuff of life, told with patience and a deep humanity, and Enyedi trusts the audience to settle into the slow changes of time.

Almost two and a half hours long, Silent Friend never feels its length. The movement between the stories and the rhythms of the world are peaceful, but never boring, and I would happily have spent just as long again with the great ginkgo and its human companions.

Sky Kirkham

The Wizard of the Kremlin

Vadim Baranov (Paul Dano) is Putin's (Jude Law) right-hand man in The Wizard of the Kremlin. (Supplied)

Sometimes, the best approach to a biopic is to simply abandon the truth.

Fast facts about The Wizard of the Kremlin Starring: Paul Dano, Jude Law, Alicia Vikander Directed by: Olivier Assayas Where: In cinemas now

The titular wizard of this film, Vadim Baranov (Paul Dano), does not exist. Initially conjured out of thin air by author Giuliano da Empoli in his 2022 debut novel, also titled The Wizard of the Kremlin, Baranov is a composite of shadowy figures within Russian government: a theatre artist-turned-reality TV producer-turned-spin doctor for Vladimir Putin (Jude Law).

The ethos of this political thriller is defined by real-life media oligarch Boris Berezovsky (Will Keen) as he mentors Baranov: "Stop making stories, start inventing reality."

The nefarious rise of Putin is skewered in this satirical drama Cannes darling Oliver Assayas tackles the shadowy forces of our time in his latest film, The Wizard of the Kremlin.

As director Olivier Assayas (Irma Vep) burrows into the political machinations underpinning modern-day Russia, the dialogue has a habit of condensing itself into these kinds of tired aphorisms, struggling to easily reconcile how our political landscape has been fundamentally destabilised by forces beyond our control.

It's no Chernobyl, but it generally succeeds as a stylish drama that burns through juicy backroom dealings taking place inside the Kremlin, industrial bot farms and the glistening French Riviera.

Baranov himself is a softly spoken enigma; it's almost impossible to detect any emotion on his pillowy face. (Somehow, Dano convincingly plays the same character across 40 years without extensive de-aging tech). And as tiring as it is to watch actors embody famous politicians, Law's terse evocation of Putin is a welcome example of how great imitation extends far beyond extensive prosthetics or even an accurate accent.

The question still remains: if you're going to invent reality, why not make it more interesting than this?

World.title: Billions of dollars are failing to lift production of AUKUS submarines
World.content:
Exclusive WorldNorth AmericaAUKUS Billions of dollars are failing to lift production of AUKUS submarines Michael Koziol July 24, 2026 — 5:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Billions of dollars of additional funding for the US defence industrial base have not improved the production rate of Virginia-class submarines, a top Pentagon official says, casting further doubt on whether Australia will receive its AUKUS subs on schedule. Austin Dahmer, a senior policy official at the Defence Department, told a hearing on Capitol Hill that while undersea forces were the decisive instrument in denying Chinese domination of the Pacific, they were also the forces the US was the least able to produce. The production rate of the Virginia-class submarine has not improved despite the billions of dollars thrown at the problem. AP “Virginia-class boats have been delivering at roughly 1.1 to 1.2 a year since 2022, against a requirement of two to 2.33, counting AUKUS pillar one,” he said. “Two per year is not now expected until roughly 2032 … The strategy is sound. Production capacity is the point of failure.”



The US Congress has approved billions in additional funding to build submarines, while Australia has tipped in at least $US2 billion ($2.84 billion) with another $US1 billion to come. But Dahmer said the extra money had not helped. “I would underline that Congress has already appropriated [funds] substantially, and the rate has not moved,” he said. “Any recommendations that consist of more money without a mechanism to materially compress those timelines will not change the outlook.” Senior Pentagon official Austin Dahmer, right, touring the USS Mississippi Virginia-class submarine at Pearl Harbour this month. US Navy / Omar A. Dominquez Dahmer is a deputy to Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defence for policy who has in the past expressed scepticism about AUKUS. He made the comments to the National Commission on the Future of the Navy on Wednesday (US time) during a hearing on ways to improve US sea power. Afterwards, he told this masthead the navy was working hard to improve delivery of the Virginia-class submarines so that a future administration would be in the best possible position when it decides whether to transfer a vessel to Australia.



“We’re full steam ahead … It’s incumbent on all parties – us and the Australians and the British as well – to ensure that we’re meeting those conditions on the timelines agreed upon,” he said. “It’s a conditions-based agreement; it’s not a time-based agreement. So we have time to improve – we’re just being clear well ahead of time that we’re not there yet.” Defence Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles has staunchly defended AUKUS in the face of criticism from fellow Labor members. AP Photo The comments underscore the practical hurdles facing AUKUS despite the political commitment from all three countries, and come as Australian Labor Party members prepare for a possibly fiery debate about the pact at their national conference in Adelaide. Under the $368 billion-plus agreement, Australia is due to receive at least three nuclear-powered submarines from the US starting in 2032, before building a new class of the vessel, the SSN-AUKUS, with the UK.



The US has now clarified all three of the submarines it proposes to sell to Australia will already be in service, rather than new. But the president of the day must approve the transfer and be satisfied it does not degrade US war-fighting capability. Related Article AUKUS AUKUS will not run on time or on budget, Christopher Pyne says Arthur “Trip” Barber, a retired 40-year veteran of the US Navy and the Pentagon, who now sits on the National Commission on the Future of the Navy, said the fundamental problem was shipyard wages, and their inability to retain workers. “We need to pay shipyard workers a compelling amount of money so they stay on the job,” he told this masthead. Barber said Australia made the correct decision to acquire nuclear-powered submarines. “Everything about the decision was right until you get to the point of, ‘well, can we actually make them?’ That’s a struggle.



“Can we sell submarines that are in service and take the inventory dip? The plan was that we would be building new ones. Well, that’s not working out real well. I have no idea how that’s going to end.” AUKUS sceptics in Australia are currently holding an independent public inquiry into the defence pact, which has heard from figures including former Liberal defence minister Christopher Pyne. A staunch AUKUS supporter who is now a defence lobbyist, Pyne told the inquiry he did not believe the project would be delivered on time nor on budget, but “they’ll give it a good go”. Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles was contacted for comment. His office referred inquiries to the government’s Australian Submarine Agency.



“All three AUKUS partners are investing significantly in our respective industrial bases to ensure the success of AUKUS, to meet respective requirements and timelines, including the delivery of three Virginia class submarines to Australia by the US,” an ASA spokesperson said. “The Australian government is satisfied that it has the appropriate bilateral and trilateral agreements and arrangements, and governance structures.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Tornadoes, cold snaps, heavy rain and some sun: 'Every type of weather' forecast this weekend
World.content:
Heather Keats with details of this weekend’s cold snap Morning Report Download MP3 4m

It is shaping up to be a wintry weekend with a blast of polar air set to bring snow, severe frost and icy conditions across parts of the country.

Heavy rain and strong winds are also expected, with the potential to spark tornadoes. Weather watches were already in place for parts of the South Island and lower North. About half-a-dozen homes flooded overnight in the Grey District, and there was a slip on a road on Cobden, with more heavy rain likely on the way.

MetService head of weather Heather Keats agreed with suggestions it could be an 'inside' end to the week' - at least on Friday and Saturday.

"Sunday's okay, but today and tomorrow, very much looking messy," she told Morning Report on Friday morning.

"We've got a bunch of fast-moving features and fronts tied up and that will be thunderstorms, snow, heavy rain, maybe even some small tornadoes and water spouts. And that'll race up and over the country - the North Island - tomorrow, and then it kind of races away.

"But then we're left with a very cold southerly flow. So we've got every type of weather coming over the next sort of 48 hours."

Overnight already thunderstorms hit Westland Fiordland, she said with about 250 lightning strikes.

"Nothing crazy, but that's just the start of it."

Presently the heavy rain was hitting Buller and Nelson Lakes.

A formal heavy rain watch was in place Friday and Saturday for the Tararua Ranges, north of Wellington, with a moderate chance of being upgraded to a warning. More were likely to come, with tornadoes possibly in the mix, Keats said.

"The entire western coastline of New Zealand, I'm talking all the way up around Northland and the Coromandel Peninsula and then it'll track a little bit over to the eastern side as well.

"Thunderstorms, really strong wind gusts and the conditions are right to see some water spouts and some small tornadoes. We don't say that lightly. Not all thunderstorms produce thunder, not all thunderstorms produce tornadoes. But we are seeing that signal in the models. So it's going to be a watch-this-space today.

"If you are anywhere sort of near those western coastlines, keep an eye on your app because if we do see a severe thunderstorm, we will put out that warning. opportunity for you to get safe."

As for temperatures, among main centres Christchurch was likely to get bragging rights for the coldest, with it dipping below zero.

Snow was likely for Ruapehu and possibly the Desert Road, Keats said, and a couple of centimetres on Crown Range Road. The latter and Milford Road (10-15cm) both had road snowfall warnings in place.

"But because it's fast-moving, won't be hanging around for long.

"But then once it clears out on Sunday, and we will have sun, we will have some nice weather coming for most of the country on Sunday, it just drops to be freezing. So we're talking -4C for Christchurch.

World.title: Rescue jetskis parked by FENZ last year to be allowed back
World.content:
Waikato is getting back its rescue jetskis that were parked up by Fire and Emergency (FENZ) last year sparking a public outcry.

Locals warned someone would drown as a result of FENZ saying local volunteers were no longer allowed to use motorised boats because it was too risky.

A request by the Cambridge brigade over jetskis it wanted to deploy with local fundraising is understood to have triggered what became a national directive from Wellington fire commanders, that only trained firefighters in rafts were allowed to do water rescues.

RNZ revealed this last October prompting online comments such as, "Huntly ... had a really good water rescue unit until FENZ Numpties banned it."

But now a group separate from FENZ is being set up to run jetski rescues on the Waikato River covering volunteers from all three local brigades - Huntly, Ngārauwāhia and Cambridge.

"It's looking positive and we are hoping to get back on the river pretty soon," Huntly brigade chief Kerry Holland told RNZ on Thursday.

This looks like it would be finalised in a meeting next week.

FENZ chief executive Kerry Gregory had been grilled by MPs earlier this year about taking a hard line on motorised water rescues, which he defended by saying this fell outside what they were funded for, trained for or had set health and safety standards around.

This suggests the new move in Waikato depends on FENZ not being in charge. RNZ expects to get more details from FENZ later on Friday.

FENZ chief executive Kerry Gregory. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The jetskis came up again at Parliament on Monday this week - when Gregory was able to deliver different news to a select committee inquiry looking into fire truck fleet problems.

National MP Tim Costley had asked if some local brigades felt they needed to "hide" trucks or jetskis they had bought themselves with local fundraising.

"Because when we had the annual review hearing [in January], I know there was a large discussion around jetskis, swift water rescue, but are brigades, where the brigade owns something, whether it's an appliance, a jet ski, a buggy, or whatever it might be, are they able to use it or are they going to have that taken off them?" asked Costley.

World.title: How New Zealanders are cutting the cost of their insurances
World.content:
Insurance costs have been a major pain point for many households in recent years, but data from insurers shows many of us are finding solutions.

It was reported mid last year that insurance had the largest increase of any item in the consumer price index since 2000, up 916 percent.

Insurance experts told RNZ that some health insurance policies lifted 50 percent last year.

But while there are signs that premium rises may be moderating, some policyholders are finding other ways to reduce their costs.

What if you don't want a slice of the AI hype? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 13m

Higher excesses

Generally, if your insurance policy has a higher excess, you may be able to pay lower premiums.

Excess is the amount that a policy-holder pays when they make a claim, before the insurer chips in the rest.

Vero said its research showed 57 percent of the 1172 insured homeowners it surveyed had home insurance excesses of more than $500, even though "standard" was $300 to $500.

Nichola Young, executive manager of pricing and underwriting, said Vero had noticed customers had been opting for higher excesses since mid-2022.

She said more people were choosing an excess of $1000 excess, while $400 excesses were becoming less popular.

She said a very high excess, for example of more than $5000, could reduce the cost of an average premium by about $300 a year, although other factors would affect it.

"We've seen more customers voluntarily increasing their excess, and we noticed that this shift coincided with broader cost-of-living pressures."

Vero's research found affordability was the main driver for the higher excesses, and 66 percent of homeowners who had increased their excesses said they did so to lower the cost of their insurance.

"It shows that our customers are making trade-offs to balance the cost of premiums with the level of risk they're willing to carry. The choice ultimately sits with the customer, but the important thing is understanding what that means if you ever need to make a claim."

Young said it would not help in every situation.

"It's important to understand that increasing your excess won't necessarily offset every driver of rising insurance costs. Premium increases in recent years have been influenced by factors such as the growing cost of natural hazards, and increased taxes and levies. If your premium is higher because your home faces greater flood or weather risk, increasing your excess is unlikely to significantly reduce your premium."

The research showed 9 percent of people who had a higher excess said it was a temporary measure.

Justin Lim, founder of insurance comparison website Quashed, said his site had recorded a 19 percent increase in excesses for house insurance year-on-year, a 14 percent increase for car insurance and 6 percent for contents cover.

Changing cover type

Lim said people were also looking for cheaper insurance options.

He said some vehicle owners were considering third-party covert rather than comprehensive insurance.

"While most consumers still ultimately purchase comprehensive car insurance, year-on-year growth in comparison activity for third-party was double that of comprehensive. Consumers are actively exploring cheaper, more basic options."

Dropping cover

Some people are dropping policies completely. Southern Cross reported a drop in membership numbers in the year to June 30, 2025, of 3493 members, bringing total membership to 951,808.

The Insurance Council said surveys showed New Zealanders still had relatively high levels of insurance cover overall, and the percentage of homes with house insurance was in the mid-90 percent range.

Shopping around

Lim said people could often save money by comparing their options.

He said people who looked at what else was on offer could find they could save up to $1500 a year.

He said the chances of finding a cheaper policy were eight out of 10 for car cover, seven in 10 for contents, and six in 10 for home insurance.

Reducing risk

You may sometimes be able to reduce your insurance costs by reducing the risk to the insurer.

For health or life cover, that could mean quitting smoking.

For vehicle insurance, you might be able to install an immobiliser or park in a garage rather than on the street.

The Insurance Council said home insurance rose only 0.4 percent in the year to March and vehicle insurance was down 2 percent.

World.title: Police reopen sexual assault case after review finds sportsman's career prioritised over complainant
World.content:
A police sexual assault investigation into a young man with a "promising" sporting career was so flawed that the case has been re-opened, with the officer in charge of the case also under investigation, RNZ can reveal.

An internal police review has found an investigation by former Detective Senior Sergeant Darren Folau was "poor", that the complainant was "not listened to and not believed" and that the young man's sporting career was "prioritised over [the complainant] and any offending against her".

The review also said that based on its review of the original investigation the sportsman did not have a defence and was culpable of sexual conduct with a person under 16 years old.

The sportsman has been granted an injunction after he was approached by RNZ. The injunction means RNZ is not able to report his identity.

The original investigation into the sportsman and another man has been re-opened, meanwhile the former police officer is also under investigation.

Territorial Superintendent Ross McKay confirmed in a statement to RNZ that police had reopened an investigation into historical claims of sexual assault dating back to 2010, after an initial review in 2025 found "concerning management of the original file".

"An independent investigation team from another district is now leading the reinvestigation, and review into the handling of the original inquiry."

Territorial Superintendent Ross McKay, pictured in 2015. RNZ / Max Towle

The sportsman said in a brief statement to RNZ he understood police were re-investigating the matter.

"So, it would be improper of me to make any comments at this stage. I have complete trust in the police."

RNZ approached Folau for comment on Wednesday. He said he was "not in a position to make any decisions or commentary".

In response to further questions, Folau said because of the little information he had, he did not think he could make any comments.

"The context I have is that I understand a review of an historical case is underway.

"I am comfortable that any recommendations I may have had input into will have been evidence based."

The woman who made the complaint says she's "angry and hurt".

"I'd spent half my life feeling like what happened to me wasn't bad enough for the police to do anything, felt shame and blame…" she said.

"It was like no one had given me a second thought… no one cared about the impact on me. I just feel used and discarded, and I feel naive for believing in the police in the first place."

The complainant, then 16, went to the Christchurch Police Station in 2011 wanting to report a sexual violation which allegedly happened in June 2010 when she was 15.

The old Christchurch Police Station, pictured in 2014. RNZ / Diego Opatowski

The complainant said she had gone to a party with some friends. She remembered waking up the next morning without any clothes on next to a man who was 20 years old.

She said the following day she was contacted by the sportsman who told her she should have the emergency contraceptive pill as they had sex the previous night. At the time the woman could not recall having sex with him.

No charges were laid as a result of the investigation.

Then, in June 2025, the complainant contacted police requesting the investigation be reviewed.

The review, seen by RNZ, was carried out by Detective Inspector Scott Anderson.

"It cannot be considered a quality investigation," Anderson said of the original investigation carried out by Folau.

The review said that after the complainant went to police in 2010 a detective did a "scoping interview" and prepared a file which was coded unlawful sexual connection with a female 12-16.

The file was then received by Detective Senior Sergeant Darren Folau from the Child Protection Unit who contacted the woman's parents for a meeting on 27 June.

Folau then conducted inquiries into the suspects with the offence of sexual conduct with a person under 16 years old in mind before the complainant was interviewed and the details of her complaint recorded, Anderson said.

Folau's inquiries revealed that the 20-year-old had left New Zealand for Australia in March and had not returned.

Then on 22 June Folau spoke to the sportsman, then 20, in the presence of his parents at their home.

"It is recorded that [the sportsman] had an honest belief that [the complainant] was 16 as she is his sister's best friend, and his sister is 16," the review said.

Anderson said the complainant's evidential interview on 30 June created "a number of lines of inquiry" that should have been pursued prior to the sportsman being interviewed.

Anderson said that while there was "absolutely no criticism" of the complainant reporting approximately one year later, it did preclude some lines of inquiry such as a medical examination, search warrants for messages and photos from the man's phones and statements from witnesses in relation to the complainant's intoxication state.

Detective Inspector Scott Anderson. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

In Folau's five-page report on the investigation, seen by RNZ, he concluded that he did not believe any sexual activity took place between the complainant and the 20-year-old.

In relation to the sportsman, Folau said he believed he had "formed sufficiently reliable grounds" at the time to believe the complainant was 16.

This included that the sportsman believed she was the same age as his sister, who was friends with the complainant, who was at the time over 16. Folau said at the time of the incident the complainant was 15 years and 7 months, and the sportsman was 18 [the sportsman was actually almost 20].

Folau had told the complainant's parents that his recommendation was that no prosecution could take place.

"The view of [the complainant] is that [they] only wanted the matter brought to [the sportsman's] attention that at the time of sexual intercourse, she believed she could not have been in the frame of mind to consent, although that cannot be forensically established due to the time delay of the reporting."

Folau then said the sportsman had just been offered a contract to play sport professionally "and it appears that he has a promising career as a professional athlete".

"I believe this to be an occasion where alcohol is a factor for both [the sportsman] and [the complainant], where it has impaired good judgement.

"It cannot be established in any way whether consent was an issue or not for both parties. I am of the firm belief that there is a defence available for [the sportsman] in relation to the charge of sexual conduct with a girl under 16 years."

Folau said his recommendation was that there be no prosecution against the sportsman, "however a warning would be appropriate".

The investigation was reviewed by a Detective Senior Sergeant who agreed on Folau's assessment that there was insufficient evidence to proceed with a prosecution.

Anderson said in his review that it was a "poor investigation" and that the complainant deserved an apology.

"It appears that [the complainant] was not the centre of this investigation, not listened to and not believed."

Anderson said the "red flag" was that on the evening of the party the complainant and the sportsman's sister were 15, not 16.

"The [sportsman] would have known that his sister was 15 years old… he does not have the defence that he believed [the complainant] was 16 years old, the same age as his sister."

Police have reopened the case. RNZ / REECE BAKER

Anderson added that it appeared no fact checking had been done prior to speaking to the sportsman.

"This is in part due to this being done prior to [the complainant's] EVI."

Anderson said that the sportsman did not appear to have been treated as a suspect.

"There is no record of a suspect recorded interview on the file, being spoken to in front of his parents given that he was 20 years old, also the fact that he was spoken to as a suspect before [the complainant's] EVI does not follow best practice."

In relation to culpability, Anderson said he believed the sportsman was criminally liable for sexual conduct with a young person under 16 and did not believe he had a defence.

"[He] would have known that his sister was not 16 years old and therefore could not have reasonably believed that [the complainant] was over 16 years. It is of no matter if [she] consented."

Anderson also believed the 20-year-old was criminally liable for sexual conduct with a young person under 16.

"Although investigations such as these are difficult and not helped by being historic, objectivity is the key.

"It is my opinion that DS Folau had formed his belief that no prosecution was going to be proceeded with very early on, and his report is reflective of that. It is my belief that [the sportsman's sporting] career was prioritised over [the complainant] and any offending against her."

He said it was unclear if the sportsman had been warned by police.

"If DS Folau believed [the sportsman] had a defence, then why is there a need for a warning! There is no record of [the sportsman] actually being warned and the File stats do not reflect a warning."

Anderson detailed some of the options the complainant had going forward. This included doing nothing further with the police investigation or requesting that the investigation be investigated further "with a view to prosecution".

"It would have to be explained that once the investigation is completed the Solicitor General Prosecution Guidelines would have to be meet for a prosecution and this may require a legal opinion (e.g. [the sportsman] being warned in 2011, if in fact he was).

"There is no guarantee a prosecution would be commenced and accordingly if a prosecution was commenced there is no guarantee of a conviction."

There was also an option of some other sort of restorative justice resolution.

The complainant also lodged a complaint with the Independent Police Conduct Authority (IPCA) about a meeting she had at the Wellington police station to discuss the investigation.

Wellington Central Police Station. RNZ / REECE BAKER

Correspondence from the IPCA, seen by RNZ, referred to Anderson's review.

"[He] found that your original complaint was poorly handled and there were multiple issues with the investigation. There has subsequently been a conflict of interest identified between [the sportsman] and former Detective Sergeant Folau."

The letter also referenced a meeting the complainant had with two police officers to discuss her case.

"They acknowledged the original investigation was poor and [a police officer] apologised on behalf of New Zealand Police and told you that an investigation into the conduct of former Detective Sergeant Folau with the view of identifying any attempts to pervert the course of justice by him will be completed by Canterbury Police."

In relation to the complainant's case about the other two police officers she had spoken to earlier, they said they were "professional and empathetic and say they did not dismiss what you were saying".

"However, Police acknowledge that, despite the officers' intentions, you found the meeting very distressing.

"The officers accept that they talked about the CIB caseload but say this was an attempt to give you realistic expectations about possible timeframes for any action. They appear to have relied on the previous investigation report in discussing the detail of your case, and I acknowledge that Police now accept that that investigation was poor."

As there was no record of the meeting, the IPCA was unable to assess the tone of the conversation.

"We consider it is reasonable for Police to try to make sure complainants have honest and realistic expectations about the process and likely timeframes, but we expect officers to explain these matters in a respectful and empathetic way."

The IPCA closed the complaint.

The complainant told RNZ she asked police to reinvestigate her 2011 complaint.

"I just want accountability. I suppose I'm not hopeful that they'll lay charges, because I don't have much trust in them as an organisation anymore, but I feel that I owe it to my younger self to have the investigation carried out, that's what I wanted back then, and I don't have anything to lose."

Folau, who worked in Police for 28 years, was awarded a Queen's Service Medal for services in the Solomon Islands in 2004.

He holds several roles including board member of charitable trust STOP, a community based organisation that says it provides support and therapy for people "who have engaged in, or are demonstrating, concerning or harmful sexual behaviour".

In May he was announced as the co-chair of the Brainwave Trust Aotearoa board.

The announcement said Folau "contributes to a number of governance and advisory roles, including Oranga Tamariki, STOP Trust, and Moana Vā, supporting Pacific Rainbow+ communities".

World.title: Live: Glasgow Commonwealth Games opening ceremony
World.content:
The Glasgow Commonwealth Games will officially begin on Friday morning (NZT), after four years of doubt over their survival.

Since it was first awarded to Birmingham, the 23rd edition of the event has become something of a hot potato, with several potential hosts bailing out on financial grounds.

Thank goodness for the brave Scots, who will stage the Games - albeit a trimmed-down version - at Glasgow for the second time in 12 years.

World.title: Report on child poverty reveals 'national shame', Children's Comissioner says
World.content:
The Children's Commissioner says the latest report on child poverty reveals the country's "national shame".

The Ministry of Social Development published its Child Poverty in New Zealand report on Thursday.

It revealed a growing number of children in material hardship, reaching 13 percent between 2023 and 2024, up from 11 percent three years prior.

Children's Commissioner Dr Claire Achmad said the government was failing to protect the rights of the 170,000 children living in poverty right now, up by 47,500 in 2022.

Achmad said the report "shines a light on what has become a national shame in our country".

New Zealand did better than the European Union average of 14 percent,.

But it was overtaken by several other countries - Lithuania, Latvia, Italy, Portugal, and Cyprus - it had previously done better than,

"New Zealand is a small, relatively rich country. It's inexcusable for us not to be at the right end of these rankings internationally," Achmad said.

"What material hardship means, for example, is that we see children who are going hungry. They are cold because they are in severe housing deprivation.

"They're also experiencing preventable respiratory illnesses, which can actually lead to death and can have a lifetime impact on their health."

She said childhood poverty could have a lifelong impact on health, education and justice outcomes.

"Preventing child poverty is absolutely urgent, because to not do so means that children are missing out on their basic rights in childhood."

Poverty in New Zealand was preventable but required bold cross-party action and clear policies, Achmad said.

"We need to see policies that are going to prioritise children's basic rights to things like housing and their health."

Achmad sent an open letter to party leaders earlier this week, calling for a commitment to a child poverty accord, to fight inequality.

She said child poverty needed to have the same significance as given to other issues.

"If we can agree a national infrastructure plan, then surely we can do the same when it comes to the rights of our children and young people in New Zealand.

World.title: Long-time Wellington party flat shut down by council
World.content:
Walking into 13 Garrett Street in the Wellington CBD, you're welcomed by a wallpaper of gig posters over concrete walls, a display of the home's legacy.

But no more posters will be added, as a complaint to Wellington City Council has forced the cancellation of all events, and the tenants will be exiting to make way for redevelopment.

The home nearby Cuba Street shops has been the place for gigs, markets, poetry readings, movie nights, and more since as early as possibly the late 90s.

The three story building is set to be turned into offices on the upper floors, and a new venue space on the bottom.

The tenants of the home who will be leaving in November - all 16 of them - say the Capital is losing a space for community.

The Wellington City Council received a complaint alleging that the building had been hosting paid live events, which it did not have the permits for.

A pillar of music and arts scene

Flatmates Ollie Warren and Sarah Lee sit on their couch remembering their time hosting.

"It's become quite a pillar of what Wellington music and arts community can look like," Warren said.

A floor to ceiling shared wardrobe sits in the entrance hall, by the front room full of murals and speakers, along with mismatched vintage furniture.

A wooden stage stands at one end of the room, which while it looks peaceful in the daylight, comes alive at night.

In just the past four years, the flatmates said hundreds of people have performed.

In its history of performances, names like Mac Demarco pop up, Welly band Heavy Chest, and founder of music collective Eyegum, Joel Cosgrove who they say had his first gig there at 17.

"Garrett is a place for people to be prototyping and sharing things that aren't quite ready," Lee explained.

A wooden stage stands at one end of the Wellington flat's living room. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The flatmates said they made no income from the events, and any money from ticket sales went to the artists and organisers.

They said they always tried to operate events with safety in mind, and they respect the council trying to keep everyone safe.

"Obviously the council were going to catch up on us at one point," Warren said.

The group has had to cancel over a dozen events planned for this year as a result of the complaint.

Wellington City Council said it had set out its vision and partnership with the creative sector on supporting groups and artists, and providing access to new and under-utilised spaces to host events.

However, it said this support still needs to comply with building and planning regulations, for safety reasons.

The front room is full of murals and speakers and mismatched vintage furniture. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Music journalist Martyn Pepperell remembered going to the flat as a teenager in the late 90s.

He said the music changed with each group of tenants - from techno, drum and bass, electro punk, new rave, to indie dance.

Pepperell said people would team up and do multi-level shows, even on the roof.

A floor to ceiling shared wardrobe sits in the entrance hall. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He compared its closure to if the famous Cuba Street Bucket Fountain vanished.

"For some people this has just been part of the fabric of their life for decades."

Now, Pepperell said the building was at a crossroad moment, and Wellington would have to wait and see how the new venue fit into its history.

"In 10 years time, we may find that that's just another chapter in the bigger story of 13 Garrett Street."

Owners' plans

The owners of the property, Emily and William Broadmore, bought the building late last year with the plan to earthquake strengthen it for redevelopment.

They said the top half of the building will be turned into character offices, and the bottom half will be a venue.

The owners are working with DJ and promoter, Jack Parry, and architect and interior designer Allistar Cox, to develop the bottom floor of the building into an official venue.

The owners said they always knew the home was a party flat, but not that events were being ticketed and publicly advertised.

"This is not how we wanted the end of the era for them."

Flatmates Ollie Warren and Sarah Lee say the flat became a pillar of what the Wellington arts and music community can look like. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

While the owners said an end of the tenancy was always planned for earthquake strengthening and redevelopment, they said they had to begin this conversation sooner than anticipated because of the complaint.

"They always knew this day would come. It's just a real shame that it came as a result of a complaint from council."

With earthquake strengthening starting on the upper floors, the owners said it's possible that lower tenants - thrift shop Dirty Laundry and coffee spot Pour & Twist - could stay slightly longer.

Neighbours say the flat was never a problem

Speaking with neighbours, they say the party flat never bothered them.

Victoria Court Motor Lodge - a hotel next to the flat - said the noise was never an issue.

Owner Liam Wang said the noise didn't worry him, as the city was noisy regardless, and other music venues like The Rogue and Vagabond are close by.

However, he said if the home didn't have the right permits, it was fair for the council to shut it down.

Neighbour Dan Craig said he went to a gig at the flat 20 years ago, and felt it was a real shame it had been shut down.

"That's pretty rank bro."

He said it was part of the fabric of Wellington.

"It's like a little hidden secret, it's a shame."

Could the legacy continue?

While 13 Garrett Street itself is closing, the tenants hope the idea of it can continue at a new address.

The flatmates said they want to continue living in large numbers, and are looking for houses with six-plus bedrooms, where they could continue to host.

World.title: Woman who almost died in Auckland swimming pool returns to thank her saviours
World.content:
The last time Lorraine Moser visited the Onehunga War Memorial Pool, she almost died.

Now she has returned to thank the heroes who brought her back from the brink.

"I'm just so blessed that I was in the right spot and we had the right people that knew what they were doing and and didn't give up," she said.

"I really want to give them a heartfelt thank you, and encourage them to keep doing what they're doing."

On 19 May, Moser was halfway through her usual three kilometre swim when her heart gave out, and she started drowning in the middle of the pool.

She was rushed to hospital in critical condition, RNZ reported at the time.

"A really strange feeling, I just got this really strange feeling over my body and I thought 'oh gosh I better stand up.' But before I even had a chance to stand up, I was out," she recalled.

"I was told by numerous people in the pool that they just gave CPR for well over 15 to 20 minutes and they didn't stop and that's really what saved my life."

A fit and avid swimmer, she said the sudden cardiac arrest came as a complete shock.

But 19-year-old lifeguard Tash Corbin and 18-year-old Damon McKinstry wasted no time.

The pair took turns performing CPR until the ambulance arrived.

Damon McKinstry (left) and Tash Corbin (right). Nick Monro

"I know for me my first instinct just kicked in and I just jumped in straight away to grab her," Damon McKinstry said.

Tash Corbin said the 15 minutes they spent doing CPR felt like hours.

"Every now and again she would give like little signs of life and, I mean, I was on the verge of tears nearly when I was doing it," she said.

"There's just no really thought going through your brain, you just got to keep going."

Despite being celebrated as heroes, the young lifeguards were staying humble.

"We do it in training, we've trained for it but I never actually thought I'd have to use it, so it is a pretty good feeling, I'm not gonna lie," Corbin said.

"Yeah it's a good feeling but it's just like another day at work," McKinstry added.

"Exactly, I mean it's part of the job."

But Moser's friends, who she swam with regularly, said Corbin and McKinstry deserved to be celebrated.

"I felt really quite helpless, but that was when the lifeguards got involved," fellow swimmer Tony Walker said.

Another swimmer, Russell Brown, said he was stunned by the lifeguards' composure.

"Not only did they know what to do but they just did it without fluster. You know, most people, even I was in a flap, and I was just so impressed with how composed the kids were."

Lorraine Moster swimming at Onehunga War Memorial Pool and Leisure Centre. Nick Monro

Lorraine Moser said she was eager to join her crew in the water again.

But after spending five weeks in hospital, where her lungs were drained and she underwent open heart surgery, she planned to take it slow.

"Part of it's psychological, and not just for me, for people around me, that they feel safe when I'm back in the pool," she said.

"So I think I will get in the pool in stages, do a little bit of flutter board, and then yeah, absolutely want to get back in the pool."

Moser said it would be about six months before she was back in peak form, but her recovery was going swimmingly.

World.title: Netball agents frustrated as pay talks roll into Glasgow 2026
World.content:
Has netball learned much since 2023? You be the judge.

The messy and drawn-out pay negotiations that dominated headlines during that World Cup year are once again overshadowing a major tournament for the sport.

The Diamonds are aiming to defend gold at the Commonwealth Games, and that mission starts on Saturday night in their opening match against Tonga at 8pm AEST. But the world number one team hit the court in Glasgow with uncertain futures.

The current Super Netball collective player agreement (CPA) expires on September 30, meaning all 88 players will be off contract. It is a chaotic way of doing things and leads to a mad scramble for everyone involved, with so many trying to secure opportunity at the same time.

Netball Australia surrenders, as players win long and bitter pay war Netball Australia has finally agreed to a modest revenue share partnership with its players, but how much have its brutal tactics throughout the pay negotiations damaged the game?

The 2027 signing window was supposed to open the Monday after the grand final on July 4. That has been delayed a month so the athletes can focus on their international duties while the terms of the next deal are worked through.

There are several sticking points that the national sporting organisation and the Australian Netball Players' Association (ANPA) cannot agree on. More on that later.

It is important to note that ANPA provided a detailed submission late last year to try and get the ball rolling. Netball Australia wanted to wait and sort out its new broadcast agreement with Nine, which underwrites the majority of the costs of the CPA first. That was done in April.

Although from the sport's point of view, discussions are more respectful and constructive this time, with greater transparency of information shared amongst parties, the players are incredibly frustrated. And so are their agents, who argue they are unable to make meaningful progress on behalf of their talent.

There is no prohibition to hold non-binding conversations with your own club or another right now, yet a request to allow non-binding written offers while CPA talks take place was denied. The agents believe this would've freed up the system and given players more certainty.

Kathryn Deiulioi is the founder of Behind Your Brand, which manages several Diamonds athletes, including the Australian captain. (Image Supplied)

Kathryn Deiulio, the founder of Behind Your Brand, said it was her understanding that the Diamonds players did not ask the sport to push back the contracting window and wanted discussions to continue. There are concerns this kind of assumption could create a divide amongst the group, positioning some as more important than others.

"This misunderstanding creates the impression that they didn't consider the impact it could have on the remaining 60-70 players not playing at the Games," Deiulio told ABC Sport.

"It is our role to continue contract negotiations on their behalf, and it would have created an additional layer of complexity, given the time difference and the need to carefully manage communication with players so as not to distract them from their performance.

"However, ultimately, that is part of our role as agents and something we are equipped to manage … These are professional athletes who dedicate their lives to their sport, and they deserve the same level of security around employment expected in any other profession."

Australia won gold at the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham. (Getty: Sue McKay)

Jace Bode is the chief executive of W Sports & Media, which works across a range of elite codes, such as cricket, Aussie Rules, football, golf and tennis.

"The fact that 80-plus athletes have once again been put in this position is incredibly disappointing and challenging to manage from our perspective," Bode told ABC Sport.

"We have the best netball competition in the world, and it is frustrating to watch these athletes continue to navigate uncertainty around their careers when it has so much potential."

This CPA will only be a 12-month deal, allowing Netball Australia to try and bring in more revenue from 2027 onwards with the free-to-air broadcast agreement and present a stronger offer. But both agents worry that without a longer CPA in place we may be right back here next year, ahead of a World Cup on home soil.

The Diamonds players have been in camp since Friday July 10. (Supplied: Netball Australia)

According to the new dates, contracts will open for clubs' own players from August 4-16. Non-binding written offers are permitted for all players during these 12 days. Then, from August 17-28, contracting officially opens for those looking to switch allegiances.

The agents argue this process favours those who intend to remain at their existing club, while placing players who may be looking elsewhere at a significant disadvantage. The time frame is also not ideal for those weighing up their options overseas, with the English Superleague contracting window already in full swing.

Complicating things further, in other sports it is normally the responsibility of the governing body to handle CPA talks with the players' association, but here the clubs appear to have taken greater control of the wheel.

All eight Super Netball franchises are likely to have competing ideas slowing progress further, and it is unclear if their vested interests will be prioritised over what is best for the sport as a whole.

Shimona Nelson represents Jamaica at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games. (Getty: Mark Kolbe)

The delay has wide-reaching implications beyond the Australian team at the Games.

In-form Melbourne Mavericks star Shimona Nelson had already flagged with Netball Jamaica that she would be unavailable for selection for Glasgow ahead of the Super Netball season. The goal shooter needs to get her tonsils removed and deal with a knee issue.

Although the Sunshine Girls did try and get her to change her mind, an appearance at the major tournament would be risky. Should she injure herself, with only one-year contracts being offered, where would that leave her?

It makes sense that Nelson has put herself first, considering the history of her career. After the Collingwood team disbanded, Nelson had to forge her way back into the league as a No.11 player with the Mavericks, working hard to return to a full-time contract the next season.

It is unfair that athletes are being forced to make these tricky decisions based on what is happening in Super Netball, and what is right for each of them is extremely individual.

Shimona Jok keeping an open mind as 11th player signing confirms she's eligible for Diamonds Super Netball import Shimona Jok was in the headlines after the Mavericks found a loophole to sign her as their 11th player. But now her eligibility for the Diamonds has been confirmed, would she ever go there?

There has been a rumour that Nelson isn't playing because she instead wants to represent the Diamonds at the next World Cup.

Nelson indeed plans to get her citizenship in September, purely to cement her status in a country she has lived in for almost 10 years and now classes as home.

At this point, there have been no discussions between the Australian camp or Shimona's about the possibility of her playing for the Diamonds.

So, what are some of the sticking points of the CPA talks?

Currently on the table is a 25 per cent pay increase for those on the minimum wage and a three per cent pay increase for everyone else.

This all sounds rosy until you do the numbers. Australia's consumer price index sits at four per cent. Once these changes are factored into the salary cap, with increased superannuation contributions and the rising cost of living, the take-home pay for many of the athletes could actually be worse off than they were this year. It may lead to a pay cut in real terms.

Former Thunderbird and Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the chief executive of the players' association. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Despite this, the sport will continue to restrict player opportunities to make extra cash in sponsorship deals. The cap for commercial arrangements with an existing team sponsor or partner is going to be raised to $50,000 but the agents want the cap removed entirely.

There are no monetary limits on a player's commercial agreements with third parties, but agents find the amount of compliance their talent must go through to get approval is unreasonable and leads to sponsors turning to athletes from other codes.

"When athletes are able to work with brands and authentically leverage their own platforms, they bring different eyeballs to the sport … This should be viewed as a positive, not a threat," Bode and Deiulio said.

"If netball does not evolve in this increasingly competitive female sports landscape, these limitations will have a broader impact on its growth and visibility."

World.title: Australia gets first win with Glasgow asleep and the Games yet to open
World.content:
In a world where everything costs a bit too much and "free summer holiday activities" is high in your auto-complete drop-down, a spot of barefoot bowls remains a glorious tradition.

The sun shining, warming your carbonated beverage to a few degrees warmer than is pleasant, baffling yourself with how you can be so bad at a sport that on its face seems so simple, all while trying to stay alive to the prospect of your mates accidentally breaking your toe with wildly flung rock while misquoting half-remembered lines from Crackerjack.

That wasn't quite the case as the sport kicked off the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

The city of Glasgow was still waking up as athletes, officials and a handful of fans filed into the Scottish Event Campus (SEC) for a 9:30am start to Commonwealth competition on Thursday.

Not least of which because the event isn't on lawn of any sort; it's being played on carpeted greens indoors at the SEC Centre.

It serves as a reminder of organisers' decision to hold as many events in existing halls and venues, and gives the in-house DJ prime acoustics as he tries to pump up a crowd described as "small but mighty" by the MC team.

Already the only sport running on every day of the Games, organisers added an extra session on Day Zero before the opening ceremony due to "unprecedented demand" for the sport at a distinctly Scottish Games.

The sport has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

But making that widely known to punters may have fallen by the wayside for an organising committee feeling the pinch as their rapid 22-month planning period suddenly reached its end.

Along with bowls, the SEC will host more than half – boxing, judo, 3x3 basketball, netball, weightlifting and para powerlifting – of the cut-down list of sports in Glasgow.

Everything from Naughty By Nature to drum and pipes renditions of ABBA and Tina Turner echoed through Hall 3 as the countdown began and pyrotechnics welcomed the athletes to the rinks, with Australia's 2018 gold medallist Kelsey Cottrell the consensus "one to watch" as eight women's pairs rollers and four in the men's singles stepped onto the field of play.

But the first competitive moments of Glasgow 2026 arrived with a startling lack of fanfare, at least for the uninitiated.

There was fanfare welcoming the first Commonwealth Games athletes to the arena. (Bowls Australia: Aidan Davis)

The in-arena announcer made sure to point out their warm-up rolls had no bearing on the scores, but the only marker that Jackaroos Cottrell and Dawn Hayman were officially kicking us off came when the scoreboard clicked on at the far end of the Siti Zalina Ahmad Rink.

Cottrell and Hayman got it ticking over straight away with a 4-0 lead after the first end of the first set against Gertrude Siame and Foster Banda.

It was the sort of lead you see sometimes at these sorts of meets, where one team is simply outclassed.

That was certainly happening in the concurrent men's singles, where 39-year-old former world champion Shannon McIlroy was kicking the tar out of 17-year-old Tongan Liam Hill, and Northern Ireland's Gary Kelly was rolling Frederrick Tafatu of Niue.

The biggest cheers of the morning came from Botswana's crew whenever bucket-hatted Diza Mphotho won an end, a raucous reaction that cracked through the polite hum and mild applause accompanying some of the other victories.

Meanwhile, the Zambian pair fought back before Cottrell got the Aussie team rocking on the sidelines with a clutch final roll to secure the 6-4 win in the first set.

A vocal Zambian team gave the Aussies a scare. (Bowls Australia: Aidan Davis)

"Just breathe through the nerves a little bit when you feel that adrenaline pumping on the mat," Cottrell said.

"Take that extra second; time is precious [with a 30-second shot clock], but take that extra second and breathe through it."

The heavily favoured Aussies looked more like themselves in the second set as they romped to a 2-0 win against a team that had never played on carpet before.

Even as they were getting walloped 14-0 in the second set, Zambian skip Banda was vocally gassing up her partner – "Come on Gertrude, you are trying my darling" – and apologising for her own performances.

It was a welcome distraction for the Australians as they tried to keep their own adrenaline in check.

"They're always very chatty," Cottrell said.

"It's just that fine line, being able to walk away and focus when we need to, but also it's kind of good to engage in it because it keeps us cool, calm and collected as well. Really lovely girls."

Hayman and Cottrell will walk in the opening ceremony at the Hydro from 5am on Friday (AEST), but they have already truly opened the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

World.title: Penrith flyer breaks record in comeback Panthers win
World.content:
Penrith have survived a scare at the hands of rivals Parramatta, claiming a 24-18 win to strengthen their outright lead in the race for the NRL's minor premiership.

The Panthers moved four points clear of the second-placed Warriors, who face Canterbury on Saturday, with an unconvincing victory in which they were forced to play 20 minutes with just 12 men.

Tom Jenkins and Isaiah Papali'i were both sinbinned for professional fouls at Parramatta Stadium on Thursday but the Panthers, who didn't take the lead until the 57th minute, were able to prevail.

"That wasn't our best stuff but that was the first time this year when we've had to sort it out and come back," said Panthers coach Ivan Cleary.

"The sinbins … we had two good periods but the end was super disappointing.

"We got away with a win and there was some good resilience shown which we did last week (in a loss to Brisbane) … but it's just a game in a season and we'll have to do a lot better than that."

Jenkins scored his 26th try for the year to surpass Rhys Wesser as the most-prolific Panthers player across a single campaign and remains a chance of running down Dave Brown's 38-try season in 1935.

"His all-round game this year has been very consistent and that's why he's getting the tries," Cleary said.

"Rhys Wesser was a try machine and a bit of a legend in our club so it's pretty cool."

Parramatta, meanwhile, will remain in 15th spot and will feel this game was a valuable win they let slip from their grasp.

The Eels had the Panthers on the ropes early when Mitch Moses and Jack Williams put the home side 12-0 up.

Moses was in excellent touch for the battling Eels. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Parramatta failed to score across either period while the Panthers were down to 12 men and then let their rivals off the hook in the second half with barge-over tries and pressure-relieving penalties.

"Unfortunately fight and effort only get you so far," said Eels coach Jason Ryles.

"It's a six-again on the last play a couple of times and penalties on play one out of yardage … they are things that are avoidable and are a little bit around our game awareness that we need to improve."

Jenkins was the catalyst for dragging the ladder-leaders back into the game, catching and offloading a Nathan Cleary kick for Casey McLean to touch down on the left.

Penrith flyer Jenkins was sinbinned on the stroke of halftime for pulling back Brian Kelly as the Eels winger chased after his own grubberkick.

Henry's try proved to be crucial for Penrith's comeback. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The Panthers trailed 12-6 at the break but Parramatta were unable to use the one-man advantage to their benefit.

And just as Jenkins returned, Liam Henry crashed over under the sticks and Cleary tied the game up with a conversion from right in front.

Liam Martin was next over to push the Panthers six points ahead.

But any hope Parramatta had of getting back into the game was undone by their own ill-discipline as they failed to capitalise when Papali'i was sent to the bin.

Jenkins crossed for his obligatory try afterwards before Williams grabbed a consolation try for the Eels at the death.

Re-live the action in our live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our Score Centre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.
