World.title: Pies make statement with impressive win over listless Crows
World.content:
Another Nick Daicos masterclass has propelled Collingwood to a comeback 34-point away victory over Adelaide.

Daicos (39 disposals, one goal) helped the Magpies overturn a 25-point second-quarter deficit in a stirring 16.12 (108) to 11.8 (74) triumph on Thursday night.

Collingwood extended their winning streak to six games and climbed to seventh on the ladder.

Adelaide great Taylor Walker kicked his 700th career goal but the fifth-placed Crows blew a chance to rise to third spot.

Adelaide held a 25-point lead nine minutes into the second term, when Walker had already booted three majors.

But the Magpies climbed from the canvas in style, scoring 13 of the next 16 goals to stun the 50,109-strong Adelaide Oval crowd.

Daicos was instrumental, as were ruckman Darcy Cameron (23 disposals, six clearances, 37 hitouts) and veteran Scott Pendlebury (29 touches, one goal).

Magpies Dan McStay, Tim Membrey and Ed Allan kicked two goals each, and defender Isaac Quaynor (20 possessions) and 200-gamer Jordan De Goey (20, one goal) were also standouts.

Quaynor was booed by sections of the Adelaide Oval crowd throughout the game. Adelaide's Izak Rankine was suspended last year for using a homophobic slur against Quaynor in a game.

Adelaide's Walker couldn't add to his early three goals while Riley Thilthorpe also finished with three.

Crow Sam Berry collected 30 disposals and 10 clearances, Izak Rankine — facing the Pies for the first time since his homophobic slur suspension — had 25 touches, and defenders Wayne Milera (24 possessions) and Josh Worrell (21, seven marks) were busy.

Look back how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Bomber Caddy to face Hawks after heart scare
World.content:
Essendon interim coach Dean Solomon says Nate Caddy will play in Saturday's match against Hawthorn following his recovery from a heart scare.

Caddy was taken to hospital during last Sunday's three-point win over GWS due to an elevated heart rate.

Bombers star cleared for return Nate Caddy is expected to fully train and play next weekend despite experiencing an elevated heart rate during Essendon's win over GWS.

The 21-year-old was released from hospital after being given the all-clear.

The club's medical staff has since given its approval for Caddy to face the Hawks.

"He'll be good to go," Solomon said.

"They said there's no risk with what happened and he's fully good to go. I trust our medical staff, and Nate's in a good headspace as well.

"He spent a lot of time with the docs and medical staff, gone through it all and has a good understanding that there's no risk at play here, and he's really confident.

"So we've just got to trust our medical staff."

Essendon has lost Xavier Duursma (hamstring) for the rest of the season, while Kyle Langford will miss the Hawthorn match due to suspension.

McKay sits out Blues training

Star Carlton forward Harry McKay failed to participate during the Blues' main training session on Thursday.

McKay suffered a minor tear to his meniscus, as well as bone bruising to his knee, during Saturday night's 21-point defeat to Collingwood.

The 28-year-old was ruled out early in the match after his knee knocked into teammate Sam Walsh.

Harry McKay was forced from the field against the Magpies last weekend. (Getty Images: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

But speculation around McKay ran rampant, with Fox Footy commentator David King questioning the one-time Coleman medallist's injury.

The Blues were privately seething with McKay's character being criticised, before the severity of the injury was confirmed on Sunday.

Interim Blues coach Josh Fraser said he "didn't spend a lot of time thinking about" the commentary surrounding McKay.

"Whenever there's an injury, your mindset goes to the care and support for the player," Fraser said.

"We act on the information we're given from our medical team, the commentary around all of that, I probably push it to the side.

"I can only judge him on the way he's presented and he's presented his usual self.

"Great energy around the group, trying as hard as he can to play and leading internally around the club."

Carlton's wildcard hopes will go on the line on Saturday when it host out-of-form Gold Coast at Docklands.

AAP

World.title: Aussie captain relishes 'special' chance 'to take time to be a dad'
World.content:
Water polo is a brutal sport.

Relentless swimming. Incessant wrestling. Elbows and fists flying around as if the combatants were half-submerged within a flooded UFC cage.

To put it mildly, it is not a place for the faint of heart.

So it is somewhat incongruous, then, to see Australian Sharks captain Nathan Power sitting on the side of the Griffith University pool on the Gold Coast with his son, Sebastian in his arms, feeding him a bottle.

Power, 33, will lead the Australian men's water polo team at the World Aquatics Water Polo World Cup event in Sydney this week, with the Sharks taking on reigning world champions Spain on Thursday.

He is also on six months of parental leave from his role as a manager with KPMG, giving him valuable time to be a dad as well as skippering his nation.

Nathan Power will skipper the team in his home town of Sydney. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"It's been fun to get to do this," Power told ABC Sport, with Sebastian still in his arms.

"To get an opportunity to take time to be a dad, it's really special."

It's created some changes within the team environment too.

"This is the first time in my time with the men's team that there's been a baby on tour — and there's actually two at the moment, Blake Edwards has his son Jude here as well," Power said.

"It makes for a bit of a shift; even at breakfast time now, the boys all roll in and it's a case of, who's gunna take hold of the baby and who wants to look after a baby.

"It's amazing to see how a large group of men have all very quickly clicked into dad mode to help out where they can."

Australian Sharks Water Polo coach Tim Hamill (left) says the addition of kids to camp has been great. (Supplied: Zac Hudson)

Head coach Tim Hamill, who has led the Sharks since taking the reins post-Tokyo in 2021, also made note of the positive changes to the dynamic young children can have.

"It's a first for us," the former international player told ABC Sport.

"One of our values as a team is around family, so we talk to that in having those families here.

The 'precious' bond driving the Stingers to success Australia's women's water polo team, the Stingers, were the most successful Australian team at the Paris Olympics, winning a stunning silver medal. This is the secret to their success.

"We're really fortunate to have a nice balance of the group, we've got the spectrum covered in terms of interests and ideas and for the first time, in this preparation, we've got two of our players who have children, which we've never had before.

"So that changed the dynamic of the group.

"A lot of people have spoken about Paris and how do we get those results [that we got] and I'm conscious to talk culture because it's that overused word in sport at the moment.

"But for me, culture as a word is derived from that care, there's real care in this team.

"We know that our culture needs to be the best in the world, we know that our team care needs to be the best in the world, otherwise we can't compete, so we invest time in all of that, and that's conversations with those 18s all the way through to 30 plus year olds and now fathers."

The topic of keeping mothers in sport has been a hot one in the Australian space for a while now.

In December, the Australian Olympic Committee created the Olympians Future Fund, with a key pillar of that designed to help support female Olympians return to high-performance sport after giving birth, making them eligible to receive $10,000.

Although Power's situation is different, he noted that the support that he has received from KPMG and Water Polo Australia was just as valuable to him in order to allow both he and his partner Maddy to continue their careers.

Water polo is not exactly a gentle sport, as Power shows while wrestling Spain on their way to the world championship title last year. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

"That's kind of the thing that can maybe get lost at times, but really it's support for the family," he said.

"With the support that I get through my work at KPMG, that then enables Maddy to get back into work; the support I get from Water Polo Australia, that enables us as a family to be here.

"We both get to keep on pursuing what we want to pursue, but also get to spend some really meaningful time with Sebastian too.

"It's been awesome to come home from training and the first thing I see is a silly smile from the window, him looking out at me.

"It's a new, fun way to come home from training when you're a bit cooked and tired and maybe a bit grumpy."

Power beamed with joy when recounting how much Sebastian was enjoying finding his feet in the water during his lessons, adding that fatherhood has "massively" changed his perspective.

Nathan Power has competing priorities now. (Supplied: Water Polo Australia)

"I think, obviously parenthood becomes that key identity that you have and you see yourself as," he said.

"It's also something which for me, at 33, I guess we can probably confidently say I'm closer to the end than the start of my career, so it means you also get to take some moments and really appreciate that this isn't normal to get to do this and to share this experience with your family.

"It gets you to appreciate these experiences you have with the team too, because they can be very fleeting."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The World Cup Final is the first time Australia has hosted a major water polo championships since the 2007 World Championships in Melbourne, and the first time Sydney has hosted a combined event since the 2000 Olympics.

Power said the opportunity to compete in front of friends and family will never be undervalued by the squad.

"The importance of it and the rarity of it is not lost on us," Power said.

"I've had teammates who've started their career and gone through their career and finished their career and didn't get that opportunity to be able to play in an event at home like that.

"Obviously, as we move towards Brisbane, this is one of those good examples of something which can hopefully lead to more of these events occurring as well."

World.title: Nina Kennedy knows now is the time to soak it all in — if she remembers to
World.content:
For most of us, falling for 5 metres is terrifying. For Nina Kennedy, provided there's no bar following her down, the fall is the fun part.

But last year introduced her to a fresh fear: the fear that it might all be over.

The reigning Olympic and world champion in pole vault tore her hamstring early in April last year.

Despite the long recovery from surgery, Kennedy was initially named in the Australian squad for the World Athletics Championships in September, but a strained muscle just a couple of days later dragged her back to reality.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She had to watch as American rival Katie Moon won outright the title they shared two years earlier.

Yesterday, she was named Australia's flag-bearer for the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony, which felt like a long shot when she was in the depths of rehab less than a year ago.

"Whenever you have a major surgery and you're out for the whole season, there's definitely that doubt of, 'Will this get fully better and will I return to my best and better?'" she said after flying out of a pre-Games athletics training camp early to accept her flag-waving honour.

"You have those thoughts, but you put in the work you do the rehab, you listen to your team, speak to your sport psychologist and never stop dreaming.

"I'm so proud of myself. Of course there were doubts, but I'm lucky enough to do this as a job and I'm pretty damn good at it. I work my arse off every day. So I'm not surprised but I am really proud of myself.

Kennedy has warmed back into the 2026 season after a torn hamstring last year. (Getty Images: Marco Mantovani)

"As athletes we try and get the best out of ourselves, so my mind always goes to, 'What if I don't get to defend my Commonwealth title? What if I don't make it back to the Olympics? What if this hamstring goes again and my career's over and I haven't really soaked up the last few years like I should have?'"

Kennedy has been representing Australia on the world stage for more than a decade, but the past five years since turning to the sport full time have seen her conquer the world and set the Australian women's pole vault record 10 times, including just two weeks ago in Monaco.

The 29-year-old admitted the Brisbane 2032 Olympics would probably be a bridge too far for her, so it was time to look around and enjoy what was happening while she was still on the field.

"Sport can be so fleeting so I've really learned to enjoy every step and this is such a special honour. I'm really going to try and soak this in and make some good memories," she said.

Unfortunately, she knows herself too well and is pretty sure she will not nail it when she leads her teammates into Glasgow's Hydro for the opening ceremony tomorrow morning (AEST).

"I'll be thinking, 'Soak this in, soak this in, soak it in,' and then I won't soak it in," she said.

"That's what will happen."

World.title: Why netball is growing into a sport of choice for men and boys
World.content:
When Daniel Statton was plotting a move from Far North Queensland to Geelong, the prospect of playing more competitive netball was part of the attraction.

The 19-year-old is one of a growing number of Australian men and boys taking up the sport.

He has now been selected for Australia's national men's netball team, the Kelpies.

"I'm just still hungry for more," he said.

"There's still more to achieve in netball, and I'm just wanting to get after it."

Daniel Statton looked forward to more competitive netball after moving to Geelong from Cairns. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

Statton has represented Australia at under-18 level and played for Queensland in the Australian Mixed and Men's Netball Association national championships in Perth earlier this year.

"I'm pretty athletic and agile, so the coaches love that,' he said.

" I always love to get up and get a bit of an aerial ball and get the crowd going a little bit. "

Born and raised in Cairns, Statton was the only boy playing netball in his sister's teams until he was about 12.

After that, age restrictions for boys forced him to switch to football and basketball.

Lynton McKay helped found the Cairns men's netball league. (ABC News: Bridget Herrmann)

He was not able to return to the game outside of mixed competitions until he was about 16.

"It was really exciting to know there were more like-minded athletes who enjoyed playing netball," he said.

Taking a shot

Before moving to Victoria for further study, Statton played in the Cairns men's netball league, one of the only men's competitions in Queensland.

Now in its third season, the Cairns competition has grown to four teams.

Lynton McKay grew up playing basketball, but after trying netball more than a decade ago, he never looked back.

Daniel Statton has represented his state and country in netball. (ABC News: Jonathon Kendall)

He founded the Cairns men's competition so he could continue playing the sport after moving back to the region from Melbourne.

"There wasn't really anything on the scene other than mixed indoor [netball]," he said.

He said once men and boys had the netball itch, the sport was hard to give up.

"It's not as easy as it looks; it's quite tactical," he said.

Lots of talent emerging

Mr McKay said one of the biggest challenges to growing netball in regional areas was the smaller pool of players with competition from many other sports.

He said there was still a stigma about netball being a female sport, "probably more so in a regional place than a big city like Melbourne or Brisbane".

"But I do think that stigma is dropping," he said.

The popularity of netball among boys and men in Australia is growing. (Supplied: Queensland Suns)

"I'm also a teacher, and I do find there's huge participation now among boys. They all seem to really enjoy netball when they come down and give it a try."

Mr McKay said the Cairns men's competition was "still a work in progress" but said the region had some "really talented players", including some recent high school graduates who had represented their state.

"Considering we've only got four teams, it's a testament to the talent we have here in Cairns," he said.

Leprechaun Netball Club men's team co-captain Damian Nowak said the sport was a safer option for people's joints.

He said the social aspect was also a big drawcard.

Netball has to compete with other sports such as football and basketball for male talent. (Supplied: Clusterpix)

"We're just down here to have fun, a good bunch of mates, a good bunch of dads," Mr Nowak said.

Mr McKay said the best way for netball competitions to attract more players was to "keep pushing".

"I've noticed when we have school carnivals there are a lot of schools now starting to enter boys' teams," he said.

"This didn't happen five years ago."

Tech.title: Patreon is laying off 20 percent of workers
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Patreon is laying off 20 percent of its workers, or around 93 employees, as reported earlier by 404 Media. In a memo to employees, Patreon CEO Jack Conte writes that the company isn’t making these changes “because we believe AI replaces humans,” but says AI has “fundamentally transformed the tech industry, including how we work, how we build products, how we communicate, and more.”

That shift has changed “how we operate and organize,” Conte writes.

During an interview on Decoder, last month, Conte laid out his stance on AI, saying that the company is “100 percent embracing” AI tools internally to continue serving creators:

If Patreon does not fully embrace these tools as a product and engineering company — and we are ultimately a product and engineering company — and use them to give the power back to creators, we, as a company, will be dead in three years.

Patreon previously laid off 17 percent of workers in 2022, as well as closed its offices in Dublin and Berlin.

Tech.title: Corsair’s PC case with a panoramic glass design is $70 off
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On the hunt for a PC case that’s loaded with features and has a unique look? Amazon, Best Buy, and Corsair are selling the Corsair Frame 4500X RS for $119.99, a $70 discount from the usual price. The versatile case supports motherboards up to EATX, GPUs up to 460mm in length, and has a seamless panoramic glass window that wraps around its front and left side. The case includes three fans with reverse rotors mounted to its right side, letting the ARGB lighting shine into the case while they pull in air.

While the panoramic window might draw more attention, one of this case’s standout functional features is Corsair’s Infinirail system. Rather than having individual holes for fan screws, there are long slots on sliding rails, giving you more flexibility with cooling components and configuration. As a result, you can fit radiators up to 280mm or 360mm on the top or side of the case, depending on whether you opt for 120mm or 140mm case fans.

The case also supports rear connection motherboards like this Gigabyte X870 Aorus for cleaner cable runs, and is ready for vertical GPU mounting if you buy a riser cable. There are some other nice inclusions as well, like an anti-sag GPU support arm, and the screws come in a reusable box rather than a series of tiny plastic bags. The case includes a two year manufacturer’s warranty.

Tech.title: Tesla’s robotaxi promises are clashing with reality
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In an earnings call yesterday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk did his best to paint a positive portrait of the company’s robotaxi program. New cities are being added, more miles are being driven, and more people are experiencing Tesla’s unsupervised vehicles.

But Musk’s typical bullishness seemed to be absent from the call, as the occasional trillionaire sought to temper expectations about the program’s future.

“We’re going as fast as humanly possible in scaling Robotaxi,” Musk said, “while trying to ensure that we do not harm anyone at all and ideally do not even run over a pet.”

Musk’s insistence that Tesla’s robotaxi service was growing is clashing with the reality of the situation: Mileage is basically flat, the number of vehicles appears to be shrinking, and despite the Tesla executive team’s claims of “zero notable incidents,” the safety of the company’s technology appears to be an open question.

Tesla did it’s best to frame the situation as headed in the right direction. Ashok Elluswamy, the company’s head of AI, said that Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxis have driven 380,000 miles across six cities in two different states. And according to Musk, that was increasing at a rate of 10 percent a week in terms of miles driven.

Tesla did it’s best to frame the situation as headed in the right direction

Elluswamy couldn’t help but take a swipe at Tesla’s competitors who use lidar sensors, as opposed to Tesla’s camera-0nly approach. “Historically, the so-called experts have always claimed that you need lidars, radars, HD maps, and the entire kitchen sink to drive safely,” he said. “Here we show that such is not true. You can have safe, comfortable, and affordable autonomy with just cameras. This record should be a huge validation of Tesla’s entire AI approach.”

But even the numbers that Tesla reported seem to betray that message. Waymo, which uses lidar sensors and radar as redundant sensors in addition to cameras, typically drives around four million miles a week. Tesla’s total mileage, a year into its robotaxi program, is less than 10 percent of that figure. This reality is starting to spook investors, with BNP Paribas Equity Research senior analyst James Picariello calling it “an alarming decline” in a research note to clients.

Tesla uses a mix of unsupervised and supervised vehicles as part of its fleet, but that ratio appears to be in a constant state of flux. According to the crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker, the company currently only has 16 unsupervised vehicles in Austin, four in Dallas, and one in Houston. During the earnings call, Elluswamy was asked what was preventing Tesla from flooding the zone in Austin, where it first launched its robotaxis a year ago, as opposed to dropping a small number of vehicles in new cities.

“The reason we have been expanding across different cities, instead of just doubling down on a single city, is that we want to make sure that our stack is a very general one,” Elluswamy said. “It is a general one. We just want to like, you know, both prove to ourselves and to other folks that it is working across a lot of different cities without too much effort per city.”

Another limiting factor is state regulations. New Jersey is considering a bill that would essentially ban robotaxis without multiple sensors, like radar and lidar. Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco flagged this on the call, noting “there seems to be some evolving regulations at the state level, potentially around sensor requirements.” To which Tesla’s vice president of vehicle engineering Lars Morvay acknowledged “obviously the stuff in New Jersey, you know, is a little bit disheartening.”

A more restrictive regulatory environment could limit the total addressable market for Tesla robotaxis, which would clash with the company’s message about a more generalized service that can drive anywhere, under any conditions.

Safety is another obstacle. Musk’s comment about wanting to avoid running over anyone’s pet appeared to be a subtle swipe at Waymo, which has hit and killed a number of animals over the past several years. But Tesla’s safety record is a mixed bag. We don’t have a lot of great insight into Tesla’s robotaxi crashes because the company tends to redact a lot of the important details.

According to the Robotaxi Tracker, the company’s fleet has been involved in approximately 18 incidents, 56 percent of which were the fault of another driver. And Tesla’s Full Self-Driving is under investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, with the potential for a future recall. Tesla’s robotaxis are currently running version 15 of FSD, as compared to version 14.3.6 on its customer vehicles.

Tesla is asking investors, supporters, and customers to look past these shortcomings as it continues to push the message that it’s robotaxi program is growing. But the company continues to run into a reality that contradicts that message.

Tech.title: Geekbench 7 will push your computer or phone even harder for better benchmarking
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Primate Labs is releasing Geekbench 7, the latest generation of its popular benchmarking tool. Geekbench 7 features new video and audio encoding / decoding tests, a redesigned multi-core test, and larger, more demanding datasets for CPUs and GPUs to crunch through. It otherwise looks and acts just like Geekbench 6, and a Pro license will cost the same $99 (discounted to $79 until August 6th).

A Geekbench 7 Pro license allows for offline benchmarking that doesn’t get uploaded to the Geekbench Browser, and it still covers all compatible desktop platforms of Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Geekbench be looking like Geekbench. Image: Primate Labs

Geekbench is one of the mainstay synthetic benchmarks we use in reviewing laptops here at The Verge. I’ve always liked how simple and fast Geekbench is to run, but its short duration also means it’s a better test of quick bursts of computing rather than sustained loads that can throttle some CPUs and GPUs. (One of its tests involves rendering a 1.5MB PDF file, which must be near-instantaneous for most modern chips.)

Primate Labs claims Geekbench 7 uses “more demanding data sets to more accurately capture the hardware demands of modern applications.” The new audio / video tests also now include AV1, Opus, model video conferencing, streaming, and content consumption workloads. And multi-core benchmarks are designed to better reflect real software behavior since the new workloads will only run multi-threaded when the modeled tasks run that way.

These all sound like marked improvements, even if Geekbench 7 tests still only take a few minutes to run. Scores from Geekbench 6 are of course not compatible with Geekbench 7. So if you’re the testing type, feel free to spiritually join me in a whole bunch of new benchmark testing and retesting. Always be testing.

Tech.title: OpenAI is making big claims as it rolls out ChatGPT Health to everyone
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is rolling out ChatGPT Health to everyone in the US on Thursday, allowing more people to connect their medical records and health-tracking information to the chatbot. During a briefing, Ashley Alexander, OpenAI’s vice president of health product, says the company’s models “are now capable of reasoning at levels that are better than clinician level.”

When asked for more information about how the performance of OpenAI’s models stacks up against human clinicians, OpenAI health lead Karan Singhal says that he would “temper” the claim that they are reasoning at better levels, but that “there have been individual studies that have been pointing in that direction,” like this one from Harvard and Stanford. On Wednesday, a Florida pastor sued OpenAI over claims ChatGPT provided him with “extremely dangerous medical recommendations,” allegedly leading him to put off medical care for a pulmonary embolism.

Image: OpenAI

The broader release of ChatGPT Health comes just weeks after OpenAI launched its new GPT-5.6 Sol, which it claims is its “strongest model yet for health.” ChatGPT Health will run on the company’s latest models.

With this update, OpenAI will now allow users to ask questions about their connected medical information in the main chat experience, rather than having them navigate to the dedicated ChatGPT Health tab. ChatGPT will ask for permission before using your health information to personalize its response, adding that “all conversations are encrypted at rest and at transit,” while information connected in Health “receives additional encryption protection.”

Image: OpenAI

Users can also review and change the kinds of health data they connect to ChatGPT, including post-visit notes, notes from their care team, lab results, and medications. Currently, users can connect their data from health providers, along with services like Apple Health, Weight Watchers, MyFitnessPal, and Function. OpenAI notes that the ChatGPT Health “supports, not replaces, professional care.” It’s rolling out to all logged-in ChatGPT users aged 18 and older on the web and iOS across free, Go, Plus, and Pro plans.

Tech.title: Amazon puts Luna cloud-streamed games like Fallout 4 inside Prime Video
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The new strategy that Amazon gaming exec Jeff Gattis talked to The Verge about last month is getting clearer now that Prime Video has added a new Games tab on Fire TV devices. With Prime Gaming, Amazon Game Studios, and Luna now combined into one organization, it’s aiming at the more casual audience of people already using Prime Video to stream movies, TV shows, and sports, instead of trying to compete directly with “core” gamers playing MMOs and shooters.

Luna was already included in Prime, but now users in the US and UK can access it directly within Prime Video to play titles like Dispatch, Fallout 4, Hogwarts Legacy, EA Sports FC 26, and Clue. Amazon says that “details on additional devices, countries, and games” will be announced later.

The Games tab is also a place for Amazon to promote tie-in games to people who watched its content on Prime Video, like the Masters of the Universe: Legends Unite co-op card battler game, or its “AI-powered party game” Courtroom Chaos: Starring Arnold Schwarzenegger ahead of his new holiday movie for Amazon later this year.

Tech.title: Microsoft is testing free, ad-supported cloud gaming for Xbox Insiders
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Xbox Insiders can stream games from their libraries for free in ad-supported streaming sessions starting today. The free streaming sessions are limited to games you already own, and sessions are capped at one hour. However, ads will only play “before sessions begin.” It’s also optional — you won’t need to watch ads if you have a paid cloud gaming subscription.

Microsoft says the ad-supported streaming option will only be available for a limited time during a “test period.” It previously began internally testing an ad-supported version of Xbox Cloud Gaming late last year, with sources telling The Verge at the time that the test included about two minutes of preroll ads before streaming sessions.

Around the same time, Microsoft also increased Game Pass prices, but added unlimited cloud gaming to its lowest-priced Game Pass Essential subscription, which costs $9.99 per month. Previously, you needed a Game Pass Ultimate subscription for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Microsoft says the goal of its current test for ad-supported streaming is to further expand affordable ways to play Xbox games. Ad tiers have become increasingly common on video streaming platforms over recent years — the addition of ads on Xbox’s streaming service could signal a similar shift coming to gaming subscriptions.

Additionally, Microsoft notes that cloud gaming could “help Xbox One owners play newer games built for Xbox Series X/S” without needing to buy a new console. The news comes as Xbox is in a state of upheaval, including mass layoffs, studio closures, and a pivot back toward the fan-favorite Fallout franchise. On top of that, Xbox console prices are set to increase by upwards of $100 starting on August 1st.

Tech.title: The new Halo remake is a reminder of what Xbox used to be
Tech.content:
It’s impossible to talk about a new Xbox game without also talking about the state of Xbox. Microsoft’s gaming division is in freefall: Recent headlines are dominated by extensive layoffs, decimated studios, and confusing strategies, most of which stem from years of bad decisions and expensive acquisitions. But it wasn’t always that way. Through its first two generations of existence, Xbox held its own against its more established rivals Nintendo and Sony, and a big reason for that was Halo. Bungie’s shooter coupled a grand sci-fi story with nearly pitch-perfect action and single-handedly created a reason to buy an Xbox. Now, the game has gotten a full remake, reimagining the same core experience for modern audiences. In a testament to the original design, Halo remains a thrilling game more than two decades after it debuted. But the remake is also a reminder of just how far Xbox has strayed from its initial promise.

Called Halo: Campaign Evolved, the remake is exactly what it sounds like: a modern overhaul of the original game’s story campaign. That means you still take on the role of supersoldier Master Chief as he leads human forces in a war against an alien alliance known as the Covenant, before eventually being pulled into a much bigger conflict with the fate of the galaxy on the line. Halo’s story was never the most original, pulling from obvious influences, most notably Aliens, but it’s well crafted, with dramatic twists and turns that give you an incentive to push through its many battles. The game is especially great at switching tones throughout. Initially Halo puts you on the front lines of a large-scale war on an alien world before later shifting to something that approaches horror, with cramped shootouts against unsettling monsters. Campaign Evolved makes the story a touch more cinematic with expanded cutscenes that flesh out the backstory and characters, but which are still relatively short and concise.

The most notable difference in the remake is its upgraded visuals. Campaign Evolved was built using Unreal Engine 5, and it looks, well, like a first-person shooter from 2026. Everything is much more detailed and the levels are grander in scope. When you’re out on the Halo’s surface, it really feels like you’re in the midst of a huge battle, with explosions all around you and the wreckage of downed vehicles and ships dotting the landscape. That extra level of detail really enhances the game midway through when you encounter the Flood, a race of parasitic aliens that turn corpses into zombies. Now those close-quarters battles are much scarier, as the aliens explode in gruesome ways, the walls are covered with oozing growths, and you see the flash of gunfire lighting up dark spaces and the horrors lurking within. You can quibble with some of the artistic decisions — I personally miss the more brutalist alien architecture of the original — but overall the game looks great.

There are changes to the gameplay as well. Some are relatively small, like the new ability to hijack enemy vehicles or the larger arsenal of weapons at your disposal. The biggest change, though, is something that seems small: the addition of a sprint button. Early Halo games didn’t let Master Chief sprint, and the addition to Campaign Evolved makes the action feel much faster and more fluid. It’s especially useful if, like me, you spend a lot of time running away from the bigger enemies. Campaign Evolved also introduces a trio of new missions while making some changes to existing ones. Unfortunately, I don’t have the kind of encyclopedic Halo knowledge to pinpoint exactly what has changed, but I will say this: Much like the remakes of Shadow of the Colossus and Resident Evil 4, Campaign Evolved plays the romanticized version of Halo from my memory, which is exactly what you want from a project like this. The changes enhance something that was already great and smooth over (most of) the rough spots. And while I played through all of it solo, the game also supports co-op for up to four players.

While the remake is excellent, it’s unfortunately launching at a very awkward time, just a few weeks after new Xbox CEO Asha Sharma kicked off a “reset” that will eventually see more than 3,000 people laid off over the next year and iconic studios like Doom developer id Software dramatically scaled down. In many ways, Halo as a franchise is illustrative of Xbox’s fall from grace. Since Microsoft assumed full responsibility for the series through its internal Halo Studios (formerly known as 343 Industries), the gap between new releases has become larger and larger, while at the same time the company has tried to broaden Halo through mostly ill-fated ventures like a streaming TV series and a live-service push. Campaign Evolved itself represents some of this disorder. Not only is it the first new Halo game since 2021, it’s also coming to the PS5 in addition to Xbox and PC as part of Microsoft’s consistently confusing console exclusivity strategy.

So as much as I’ve enjoyed fighting off the hordes of the Flood once again, I can’t help but see Campaign Evolved within the larger context of Xbox. The original Halo felt daring, proving that action and narrative could be complementary strengths, and it went on to influence a generation of first-person shooters. In the years since, the franchise’s prominence has steadily diminished, to the point that now Microsoft is trying to reinvigorate it by going back to the beginning instead of doing something actually new. Five years after Halo Infinite, instead of the next entry in the franchise, Xbox has opted for the safe choice with a remake. And Campaign Evolved comes at a time when the future of the Xbox lineup looks increasingly murky given the dramatic studio cuts.

Campaign Evolved does a remarkable job of re-creating the experience of playing Halo for the first time. But that’s not enough to make Halo — or Xbox, for that matter — feel as essential as it once was.

Halo: Campaign Evolved launches on the Xbox, PS5, and PC on July 28th, with early access on July 23rd for those who preordered.

Tech.title: AegisAI, founded by former Google security execs, lands $36M to stop AI-driven spear phishing
Tech.content:
Hackers are increasingly using AI to launch attacks on a massive scale, with email emerging as a primary target. AI can quickly aggregate personal information—such as information about coworkers, active projects, and recent travel itineraries—allowing bad actors to instantly craft convincing messages that look authentic.

Last year, former Google security executives Cy Khormaee and Ryan Luo, who previously worked on developing safe browsing technology and reCAPTCHA, teamed up to launch AegisAI, a startup that uses AI agents to stomp out these threats, known as spear phishing.

With a decade of experience preventing email hacks, the AegisAI co-founders realized that existing rule-based systems for preventing hacks—relying on “if-then” logic—are too slow and limited to catching AI-crafted malicious emails. So they developed AI agents that quickly analyze each message as a human would, paying attention to small anomalies that even the most elaborate checklist wouldn’t catch.

Less than a year after its launch, AegisAI says its tech has been adopted by dozens of customers, including crypto payments company Mash, AI startup LangChain, and Google-owned privacy compliance platform Lokker. That demand has just helped AegisAI raise a $36 million Series A led by Battery Ventures, with participation from existing backers Accel and Foundation Capital. The fresh funding brings the startup’s total capital to $49 million.

“AI-powered attacks bypass existing controls more than half the time now, which means they’re almost twice as effective as they used to be,” Khormaee told TechCrunch. “They’ve researched you, they understand everything about you, and they’re targeting attacks that are perfectly bespoke to you.”

Khormaee claims that AegisAI’s agents can spot threats traditional email security systems may miss entirely. For instance, the startup’s AI can catch malicious PDF attachments that look legitimate at first, including ones with built-in passwords and CAPTCHAs, which are often used to fool standard spam filters.

When Dharmesh Thakker, general partner at Battery Ventures, noticed an increase in email attacks, he set out to invest in a startup that could defend against AI with AI, one aiming to replace legacy email security tools with agentic-driven defense.

“The bad guys are using email to attack us using AI at a much faster pace than we can keep up with,” Thakker told TechCrunch. “Defending against that is going to be a number one priority for a lot of companies.”

AegisAI isn’t the only startup using AI to analyze the context of every incoming email to detect fraud and impersonation attempts. Lightspeed-backed Ocean is also trying to displace established vendors like Proofpoint and Mimecast, along with newer players like Abnormal Security.

However, given that AegisAI is led by experts who helped secure Gmail, the most popular email system in the world, Thakker believes the startup has the best shot at becoming the leading new hack-prevention company.

While AegisAI is starting with email, the startup has its sights on eventually expanding to other areas of defense, such as data security. “The core idea of building customized, highly advanced agents that can do investigations is going to [determine] who becomes the next dominant security company,” Khormaee said.

Tech.title: US government says Iran-linked hackers are disrupting American water and energy providers
Tech.content:
The U.S. government is warning that Iranian state-backed hackers are actively breaking in and disrupting industrial control systems at American water and energy providers. This new alert comes months after federal agencies warned of an escalation in hacking from Iranian actors amid the ongoing war.

In an advisory updated Wednesday, the FBI, the NSA, the Department of Energy, and CISA said Iranian hackers were targeting programmable logic controllers on internet-connected operational networks, allowing them to manipulate data on their displays, causing outages and disruption.

The Iranian hackers were initially discovered earlier this year to be targeting controllers made by Rockwell, but the advisory has now expanded the types of industrial control systems under attack to include products from Schneider Electric and Siemens.

The agencies warn that “potentially all internet exposed” industrial control systems may be affected, and urged critical infrastructure owners to take action. Per the advisory, the Iranian-backed hackers were “conducting this activity to cause disruptive effects within the United States,” likely in response to the ongoing war between Iran and the U.S. and Israel.

According to the FBI, the hackers broke into one critical infrastructure provider and changed the controllers’ programming logic to disable processes that handled critical shutdowns and alarms. The feds said this allowed “systems to enter unsafe conditions without notifying operators of the anomalies.”

This is the latest in a series of cyberattacks launched by Iranian government hackers and their proxies across the region since the start of the war in February.

The hacks have ranged from the country’s typical espionage and hack-and-leak operations, such as leaking the contents of FBI director Kash Patel’s personal email account, to more atypical destructive hacks that have caused large-scale damage or disruption. Among the more notable incidents was a hack on the U.S. medical tech giant Stryker, which allowed the Iranian hacking group “Handala” to remotely wipe tens of thousands of employee devices.

Handala also took credit for a data breach affecting California water provider Cal Water in June, and claimed it could have disrupted the water supply (without providing evidence). The water provider said that it saw no evidence of unauthorized access to its operational networks, which control the water supplies.

Tech.title: Runway launches AI model router as generative media gets crowded
Tech.content:
Runway no longer wants to be just another AI model company. It wants to become the infrastructure layer for generative media.

On Thursday, the startup launched Runway Media Router through Runway Dev, its developer platform, released earlier this month, that provides API access to a growing roster of third-party image, video, and audio models alongside Runway’s own.

The Media Router is a tool that automatically selects the best image, video, or audio generation model for a request based on whether a developer prioritizes quality, speed, or cost. While model routers have become increasingly common in the world of large language models, Runway says this is the first built specifically for generative media.

“The routing really fits into that overall promise of being the easiest one-stop shop for developers to integrate with any type of generative media model,” Anthony Maggio, Runway’s chief product officer, told TechCrunch.

The launch, shared exclusively with TechCrunch, marks another step in Runway’s evolution from an AI video startup into infrastructure for companies building with generative media. Through Runway Dev, customers including Adobe, Cloudflare, ElevenLabs, Expedia, Shutterstock, and Quora can build media generation directly into their own products using Runway’s API rather than sending their users to Runway’s own app or site.

The launch of the router comes as the number of generative media models has exploded, making it increasingly difficult and time-consuming for developers to evaluate new releases. Through the Runway Dev platform, developers can access the latest media models when they’re released.

“Most developers are not spending the time to really understand the capabilities of each of these models and where they excel or differ based on various types of outputs across video, image, and audio,” Maggio said. “The unique proposition we’re bringing to the table is all of that intelligence around what the best model is for each different use case, and meshing that with preference you apply around the context of your business.”

Maggio noted that Chinese generative media models are becoming increasingly popular. However, many businesses building their own products might not be comfortable working with models that come out of China, so they could, he said, potentially set a preference for American model providers — a preference that may become more common as the Trump administration explores bans and sanctions against Chinese open AI models.

That’s just one example of preferences that developers can set, though. Maggio says customers are mainly interested in routing the model to account for token pricing and quality. Token pricing has become a hot topic in 2026 as enterprises that went all-in on agentic AI felt the sting of high token bills. In the world of LLMs, model routing for token pricing has become common, so it only makes sense that routing for generative media would follow. The Media Router launch also comes weeks after Runway replaced its unlimited subscription plans with token-based pricing, a move that drew criticism from some users.

On the quality front, deciding which models provide the best quality for any given task isn’t as easy for generative media as it is with language models, Maggio says. That’s where the router’s intelligence layer kicks in. It’s based on the expertise Runway’s in-house creative team has developed in evaluating output across every media type — things like how video models handle motion, how image models handle composition, or how voice models handle lip syncing.

Runway had already done a lot of the work building that intelligence layer for its agent product, a conversational AI creative partner that Runway launched in May to help turn text prompts into fully edited multi-shot videos and marketing campaigns.

The Runway Media Router, Maggio says, takes the same routing technology Runway built for its own products and packages it for outside developers to use.

Runway’s strategy today reflects how fragmented and competitive the current generative media landscape is, and how much the startup needs to expand and pivot to stay competitive. Runway’s last AI video model release — Gen 4.5 — was in December. At the time, the model topped leaderboards, outperforming similar models from incumbents like Google. In the same month, Runway released its first world model.

Aside from an upgrade to its video editing model, Aleph 2.0, in May, Runway hasn’t dropped a new dedicated frontier video model in months. (TechCrunch has asked when the startup plans to release Gen 5.) Today, while Aleph 2.0 ranks among the leading video editing models according to Artificial Analysis, the company’s text-to-video and image-to-video models no longer lead the rankings. In the top 20 spots are models from heavy hitters like Google and China’s ByteDance and Alibaba.

Rather than asking developers to bet on a single model staying ahead, Media Router assumes that the best model will continue to change — and it keeps Runway in the game so that it can continue to build on the frontier. If not as the best new AI model, then as the best orchestration layer.

Anastasis Germanidis, Runway’s co-founder and co-CEO, acknowledged that the startup has been known for a long time primarily for “that end user piece,” but it had to build a full stack to get there, one that includes a developer platform, a creative tool suite, and an inference layer underneath it all. He says the company has seen increasing interest from companies for Runway to live across every part of that stack.

“You need great models underneath, but the orchestration increasingly matters a lot because people are building entire campaigns with those models, or they’re building entire finished multi-scene generations out of those models,” Germanidis told TechCrunch. “It’s something that we increasingly had to build — that intelligence layer that comes on top of the pure pixel models. The router is one way in which the benefits of that come to users.”

Or as Maggio put it more broadly: “If you zoom out at the one thing Runway has been doing since 2018, it’s that we’re deeply focused on research, while building for where we think the space is going at the same time.”
